L43: ## I. Executive Summary
L44: ## 1. Summary of Regulatory Action
L45: The Applicant, TheracosBio LLC, has submitted a New Drug Application (NDA) for Brenzavvy (bexagliflozin) tablets as an adjunct to diet and exercise to improve glycemic control in adults with type 2 diabetes (T2DM). The recommended dosage is 20 mg orally once daily.
L46: Bexagliflozin is a small molecule inhibitor of the sodium-glucose linked transporter 2 (sodium-glucose co-transporter-2, SGLT2), the transporter responsible for reabsorption of the majority of glucose from the renal glomerular filtrate in the renal proximal tubule. By inhibiting SGLT2, bexagliflozin reduces renal reabsorption of filtered glucose and lowers the renal threshold for glucose, and thereby increases urinary glucose excretion. Bexagliflozin also reduces sodium reabsorption and increases the delivery of sodium to the distal tubule. There are currently four FDA-approved SGLT2 inhibitors indicated for improved glycemic control in adults with T2DM. Bexagliflozin is a new molecular entity (NME), and the Applicant is submitting this NDA using the 505(b)(1) approval pathway.
L47: T2DM is a serious and life-threatening condition that if left untreated leads to an increased risk of morbidity and mortality. Despite numerous available therapeutic options, a significant number of patients have difficulty achieving adequate glycemic control. Landmark clinical trials in both type 1 diabetes and type 2 diabetes demonstrated that improved glycemic control as assessed by hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) leads to substantial reduction in the incidence of microvascular complications, including diabetic retinopathy, nephropathy, and neuropathy (Control et al. 1993; Ohkubo et al. 1995; UKPDS 1998). Improved glycemic control demonstrated by reduction of HbA1c is considered a surrogate for reduction of microvascular complications of diabetes and has served as the basis for traditional approval of drugs and biologic products for a glycemic control indication in people with diabetes (FDA 2022).
L48: The Applicant demonstrated substantial evidence of effectiveness for the proposed indication with data from six phase 3, adequate and well-controlled investigations, including four placebo-controlled trials and two active controlled trials.
L49: Bexagliflozin was compared to placebo in subjects with inadequately controlled T2DM as monotherapy (C-450), as add-on to metformin (C-419), and as add-on to standard of care therapies in subjects with inadequately controlled T2DM and increased cardiovascular risk (C-476) and moderate renal impairment (C-448).
L50: The primary efficacy endpoint for glycemic control in these trials was the mean change from baseline in HbA1c. The placebo-adjusted estimate of the treatment effect in trials C-450, C-419, and C-476 (all conducted primarily in patients with normal renal function) ranged from -0.38% to -0.48%. The results were statistically significant and clinically meaningful, and collectively represent substantial evidence of effectiveness. In the active-controlled trials, bexagliflozin was statistically non-inferior to sitagliptin (C-423) and glimepiride (C-480) as an add-on to metformin, although glimepiride was only titrated up to a maximum dose of 6 mg, which is less than the maximum approved dose of 8 mg in the US. In C-423 the estimated treatment difference versus sitagliptin was 0.08 (-0.06, 0.22). In C-480 the estimated treatment versus glimepiride was
L51: -0.03 (-0.20, 0.13). In both trials, the upper bound of the 95% confidence interval did not exceed the prespecified non-inferiority margin of 0.35. In the dedicated renal impairment trial (C-448) enrolling subjects with stage 3 chronic kidney disease (moderate renal impairment, defined as estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) \ge 30 to &lt;60 mL/min/1.73 m^2), the placebo-adjusted estimate of the treatment effect was -0.27% (95% CI: -0.44, -0.09). This result was statistically significant. In contrast, no treatment effect was observed in a subgroup analysis of subjects with eGFR &lt;60 mL/min/1.73m^2 in trial C-476, the trial of patients with increased cardiovascular risk. This trial was not designed to evaluate glycemic control in patients with renal impairment; therefore, we place more weight on the demonstrated glycemic effects in the dedicated renal impairment efficacy and safety trial.
L52: Statistically significant decreases in body weight versus placebo were observed in trials where bexagliflozin was added to standard of care therapy in subjects with renal impairment (C-448) and increased CV risk (C-476). Statistically significant reduction in systolic blood pressure (SBP) with bexagliflozin versus placebo was observed in the CV risk trial (C-476).
L53: Safety findings were generally consistent with those of other SGLT2 inhibitor products. Consistent with other members of the SGLT2 inhibitor class, the Warnings and Precautions section of labeling will include the risk of ketoacidosis, urosepsis and pyelonephritis, Fournier's gangrene, genital mycotic infections, volume depletion, and hypoglycemia with concomitant use of insulin or an insulin secretagogue.
L54: An increased incidence of nontraumatic amputation was observed compared to placebo in a trial of patients with increased CV risk (hazard ratio: 1.64 (0.7, 3.8)). Lower limb amputation is a recognized complication of diabetes mellitus, and an increased risk of amputation has been identified with some, but not all, members of the SGLT2 inhibitor class. A statement advising prescribers to consider factors that may increase the risk of amputation before initiating bexagliflozin and to monitor patients for infections or ulcers of lower limbs also appears appropriate to mitigate this potential risk and will be included in the Warnings and Precautions section of labeling.
L55: Section 6 of the prescribing information will include subsections to describe imbalances unfavorable to bexagliflozin for the following adverse events: bone fracture, sepsis, rash, and dermatitis.
L56: The Applicant conducted a program-wide meta-analysis to evaluate the cardiovascular risk of exposure to bexagliflozin. The primary endpoint was time-to-first event of a four-component composite endpoint consisting of CV death, nonfatal stroke, nonfatal myocardial infarction, or hospitalization for unstable angina. The estimated hazard ratio of the composite endpoint associated with bexagliflozin relative to control was 0.80 (95% CI: 0.58, 1.09). Exposure to bexagliflozin is not expected to substantially increase the risk of MACE in patients with T2DM.
L57: Key review issues in the evaluation of benefit/risk included efficacy of bexagliflozin in subjects with moderate renal impairment, increased risk of nontraumatic amputation with bexagliflozin, overall safety of bexagliflozin, and quality of the safety database. Refer to the Sections 2.2 (Conclusions Regarding Benefit and Risk), 3.1 (Review Issue List), and the linked subsections of 6 (Assessment of Effectiveness) and 7 (Risk and Risk Management) for details.
L58: NDA 214373
Brenzavvy (bexagliflozin)
L59: All review disciplines, the clinical division director, and the office director (signatory) support approval of the application. Refer to Sections II (Interdisciplinary Assessment) and III (Appendices) for details of the individual discipline reviews.
L60: In summary, the application demonstrated substantial evidence of effectiveness of bexagliflozin as an adjunct to diet and exercise to improve glycemic control in adults with T2DM. The approved dosage is 20 mg orally once daily. Bexagliflozin is not recommended for use in patients with an eGFR &lt;30 mg/mL/1.73 m^2 and is contraindicated in patients on dialysis, because there is a progressive decline in urinary glucose excretion with accompanying loss of pharmacodynamic blood glucose-lowering effect with increased severity of renal impairment, as well as a reduction in urine output. As such, there will be minimal, if any, efficacy in this population always outweighed by the risks. Major safety issues are adequately communicated in labeling. Approval will include a Pediatric Research Equity Act (PREA) postmarketing requirement (PMR) issued to assess the safety and efficacy of bexagliflozin in pediatric patients \ge 10 to &lt;18 years of age.
L61: ## 2. Benefit-Risk Assessment
L62: ## 2.1. Benefit-Risk Framework
L63: Table 2. Benefit-Risk Framework
L64: Dimension	Evidence and Uncertainties	Conclusions and Reasons
Analysis of Condition	Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), which affects approximately 33 million people in the United States (CDC 2022b), is a chronic medical condition characterized by insulin resistance and inadequate insulin secretion, resulting in hyperglycemia.
Patients with T2DM are at increased risk for serious microvascular (i.e., retinopathy, nephropathy, and neuropathy) and macrovascular (i.e., myocardial infarction, stroke) complications (Stratton et al. 2000; American Diabetes Association Professional Practice 2022; American Diabetes Association Professional Practice et al. 2022c; American Diabetes Association Professional Practice et al. 2022d). It is the 8th leading cause of death in the United States (CDC 2022a).
Despite known benefits of glycemic control, approximately one quarter to one half of subjects with T2DM in the United States fail to achieve recommended treatment goals (Carls et al. 2017; Khunti et al. 2018; Avramidis et al. 2020).
T2DM is a serious and life-threatening condition that if left untreated leads to an increased risk of morbidity and mortality. A significant number of patients have difficulty achieving adequate glycemic control.
L65: Dimension	Evidence and Uncertainties	Conclusions and Reasons
Current Treatment Options	There are currently 12 pharmacologic classes of antihyperglycemic medications (generally with multiple members in each class), approved to improve glycemic control in patients with T2DM (American Diabetes Association Professional Practice et al. 2022b). There are different safety concerns for each class.
Published guidelines have generally recommended initiating treatment with lifestyle interventions and metformin, with the choice of additional therapies and/or alternatives based on factors such as baseline cardiovascular (CV) and renal comorbidities, efficacy, hypoglycemia risk, impact on weight, patient preference, and cost (American Diabetes Association Professional Practice et al. 2022b). Because T2DM is a progressive disease, maintenance of glycemic targets with monotherapy is often possible for only a few years, after which combination therapy is necessary. Initiation of some antihyperglycemic products are not recommended for use in patients with moderate renal impairment and/or may require dose adjustment in this patient population.
There are currently four sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitor products approved in the United States (ertugliflozin, dapagliflozin, canagliflozin, empagliflozin) (Janssen 2020; AstraZeneca 2021; Merck 2021; Ingelheim 2022).
While all approved antihyperglycemic medications for T2DM have been shown to improve glycemic control, some have also been shown to improve CV and renal outcomes, including several SGLT2 inhibitor and glucagon-like peptide (GLP-1) receptor agonist products (Janssen 2020; AstraZeneca 2021; Ingelheim 2022; Lilly 2022; Nordisk 2022a; Nordisk 2022b).
Despite the many available treatment options, many patients continue to have difficulty achieving adequate glycemic control. Further, T2DM is a progressive disorder and patients typically need additional agents added as the disease progresses. Many patients with T2DM also have renal impairment, and therefore, it is important to have available treatment options for this population.
L66: Benefit	
Six phase 3 trials that met the criteria for adequate and well-controlled investigations were submitted to establish efficacy of bexagliflozin 20 mg for the proposed indication.
These trials used HbA1c, an average measure of glycemic control over 2-3 months and an established surrogate for reduction in microvascular complications, as the key efficacy measure of effectiveness. Studies such as UKPDS indicate that a reduction in HbA1c is considered clinically meaningful because it corresponds with decreased rates of microvascular disease in proportion to the improvement in HbA1c.
Bexagliflozin was statistically superior to placebo as monotherapy, with a placebo-adjusted change from baseline in hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) of -0.38% (-0.63%, -0.13%; p=0.002), and as add-on to metformin, with a placebo-adjusted change from baseline of -0.48% (-0.69%, -0.26%; p<0.0001). This magnitude of improvement is in line with previously approved anti-diabetics.
Bexagliflozin was also noninferior to sitagliptin [0.08% (-0.06, 0.22)] and glimepiride [-0.03% (-0.20, 0.13)], two products that are approved for the treatment of T2DM, when evaluated using a noninferiority margin of 0.35% for HbA1c.
Efficacy of bexagliflozin was evaluated in trials enrolling subjects with stage 3 chronic kidney disease (CKD) (estimated glomerular filtration rate [eGFR] 30–60 mL/min/1.73 m2) and subjects with increased CV risk. No restriction was placed on background therapy for glycemic control in these trials, with the exception of treatment with another SGLT2 inhibitor product. Glycemic control was significantly improved in both populations as compared to placebo with bexagliflozin treatment (placebo-adjusted change from baseline in HbA1c of -0.27% [-0.44%, -0.09%; p=0.002]) and -0.44% [-0.53%, -0.35%; p<0.0001] in subjects with stage 3 CKD and increased CV risk, respectively).
Secondary endpoints related to change in body weight and systolic blood pressure (SBP) were evaluated. Statistically significant decreases in body weight were observed in trials where bexagliflozin was added to standard of care therapy in subjects with renal impairment (Trial C-448) and increased

The submitted clinical trial data provides substantial evidence of effectiveness of bexagliflozin for the proposed indication, as an adjunct to diet and exercise to improve glycemic control in adults with T2DM. Data from the six phase 3 trials, which evaluated the use of bexagliflozin as monotherapy and in combination with other antihyperglycemic products, showed clinically meaningful improvements in HbA1c compared to placebo and noninferiority compared to active comparators. In addition, several trials enrolled distinct patient populations, including patients with increased CV risk and patients with renal impairment. In all trials, improvements in HbA1c were considered clinically meaningful, and the benefit of this product would be relevant to many patients with T2DM.
Efficacy data support approval of dosing in patients with impaired renal function (eGFR 30–60 mL/min/1.73 m2), providing another therapeutic option for patients with both T2DM and CKD.
In certain trials, efficacy data demonstrate that bexagliflozin results in reduced body weight and/or SBP, which are other effects generally associated with the class.
The safety and efficacy of bexagliflozin in pediatric patients \ge 10 to <18 years of age is currently unknown but will be studied.
L67: Dimension	Evidence and Uncertainties	Conclusions and Reasons
CV risk (Trial C-476). Statistically significant changes in SBP were also observed in Trial C-476.
Uncertainties of Benefit:
The efficacy of bexagliflozin for pediatric patients with T2DM has not been established.
Pivotal trial populations underrepresented some racial subgroups (e.g., 5.7% were black).
In the trial comparing bexagliflozin to glimepiride, glimepiride was titrated to a maximum dose of 6 mg daily, not to the US approved maximum dose of 8 mg daily. The impact on noninferiority conclusions is unknown.
It is unknown if a bexagliflozin dose higher than 20 mg would lead to further improvement in efficacy and acceptable safety as a higher dose was not tested in the phase 2 or phase 3 trials.
L68: Dimension	Evidence and Uncertainties	Conclusions and Reasons
Risk and Risk Management	Safety findings were generally consistent with those of other SGLT2 inhibitor products. Compared to placebo, higher proportions of subjects experienced genital mycotic infections, urinary tract infections, vaginal pruritus, thirst, and increased urination with bexagliflozin. A higher incidence of genital mycotic infections was observed in females than males treated with bexagliflozin.
A program-wide meta-analysis was undertaken to establish the cardiovascular hazards of exposure to bexagliflozin. The primary endpoint was time-to-first adjudicated major adverse cardiac event (MACE+), a four-component composite endpoint consisting of events of CV death, nonfatal stroke, nonfatal myocardial infarction, or hospitalization for unstable angina. The estimated hazard ratio of MACE+ associated with bexagliflozin relative to control was 0.80 (95% CI: 0.58, 1.09). Exposure to bexagliflozin is not expected to unacceptably increase the risk of MACE in patients with T2DM.
An increased risk of nontraumatic amputation was observed compared to placebo in a trial enrolling patients with increased CV risk (hazard ratio: 1.64 (95% CI: 0.7, 3.8)). In addition, imbalances unfavorable to bexagliflozin were observed for events of serious fracture, sepsis, and rash/dermatitis.
Uncertainties in Risk
Risks associated with bexagliflozin exposure during pregnancy or breastfeeding are uncertain.
The duration of treatment exposure and follow-up in the clinical trials was not adequate to evaluate long latency events, including cancer.
There were few events of diabetic ketoacidosis, severe hypoglycemia, Fournier's gangrene, and pyelonephritis/urosepsis, limiting the interpretability of the available data.
No new safety findings were observed in the bexagliflozin clinical development program that significantly impact the overall risk profile. The reported AEs were generally consistent with the known safety profiles of SGLT2 inhibitor products.
In accordance with the SGLT2 inhibitor class, the Warnings and Precautions section in the approved bexagliflozin labeling will include the risk of ketoacidosis, urosepsis and pyelonephritis, Fournier's gangrene, genital mycotic infections, volume depletion, and hypoglycemia with concomitant use of insulin or an insulin secretagogue. As with some other members of the class, a Warnings and Precautions statement advising prescribers to consider factors that may increase the risk of amputation before initiating bexagliflozin and to monitor patients for infections or ulcers of lower limbs is also appropriate to mitigate this potential risk.
Section 6 of the prescribing information will include subsections to describe the imbalances noted for the adverse reactions of bone fracture, sepsis, rash, and dermatitis.
As with other members of the SGLT2 inhibitor class, the risks of bexagliflozin is adequately mitigated with labeling, including a Medication Guide for patients.
L69: ## 2.2. Conclusions Regarding Benefit-Risk
L70: The Applicant submitted six adequate and well-controlled investigations that establish clinical benefit for bexagliflozin for improving glycemic control in adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus, including four placebo-controlled trials and two active-controlled trials.
L71: The four placebo-controlled trials (C-419, C-448, C-450, and C-476) demonstrated superiority of bexagliflozin to placebo for the primary endpoint of change in HbA1c, from baseline to Week 24. Assessing change in HbA1c from baseline over at least 24 weeks relative to a control is the standard approach to showing benefit for a glycemic control indication for type 2 diabetes mellitus. HbA1c reflects average glucose control over the preceding 2-3 months and is an established surrogate for reduction in microvascular complications. Reductions in HbA1c were both statistically and clinically significant. Bexagliflozin was statistically superior to placebo as monotherapy, with a placebo-adjusted change from baseline in HbA1c of -0.4% (-0.6%, -0.1%; p=0.002) in C-450, and as add-on to metformin, with a placebo-adjusted change from baseline in HbA1c of -0.5% (-0.7%, -0.3%; p&lt;0.0001) in C-419. In addition, bexagliflozin was statistically superior to placebo on change from baseline in HbA1c to Week 24 in patients with increased CV risk on standard of care therapy for glycemic control (placebo-adjusted change from baseline of -0.4% [-0.5%, -0.4%; p&lt;0.0001]) in C-476. The observed treatment effect is comparable to that of some of the other approved oral agents for glycemic control in patients with T2DM. Reduction in microvascular disease in T2DM is proportional to reduction in HbA1c.
L72: While statistically significant, glycemic efficacy was more modest in C-448, the trial of patients with moderate renal impairment (i.e., eGFR \ge 30 to &lt;60 mL/min/1.73 m^2), with a placebo-adjusted change from baseline in HbA1c of -0.3% (-0.4%, -0.1%; p=0.002).
L73: Bexagliflozin also performed comparably to sitagliptin and glimepiride, two other approved treatments for type 2 diabetes in two active-controlled trials (C-423 and C-480). Trial C-423 compared bexagliflozin to sitagliptin at the recommended dose for patients without renal impairment (100 mg). Trial C-480 compared bexagliflozin to glimepiride titrated from 2 mg up to a maximum dose of 6 mg. In C-423 the estimated treatment difference versus sitagliptin was 0.1 (-0.1, 0.2). In C-480 the estimated treatment versus glimepiride was 0.0 (-0.2, 0.1). In both trials, the upper bound of the 95% confidence interval did not exceed the prespecified non-inferiority margin of 0.35. One limitation is that the glimepiride comparator was not titrated up to the maximum U.S. approved daily dose of 8 mg and glimepiride was not titrated after Week 6 in the 60-week trial.
L74: Bexagliflozin use was associated with statistically significant reductions in body weight compared to placebo in both the renal impairment trial (C-448) and the increased CV risk trial (C-476). In C-476, bexagliflozin was also associated with reduction in cuff systolic blood pressure versus placebo.
L75: Safety findings were generally consistent with those of other SGLT2 inhibitor products and can be adequately mitigated by labeling, including with a Medication Guide for patients, as has been done with the approved SGLT2 inhibitors.
L76: Consistent with other approved products in the SGLT2 inhibitor class, the *Warnings and Precautions* section of labeling will include the risk of ketoacidosis, urosepsis and pyelonephritis, Fournier's gangrene, genital mycotic infections, volume depletion, and
L77: hypoglycemia with concomitant use of insulin or an insulin secretagogue. In the clinical trials, a higher incidence of subjects assigned to bexagliflozin than placebo experienced one or more events of urinary tract infections, genital mycotic infections, volume depletion, and hypoglycemia. Events of ketoacidosis were observed in clinical trials with bexagliflozin. Fournier's gangrene is a rare, serious event associated with the class.
L78: Lower limb amputation is a recognized complication of diabetes mellitus, and an increased risk of lower limb amputation has been identified with some, but not all, members of the SGLT2 inhibitor class. Data from the increased CV risk trial (C-476) indicated an increased incidence of amputation with bexagliflozin treatment as compared to placebo (HR: 1.64 (0.70, 3.82)). The risk of amputation is higher in patients with a baseline history of prior amputation, PAD, and neuropathy, compared to patients without such disease history. The majority of amputations in both groups in C-476 were below-the-knee. Description of the observed imbalance in amputation warrants inclusion in labeling.
L79: Given the more modest treatment effect on HbA1c in patients with renal impairment in trial C-448, the safety of bexagliflozin in subjects with moderate renal impairment was considered a key review issue. Overall, considering the safety data from both the dedicated renal impairment trial (C-448) and the subgroup from the increased CV risk trial (C-476), no new safety issues were identified in subjects with stage 3 CKD, and the benefits outweigh the risks in this population.
L80: Changes in laboratory parameters in C-448 were generally consistent with data from other trials of bexagliflozin. The magnitude of transient increases in serum creatinine and corresponding decreases in eGFR was greater in trial C-448. Communication in labeling can adequately inform prescribers regarding these changes in laboratory parameters.
L81: In conclusion, the applicant demonstrated substantial evidence of effectiveness to support approval of the application. The benefits of treatment with bexagliflozin on glycemic control outweigh the potential risks in the indicated population when bexagliflozin is used according to the approved labeling.
L82: ## II. Interdisciplinary Assessment
L83: ## 3. Introduction
L84: TheracosBio LLC (hereafter referred to as the Applicant) has developed the sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitor bexagliflozin as an adjunct to diet and exercise to improve glycemic control in adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM). The SGLT2 protein is the predominant transporter responsible for reabsorption of glucose from the glomerular filtrate back into circulation. By inhibiting SGLT2, bexagliflozin reduces renal reabsorption of filtered glucose and lowers the renal threshold for glucose, thereby increasing urinary glucose excretion. The proposed marketed product is a blue tablet containing 20 mg of bexagliflozin. The tablet is to be taken once daily with or without food. There are currently four FDA-approved SGLT2 inhibitors indicated for improved glycemic control in adults with T2DM. Bexagliflozin is a new molecular entity (NME), and the Applicant is submitting this new drug application (NDA) using the 505(b)(1) approval pathway.

L97: ## 3.2. Approach to the Review
L98: Six adequate and well-controlled phase 3 trials conducted in subjects with T2DM provide substantial evidence of effectiveness for the pursued glycemic control indication (Trials C-419, C-423, C-448, C-450, C-476, and C-480; Table 3). The NDA also included a phase 2b dose-finding trial (C-449) to support dose selection and a phase 2b trial that utilized a noncommercial formulation of bexagliflozin (C-418). Other trials completed in the clinical development program either did not have a sufficient treatment duration, such that they would contribute meaningfully to the assessment of efficacy, did not enroll subjects with T2DM, or were conducted for the evaluation of bexagliflozin for the treatment of essential hypertension (e.g., C-603A, C-603B).
L99: The safety evaluation for this Application was based on the review of pooled safety data from three placebo-controlled trials enrolling subjects who were either treatment naïve or inadequately controlled on metformin (C-419, C-449, and C-450), termed the placebo-controlled pool, and the review of phase 3 trial data from active-controlled trials (C-423 and C-480) and trials enrolling specific populations (C-448 and C-476). The placebo-controlled pool was utilized to evaluate the safety and tolerability of 20 mg bexagliflozin relative to placebo in a similar patient population and was used to inform commonly occurring adverse reactions in Section 6 of the labeling. Trial C-448, which enrolled subjects with stage 3 chronic kidney disease (CKD), and Trial C-476, which enrolled subjects with increased cardiovascular (CV) risk, were evaluated independently to assess safety in these distinct patient populations. Trial C-476 was of special interest in this safety review, as it was the largest (1,699 subjects in the safety population) and longest (median duration 2.4 years) trial in the bexagliflozin clinical program. It therefore provided the most robust assessment for various adverse events of special interest (AESIs). Analyses from C-448 and C-476 are presented independently and used to inform labeling where indicated.

L119: **Table 5. Summary of General Clinical Pharmacology and Pharmacokinetics**
L120: Characteristic	Drug Information
Pharmacologic Activity
Established pharmacologic class (EPC)	Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitor
Mechanism of action	SGLT2 is the predominant transporter responsible for reabsorption of glucose from the glomerular filtrate back into the circulation. Bexagliflozin is an inhibitor of SGLT2. By inhibiting SGLT2, bexagliflozin reduces renal reabsorption of filtered glucose and lowers the renal threshold for glucose, and thereby increases urinary glucose excretion.
Active moieties	Bexagliflozin (no active metabolite)
QT prolongation	At five times the maximum recommended dose (100 mg), bexagliflozin does not prolong the QTc interval to any clinically significant extent.
General Information
Bioanalysis	Bexagliflozin concentrations in plasma were measured using validated LC-MS/MS methods.
Healthy subjects versus patients	No clinically relevant differences in bexagliflozin PK parameters between healthy volunteers and patients with T2DM.
Drug exposure following the therapeutic dosing regimen	Single dose data are presented as there is no significant accumulation following once daily dosing of bexagliflozin with the 3 mg, 10 mg, and 30 mg tablet formulation.
Following oral administration of a single dose of 20 mg bexagliflozin tablet under fasted and fed conditions, the geometric mean (CV%) Cmax was 134 (43) ng/mL and 176 (31) ng/mL, respectively, and AUC0-∞ was 1149 (30) ng*h/mL and 1276 (26) ng*h/mL, respectively.
Range of effective dosage(s) or exposure	20 mg QD was the only dose studied in the pivotal phase 3 studies.
Maximally tolerated dosage or exposure	Maximally tolerated dose is not known. The highest studied dose was 150 mg QD for 14 days in healthy subjects.
Dosage proportionality	Bexagliflozin PK is dose-proportional over the range of 3 mg to 90 mg.
Accumulation	No significant accumulation upon once daily dosing with accumulation ratio between 1.1 and 1.2
Time to achieve steady-state	Approximately 60 hours
Bridge between to-be-marketed and clinical trial formulations	Not needed as the to-be-marketed formulation was used in the phase 3 studies.

T_{max}	2-4 hours following oral administration

Mass balance results	91.6% of total radioactivity was recovered, 51.1% in feces, predominantly as bexagliflozin, and 40.5% in urine, largely as the 3'-O-glucuronide metabolite.
Clearance	The apparent oral clearance is 19 L/h by population pharmacokinetic modeling.
Half-life	The apparent elimination half-life was about 12 h.
Metabolic pathway(s)	Bexagliflozin is mainly metabolized by UGT1A9 and, to a lesser extent, CYP3A.

Intrinsic Factors and Specific Populations
Body weight	Based on a population PK analysis, body weight does not have a clinically relevant effect on the PK of bexagliflozin.
Age	Based on a population PK analysis, age does not have a clinically relevant effect on the PK of bexagliflozin.
Renal impairment	In T2DM patients with mild (eGFR: 60-89 mL/min/1.73 m2), moderate (eGFR: 30-59 mL/min/1.73 m2), and severe renal impairment (eGFR: 15-29 mL/min/1.73 m2), the AUC of bexagliflozin increased by 6.8%, 33.8% and 53.9%, respectively, compared to T2DM patients with normal renal function. The C_{max} was not affected. Consistent with the mechanism of action, the 24-hour urinary glucose excretion in T2DM patients with mild, moderate, and severe renal impairment was 17%, 60%, and 83% lower, respectively, than in T2DM patients with normal renal function.
Hepatic impairment	Based on safety and efficacy data in patients with moderate renal impairment, no dose adjustment is needed in patients with mild and moderate renal impairment (i.e., eGFR \ge30 mL/min/1.73 m2). Bexagliflozin is not recommended in patients with severe renal impairment, as it is not expected to be effective in these patients (See Sections 6.3 and 8.1).
The use of bexagliflozin has not been studied in patients with severe hepatic impairment. In subjects with moderate hepatic impairment, the AUC of bexagliflozin increased by 28.3%, and C_{max} increased by 6.3% compared to subjects with normal hepatic function. No dose adjustment is needed in patients with mild and moderate hepatic impairment.

L125: ## 5.1. Nonclinical Assessment of Potential Effectiveness
L126: Bexagliflozin is an inhibitor of SGLT2 indicated for the treatment of T2DM. SGLT2 is a transmembrane protein that actively cotransports extracellular sodium and hexose sugars into cells by relying on the electrochemical potential of sodium ions across the renal tubular (apical) cell membrane. Inhibition of SGLT2 prevents glucose reuptake from the renal proximal tubule, leading to glucosuria and a reduction in plasma glucose concentration.
L127: **Figure 1. Bexagliflozin Mechanism of Action**
L128: Source: (Fioretto et al. 2015)
L129: Abbreviations: SGLT; sodium-glucose cotransporter.
L130: Nonclinical evidence of effectiveness was obtained from in vitro studies evaluating the activity of bexagliflozin on human SGLT2, and from in vivo studies evaluating levels of glucosuria, blood glucose, and hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) in healthy animals and/or diabetic animal models.
L131: In vitro, bexagliflozin selectively inhibited human SGLT2 as compared to SGLT1 with a half maximal inhibitory concentration (IC_{50}) of 2 nM and 5.6 \muM, respectively, representing a ~2,400-fold selectivity for SGLT2 over SGLT1 (Table 6).

L156: ## 6. Assessment of Effectiveness
L157: ## 6.1. Dose and Dose Responsiveness
L158: The Applicant's proposed dose for bexagliflozin is 20 mg once daily, taken in the morning with or without food. The proposed dosing regimen is acceptable for approval based on a favorable efficacy and safety profile.
L159: We had recommended the evaluation of two dosage strengths in the phase 3 program (meeting minutes dated September 21, 2016); however, only a 20 mg dosage strength was evaluated. It is unclear whether a higher dosage strength could provide additional glycemic control without significant additional tolerability-related events.
L160: The selection of the 20-mg dose was primarily based on the HbA1c reduction from baseline in T2DM subjects from a 12-week, phase 2, dose-ranging study (C-449). In the study, subjects with T2DM received placebo or bexagliflozin doses ranging from 5 to 20 mg. A dose-response relationship across bexagliflozin dosages of 5 mg to 20 mg was observed, and the unadjusted mean changes from baseline in HbA1c at Week 12 were +0.23%, -0.28%, -0.40%, and -0.48% in the placebo, 5 mg, 10 mg, and 20 mg groups, respectively (Figure 4). A maximum drug effect (E_{max}) model was fitted to the observed data with an estimated maximum mean reduction (95% CI) of -0.82% (-0.51%, -1.1%) and an estimated ED_{50} (95% CI) of 3.0 mg (0, 7.3 mg). After adjusting for placebo mean changes from baseline, 20 mg bexagliflozin was predicted to achieve 76.8% of the maximum pharmacological effect in T2DM subjects. Additionally, the placebo-adjusted least-square mean treatment differences in HbA1c at Week 12 were -0.55%, -0.68%, and -0.80% for 5 mg, 10 mg, and 20 mg, respectively (refer to Section 11.5 in the C-449 study report). The reduction in HbA1c at the proposed dose of 20 mg was considered statistically significant and clinically meaningful.
L161: Figure 4. Change in HbA1c From Baseline at Week 12 in Patients With T2DM, Trial C-449
L162: Source: Reviewer independent analysis from Study C-449 efficacy dataset with full analysis population; see Section 14.3 Pharmacometrics Review for details
L163: Black dots, observed mean change from baseline of each subgroup by dosage shown; middle black line, model predictions based on parameter estimates; top and bottom black lines, upper and lower bounds of 95% confidence interval based on the parameter standard errors, respectively
L164: Abbreviations: HbA1c; hemoglobin A1c; T2DM, type 2 diabetes mellitus.
L165: The potential effectiveness of the 20-mg dose was also supported by dose-response relationships of 24-hour urinary glucose excretion (UGE; PD effect of glucosuria) in healthy subjects and fasting plasma glucose in subjects with T2DM (C-445 and C-402). The mean change in UGE as a function of dose ranging from 5 mg to 90 mg was well fit by an E_{max} model (Figure 5). The estimated maximum UGE was 80.7 g per day (95% CI: 71.7 to 89.8) and the estimated ED_{50} was 5.2 mg (95% CI: 2.8 to 7.6). A dose of 20 mg was predicted to achieve 79% of the maximum pharmacological effect in nondiabetic subjects. The changes in fasting plasma glucose (FPG) were determined in T2DM subjects at bexagliflozin doses ranging from 5 mg to 50 mg in a 28-day study (Figure 6). Based on the fitted E_{max} model, the 20-mg dose is expected to produce ~90% of the maximum effect in lowering FPG.

L170: ## 6.2. Clinical Trials Intended to Demonstrate Efficacy
L171: ## 6.2.1. Study Design
L172: ## Overview
L173: The six phase 3 trials used to support efficacy of bexagliflozin were all multicenter, randomized, double-blinded, controlled trials that met the regulatory standards for adequate and well-controlled studies. These studies included four placebo-controlled trials and two active-
L174: controlled trials. The placebo-controlled trials evaluated bexagliflozin as monotherapy (C-450), as add-on to metformin (C-419), as add-on to standard antihyperglycemic medications in subjects with stage 3 CKD (C-448), and as add-on to standard antihyperglycemic medications in subjects with increased CV risk (C-476). The active-controlled trials compared bexagliflozin to glimepiride (C-480) or sitagliptin (C-423) as add-on to metformin. All trials were completed at the time of this NDA review. The Applicant states that all clinical trials were conducted in compliance with good clinical practice, applicable laws, and regulations, and in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki (1996). Protocol synopses for each trial are presented in Section 15.1.
L175: ## Objectives
L176: The stated primary objective of all phase 3 trials was to assess the effect of bexagliflozin relative to comparator (placebo or active) on the change in HbA1c from baseline to the primary assessment timepoint (Week 24 in C-419, C-450, C-423, C-448, and C-476, and Week 60 in C-480). Key secondary objectives differed between trials but were generally related to evaluation of the effect of bexagliflozin on body weight, systolic blood pressure (SBP), and/or FPG.
L177: ## Trial Design
L178: The following sections present an overview of noteworthy trial design features in the phase 3 clinical program.
L179: ## Run-In Period
L180: All trials included a one- or two-week, single-blind, placebo run-in period to assess compliance and uncontrolled hyperglycemia prior to randomization. At the start of the run-in period, subjects received diet and exercise counseling and were provided with a glucometer and instructions for daily use. Subjects were not eligible for randomization if more than one dose (or two doses in C-480) of run-in medication was missed. Subjects were also generally not eligible for enrollment if they experienced uncontrolled hyperglycemia during the run-in period (e.g., FPG \ge250 mg/dL on two or more consecutive days, signs and symptoms of uncontrolled hyperglycemia).
L181: ## Study Treatments
L182: Of the six phase 3, pivotal trials, four trials were placebo-controlled (C-419, C-450, C-448, C-476) and two trials were active-controlled (C-480 utilized glimepiride and C-423 utilized sitagliptin as the active-comparator treatments). All trials evaluated bexagliflozin 20 mg utilizing the to-be-commercialized tablet formulation.
L183: ## Dose Modification of Study Treatments
L184: As the Applicant only proposes to commercialize one dosage strength (20 mg) of bexagliflozin, no dose modification for bexagliflozin occurred in any trial.
L185: In C-423, subjects assigned to the active comparator group received sitagliptin 100 mg.
L186: In C-480, optimal titration of glimepiride was required, and a titration algorithm was detailed in the study protocol. Briefly, subjects who successfully completed the run-in period were randomized to receive either bexagliflozin tablets with placebo glimepiride capsules (Group 1) or placebo bexagliflozin tablets and active glimepiride capsules (Group 2). Subjects were to receive a starting dose of 2 mg glimepiride or placebo glimepiride at randomization. At Weeks 2, 4, and
L187: 6, subjects had in-clinic visits for the assessment of glimepiride up-titration and safety evaluation. Glimepiride doses were increased if a subject met the following two criteria:
L188: - \ge 50\% of documented fasting self-monitoring blood glucose (SMBG) measurements &gt;110 \text{ mg/dL}
- No severe or documented symptomatic hypoglycemia events (defined as an event during which typical symptoms of hypoglycemia are accompanied by a measured plasma glucose concentration \le 70 \text{ mg/dL})
L189: Subjects were advised to contact the clinical site in the case of persistent hyperglycemia (more than three consecutive daily fasting SMBG measures \ge 270 \text{ mg/dL}) such that glimepiride doses could be increased earlier than the next scheduled study visit. After Week 6 of treatment, no further increases in glimepiride were to occur, and rescue medication could be prescribed by the investigator if deemed necessary for the well-being of the subject. As C-480 was double-blinded, subjects assigned to receive placebo glimepiride received mock titrations at Weeks 2, 4, and 6 based on the noted glycemic criteria.
L190: In all trials that allowed background antihyperglycemic therapy (C-419, C-423, C-448, C-476, C-480), dosing was to remain stable over the course of the trial unless a change was deemed necessary for the well-being of the subject (see “Rescue Medication” below). Protocols stated that changes to dosage and administration that occurred during trials should be documented.
L191: ## Stratification
L192: Stratification factors varied by trial as summarized below:
L193: - C-419: HbA1c \le 8.5 or not; United States or Japan clinical site
- C-423: HbA1c \le 8.5 or not
- C-448: HbA1c \le 8.5 or not; baseline insulin use or not; estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) 30 to 44 or 45 to 59 mL/min/1.73 m^2
- C-450: HbA1c \le 8.5 or not; treatment-naïve or not
- C-476: HbA1c \le 9.5 or not; body mass index (BMI) &lt;25 \text{ kg/m}^2 or not; eGFR &lt;60 \text{ mL/min/1.73 m}^2 or not; history of heart failure (HF) or not
- C-480: HbA1c \le 8.5 or not; metformin use only or metformin use +1 additional antihyperglycemic agent; eGFR \ge 90 \text{ mL/min/1.73 m}^2 or not

L212: ## **Rescue Medication**
L213: Subjects were to receive counseling regarding appropriate diet and exercise to aid in glycemic control throughout all phase 3 trials. In addition, subjects were advised to take daily fasting SMBG measurements. Rescue medication was recommended if, after diet and exercise counseling, subjects had uncontrolled hyperglycemia. While specific rescue criteria differed by trial,1 criteria were generally as follows:
L214: - More than three consecutive, daily fasting SMBG measures of \ge 270 mg/dL from baseline to Week 6, \ge 240 mg/dL from Week 6 to Week 12, or \ge 200 mg/dL from Week 12 to end of treatment.
- Fasting SMBG values \ge 250 mg/dL and associated with clinical signs or symptoms of hyperglycemia (e.g., weight loss, blurred vision, increased thirst, increased urination, or fatigue), and the signs or symptoms are severe.
L215: In C-476, subjects were to be managed with diet and exercise counseling or rescue medication (if above criteria were met) for the first 24 weeks. After the primary endpoint measurement at Week 24, changes to the medical therapy for hyperglycemia could occur at investigator discretion based on SMBG, FPG, and HbA1c information using local standards of care for subjects with T2DM.
L216: ## **Study Endpoints**
L217: The primary endpoint in all phase 3 trials was change from baseline in HbA1c to the prespecified timepoint at Week 24 (except C-480, at Week 60). HbA1c is a surrogate endpoint for microvascular disease risk reduction and is a validated surrogate endpoint (FDA 2022) to support glycemic control indications in patients with diabetes. In the bexagliflozin clinical program, HbA1c was measured using a high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) method certified to be Level 1 by the National Glycohemoglobin Standardization Program (NGSP) and standardized to the Diabetes Control and Complications Trial (DCCT) reference assay.
L218: A summary of secondary endpoints as described in the statistical analysis plan (SAP) for each trial is presented in Table 10. To control for type I error, a hierarchical testing approach was carried out for the testing of secondary endpoints. No formal hypothesis testing occurred for secondary efficacy endpoints in C-419 and it is thus excluded from Table 10. Secondary endpoints evaluated for exploratory purposes in C-419 included changes in FPG, SBP, body weight, and proportion of subjects with HbA1c \le 7\% over time.
L219: 1 C-419 and C-423 also recommended rescue treatment if HbA1c was &gt;8.0\% between weeks 12-24. C-450 did not specify a minimum fasting SMBG values or specify “severe” signs and symptoms for rescue criteria to be met for criterion #2. In C-476, two consecutive, daily, fasting SMBG values above the noted thresholds could prompt rescue treatment. C-476 also did not include rescue criteria regarding clinical signs and symptoms of hyperglycemia.

L224: ## 6.2.2. Statistical Analysis Plan
L225: This section provides a brief description of key SAP elements. Please see Section 12.2 for a detailed description of the SAP and its development history.
L226: ## Analysis Set for Efficacy
L227: The intent-to-treat (ITT) analysis set included all subjects who were randomized and was preplanned to serve as the primary set for the efficacy analyses. All analyses of the ITT analysis set were based on the randomization assignment.
L228: ## Primary Analysis Method for the Primary and Key Secondary Efficacy Endpoints
L229: During the IND stage, the Applicant first proposed an LOCF analysis, and then an MMRM method for the primary analysis of the primary or secondary endpoints with missing data. FDA continuously advised against the LOCF, and the MMRM approach that does not appropriately address missing data, as it treats the behavior of missing data for those subjects who are off-treatment to be the same as that of observed data for those subjects who are on-treatment in the same treatment group. The Applicant's prespecified primary estimand for the bexagliflozin T2DM HbA1c studies is the treatment policy estimand, which is FDA's preferred estimand. An appropriate statistical method that aligns with the treatment policy estimand in handling missing data is the retrieved- dropout-based pattern mixture multiple imputation method (MI-RD). To
L230: estimate the treatment policy estimand, efficacy data should be collected and utilized in analyses on all randomized treated subjects regardless of treatment adherence, rescue status, or other post baseline status. Missing data should be imputed in a fashion consistent with what the measurement would have been, had it been measured.
L231: Disagreeing with the proposed MMRM approach in the Applicant's preNDA meeting package (meeting date December 5, 2019), FDA recommended that where there are a sufficient number of retrieved dropouts (subjects who discontinued treatment before the final assessment window but still had an efficacy measurement in the final assessment window). FDA prefers a multiple imputation approach that models the missing final assessment of nonretrieved dropouts (subjects who discontinued treatment before the final assessment window and did not have a measurement in this assessment window) based on known measurements from the retrieved dropouts. The Applicant's pivotal trials were all completed and unblinded (database locked at on November 22, 2019) at the time of the preNDA meeting. Clinical study reports (CSRs) had been finalized before the FDA's specific recommendation of retrieved drop-out approach or return-to-baseline approach (if insufficient retrieved dropouts) analysis advice was delivered. Across the six HbA1c studies, an insufficient number of retrieved dropouts rendered the MI-RD approach analysis not feasible. Following the FDA's recommendation at a preNDA meeting, the Applicant used the multiple imputation based on return-to-baseline approach (MI-RTB) in handling missing data as post-hoc analyses. As analysis methods have been continuously recommended by FDA to estimate the appropriate treatment effect for evaluation of efficacy, these post-hoc analyses were acceptable.
L232: A three-step MI-RTB plus analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) approach was adopted by the Applicant as the primary analysis method for both the primary and key secondary efficacy endpoints; the same method was used by the FDA statistical reviewer in this NDA review. The three steps are:
L233: - MI-RTB to impute missing data: based on the baseline of the subject for an endpoint, with variance estimated from an ANCOVA model of nonmissing Week 24 (Week 60 for Study C-480) HbA1c for the treatment arms. The ANCOVA model will include the same variables as the primary analysis model. The variance, \sigma^2, for the Week 24 (Week 60 for Study C-480) data for each treatment arm will be used as the variance in an imputation model X_{\text{Week } 24 \text{ or } 60} \sim N(X_{\text{baseline}}, \sigma^2) to impute the missing Week 24 (Week 60 for Study C-480) data.
- ANCOVA model analysis: for each iteration of the multiply imputed full dataset, the primary and secondary endpoints were analyzed using an ANCOVA model with treatment and stratification factors as fixed effects and the corresponding baseline value as a covariate. The least squares (LS) mean differences between bexagliflozin 20 mg and a comparator in each study, with the associated two-sided 95% CIs were estimated from the ANCOVA model.
- Rubin's rule to combine the results: Rubin's rule was applied to combine and synthesize the results from step 2 to estimate an overall treatment effect and corresponding variability.
L234: ## Noninferiority Margin for the Active-Controlled Trials
L235: For the active-controlled trials C-423 and C-480, a noninferiority margin of 0.35% was preplanned by the Applicant and agreed upon by the FDA review team at the clinical development stage. See the Applicant's justifications for the margin selection in Section 12.2.
L236: ## Multiple Testing Procedures
L237: In each of the six pivotal studies, the study SAP prespecified a hierarchical testing sequence of primary endpoint and key secondary endpoints to control for study-wise type I error due to multiplicity. For each endpoint in the sequence, a two-sided statistical test was to be conducted at the 5.0% significance level. In each study, if the primary endpoint met the statistical significance, then the key secondary endpoints were to be tested sequentially in the order as listed in Table 10 and Table 136 [Section 16].
L238: ## Tipping Point Sensitivity Analyses for the Primary Efficacy Endpoints
L239: For each of the four superiority trials (C-450, C-419, C-448, and C-476), a two-dimensional delta-based tipping point analysis was carried out to assess the robustness of inferences from the primary analysis method to deviations from its underlying assumptions, targeting the same primary estimand.
L240: For each of the two active-controlled trials (C-423 and C-480), the FDA statistical reviewer performed a one-dimensional tipping point analysis: based on the RTB-MI imputed datasets, penalizing the missing outcomes on the bexagliflozin arm by applying a delta of size equal to the null hypothesis of the noninferiority test (i.e., the noninferiority margin of 0.35%) while keeping the MI-RTB imputed active-control arm missing outcomes unchanged.
L241: ## Subgroup Analyses
L242: For each of the preplanned subgrouping factors (age, gender, race, region and baseline HbA1c for all studies, see Section 16 preplanned subgroups of each individual study), a by-subgroup analysis was firstly performed for each subgroup level using the primary analysis method (with modifications on covariates when necessary) to derive a sample estimate of the subgroup treatment effect; subsequently, a Bayesian hierarchical model was used to derive a shrinkage estimate of the subgroup treatment effect using the sample estimates. Forests plots are used to present both the “sample” and “shrinkage” estimates and corresponding confidence intervals.
L243: To investigate for potential effect modification of baseline HbA1c levels, an additional exploratory simple linear regression analysis treating baseline HbA1c as a continuous variable was carried out for each of the four placebo-controlled studies. The response variable was the change from baseline in HbA1c at Week 24, the predictor variables included treatment, baseline HbA1c levels, and a treatment by baseline HbA1c levels interaction. The size and the significance level of the interaction term (difference in by-arm baseline HbA1c slopes) from this model fitting is an indicator of the potential modification effect.
L244: ## 6.2.3. Results of Analyses
L245: ## 6.2.3.1. Demographics, Baseline Characteristics, and Disposition
L246: ## 6.2.3.1.1. Demographics and Baseline Characteristics
L247: Relevant demographics and baseline clinical characteristics of the pivotal efficacy trials are shown in Table 11. Characteristics between drug and comparator groups were generally balanced in all trials. Trials enrolling subjects who were either treatment-naïve or inadequately controlled on metformin (i.e., C-419, C-423, C-450, C-480) were generally similar, with a mean age of approximately 55 to 60 years and an average diabetes duration of approximately 9 years. In contrast, subjects enrolled in C-448 and C-476 were older (average age of approximately 65 to 70 years) with a longer duration of diabetes (approximately 15 years) with a significant amount of baseline insulin use (approximately 50 to 55%). Proportions of male and female subjects varied by trial. Trial C-476, which evaluated subjects with increased risk for MACE, enrolled a majority of male subjects (approximately 70%). The majority of subjects in most trials were White, although C-419 and C-448 enrolled approximately 50% and 39% of Asian subjects, respectively. All trials predominantly enrolled non-Hispanic/Latino subjects.

L256: ## 6.2.3.1.2. Disposition
L257: Analysis populations and subject disposition from the efficacy trials is summarized in Table 12. Screened subjects were eligible for randomization if study-specific inclusion/exclusion criteria were met and if the subject successfully completed the run-in period. The most common reasons subjects were not eligible for randomization varied by trial but included having screening HbA1c &lt;7% and not meeting the eligibility criteria for renal function.
L258: Approximately 90 to 95% of the subjects completed each study (Table 12). The trials with the least completers were C-419 and C-480, with about 90% of subjects in both trials completing treatment in the bexagliflozin and placebo groups, respectively. While these trials had fewer completers as compared to other trials in the clinical program, the completion rate is considered acceptable, and it is reassuring that no imbalances in completers between treatment groups was observed. While data are limited, there were no discernable trends in reasons for study discontinuation between treatment arms and study. Imbalances in subjects lost to follow-up were observed in some trials (e.g., seven and one subjects in the bexagliflozin and placebo groups were lost to follow up, respectively, in C-450); however, this finding was not observed consistently, thus limiting interpretability. See Section 16.4 for additional information on disposition for each trial.

L267: ## 6.2.3.2. Primary Efficacy Results, Sensitivity, and Subgroup Analyses
L268: ## 6.2.3.2.1. Primary Efficacy Results
L269: Table 13 summarizes FDA's primary analysis results for the six pivotal efficacy studies in the bexagliflozin clinical development program. Additional detailed information on the efficacy analysis can be found in Section 16.
L270: Superiority of bexagliflozin to placebo was demonstrated for the primary endpoint of change in HbA1c from baseline to Week 24 for the four placebo-controlled trials (C-419, C-448, C-450, and C-476). Reductions in HbA1c were both statistically and clinically significant. Bexagliflozin was statistically superior to placebo as monotherapy, with a placebo-adjusted change from baseline of -0.38% (-0.63%, -0.13%; p=0.002) in C-450, and as add-on to metformin, with a placebo-adjusted change from baseline of -0.48% (-0.69%, -0.26%; p&lt;0.0001). In addition, bexagliflozin was statistically superior to placebo from baseline to Week 24 in subjects with increased CV risk on standard of care therapy for glycemic control (placebo-adjusted change from baseline of -0.44% [-0.53%, -0.35%; p&lt;0.0001]). While statistically significant, glycemic efficacy was more modest in C-448, enrolling patients with moderate renal impairment (i.e., eGFR \ge 30 to &lt;60 mL/min/1.73 m^2), with a placebo-adjusted change from baseline of -0.27% (-0.44%, -0.09%; p=0.002). Efficacy in this patient population is discussed in additional detail in Section 6.3.1.
L271: Noninferiority was achieved for the two active-controlled trials (C-423 and C-480). Trial C-423 compared bexagliflozin to sitagliptin at the recommended dose for patients without renal impairment (100 mg). Trial C-480 compared bexagliflozin to glimepiride 2, 4, or 6 mg (see Section 6.2 for additional details regarding how glimepiride was titrated in this study). Of note, the maximal approved dose of glimepiride in the US is 8 mg, and 81% of subjects in the glimepiride group received up-titration to 6 mg, suggesting that additional up-titration could have occurred if an 8 mg dosage strength had been incorporated into this trial. The impact of additional glimepiride titration (i.e., up to 8 mg) on the overall results of this trial is unclear.

L280: To date, no trials have been conducted to directly compare the efficacy of bexagliflozin to another approved SGLT2 inhibitor. Cross-trial comparison of data suggest that the efficacy of bexagliflozin may be more modest than other approved SGLT2 inhibitors. For example, when comparing data from monotherapy trials presented in Section 14 of the USPI, placebo-adjusted change from baseline in HbA1c from baseline to 24 to 26 weeks was 0.7% for ertugliflozin 15 mg, 0.7% for dapagliflozin 10 mg, 1.2% for canagliflozin 300 mg, and 0.9% for empagliflozin 25 mg as compared to 0.4% for bexagliflozin 20 mg (Janssen 2020; AstraZeneca 2021; Merck 2021; Ingelheim 2022). However, cross-trial comparisons should be approached with caution as differing trial designs and patient populations may influence the data observed in any given trial. In addition, FDA's approach to the preferred statistical analysis of trials to determine the most appropriate estimate of the treatment effect closer to realistic effectiveness has evolved over time, further limiting meaningful conclusions from cross-trial comparisons. (e.g., use of LOCF versus return to baseline for missing data imputation based on the most relevant assumption of missing data considering reasons of the missing data). Furthermore, other SGLT2 inhibitor programs evaluated two dosage strengths in phase 3 as compared to bexagliflozin which only evaluated a 20 mg dosage strength. It is unclear whether additional glycemic efficacy could be achieved with a higher bexagliflozin dose without an unacceptable increase in tolerability events. Ultimately, it is unclear at this time if, and to what extent, bexagliflozin may be less efficacious than other approved products.
L281: ## 6.2.3.2.2. Sensitivity Analysis of the Primary Endpoint
L282: For each of the superiority trials, tipping points were determined at the values of delta combinations where the statistical significance of treatment effect is lost; none of these derived delta combinations were clinically plausible (see result tables in Section 16.6). For each of the noninferiority trials, penalizing the missing outcomes on the bexagliflozin arm by applying a delta of 0.35% while keeping the MI-RTB imputed active-control arm missing outcomes unchanged, did not change the conclusion of noninferiority. These sensitivity analyses and results support the robustness of the conclusions based on primary analysis of HbA1c changes across the six pivotal trials.
L283: ## 6.2.3.2.3. Subgroup Analysis of the Primary Endpoint
L284: Subgroup analyses of the primary endpoint were conducted for all trials and are presented individually in Section 16.4. Subgroup analysis results were generally consistent across trials to demonstrate homogeneity of the favorable result for bexagliflozin, although limited data in
L285: certain subgroups impeded interpretability in some cases. Shrinkage estimates show narrower credible intervals than confidence intervals of sample estimates. The point estimate of the Shrinkage estimates are closer to the point estimate for the overall treatment difference compared to the sample estimates. No notable differences were detected using shrinkage estimates in all trials.
L286: The subgroup analysis from C-476 is presented here as a representative analysis because C-476 was the largest trial (ITT N=1700) and thus, provided more data contributing to each subgroup. As shown in Table 14, the treatment effect of bexagliflozin showed similar results to the overall population in all subgroups evaluated with the exception of a subgroup of subjects with renal impairment (i.e., baseline eGFR &lt;60 mL/min/1.73 m2). Efficacy in subjects with moderate renal impairment is discussed further in Section 6.3.1.

L307: ## 6.2.3.3.1. Change in HbA1c (%) From Baseline Over Time
L308: As discussed above, most trials evaluated the primary endpoint of change in HbA1c from baseline to 24 weeks, with active-controlled trial C-480 evaluating change from baseline in HbA1c at 60 weeks. While the primary endpoint was evaluated at Week 60 in C-480 the total trial duration was 96 weeks. Likewise, while the primary endpoint was evaluated at Week 24 in C-476, the trial duration was driven by the accrual of major adverse cardiac events (MACE+), and the average treatment duration was 2.4 years. These trials provide supportive information of changes in HbA1c (%) from baseline to longer time points for bexagliflozin.
L309: Figure 7 and Figure 8 are presented for exploratory purposes to show changes in HbA1c (%) from baseline over time using observed data only without consideration of missing data imputation. As shown in Figure 7, in C-480, maximal HbA1c reduction occurred at week 12 followed by decreases in effect over time for both drugs. C-476 provides additional long-term data for changes in HbA1c from baseline up to 168 weeks, although data at later timepoints are limited (Figure 8). As shown in Figure 8, reduction in HbA1c is maintained from baseline to approximately week 36, with a decline in treatment effect over time. However, all timepoints show a greater treatment effect in the bexagliflozin group as compared to the placebo group.

L316: ## 6.3. Key Review Issue Relevant to Evaluation of Benefit
L317: ## 6.3.1. Efficacy of Bexagliflozin in Subjects With Moderate Renal Impairment
L318: ## Background/Issue
L319: SGLT2 inhibitor products were not initially recommended for use in patients with moderate renal impairment due to diminished glycemic efficacy and safety concerns (e.g., increases in serum creatinine/decreases in eGFR upon treatment initiation, acute kidney injury) leading to an unfavorable benefit-risk assessment in this patient population. However, additional information has been obtained regarding the safety and efficacy of SGLT2 inhibitors in patients with moderate renal impairment, including the evaluation of these products in dedicated renal impairment studies and long-term cardiovascular outcome trials (CVOTs). These trials have supported expanded labeling for the use of SGLT2 inhibitors to improve glycemic control in patients with moderate renal impairment. Currently, dosing and administration recommendations for patients with renal impairment are product-specific based on the available clinical data. At this time of this NDA review, ertugliflozin and dapagliflozin are not recommended for use to improve glycemic control in patients with T2DM and an eGFR &lt;45 mL/min/1.73 m^{2}, and canagliflozin and empagliflozin are not recommended for use to improve glycemic control in patients T2DM and an eGFR &lt;30 mL/min/1.73 m^{2} because studies to support efficacy in patients with this level of renal impairment were not conducted or did not show statistically robust results.
L320: In the bexagliflozin clinical program, C-448 was a dedicated renal impairment trial enrolling patients with eGFR \ge 30 to &lt;60 mL/min/1.73 m^2. In addition, subjects were eligible for enrollment in C-476 with eGFR \ge 45 mL/min/1.73 m^2. Subjects with moderate and severe renal impairment (eGFR &lt;60 mL/min/1.73 m^2) were excluded from all other trials in the bexagliflozin clinical program and therefore Trials C-448 and C-476 are the only trials with sufficient information to inform safety and efficacy in this patient population. While glycemic efficacy was observed in C-448, efficacy was not observed in the subset of subjects with moderate renal impairment in C-476, raising uncertainties about the efficacy of bexagliflozin in this patient population. The efficacy of bexagliflozin in patients with moderate renal impairment is therefore a key review issue.
L321: ## Assessment
L322: ## Overview
L323: The assessment of renal efficacy focused on two trials: C-448, a dedicated renal impairment trial enrolling patients with eGFR between \ge 30 and &lt;60 mL/min/1.73 m^2 (i.e., stage 3a and 3b CKD), and C-476, a trial enrolling subjects with increased CV risk that enrolled subjects with eGFR \ge 45 mL/min/1.73 m^2 (i.e., stage 3a CKD). In C-476, treatment was stratified by eGFR category (eGFR &lt;60 or \ge 60 mL/min/1.73 m^2), and approximately 20% of subjects in each treatment arm had eGFR &lt;60 mL/min/1.73 m^2. Baseline demographics for C-448 and C-476 are presented in Table 11. All other trials excluded subjects with a screening eGFR &lt;60 mL/min/1.73 m^2 and were therefore not considered due to limited data. Renal efficacy data from C-448 and C-476 are discussed independently below.
L324: ## Trial C-448 in Patients With Moderate Renal Impairment
L325: C-448 was a phase 3, multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group study to evaluate the efficacy and safety of bexagliflozin 20 mg versus placebo in subjects with T2DM, moderate renal impairment, and inadequate glycemic control. The study population included subjects with T2DM, an HbA1c of 7.0 to 10.5% (inclusive), and stage 3 CKD as defined by an eGFR \ge 30 and &lt;60 mL/min/1.73 m^2 at the screening visit and at one additional time of measurement between 1 and 12 months prior to screening, which could be obtained from available medical records. Subjects were excluded if there was a &gt;20\% change in eGFR between the historical value and the screening visit. Subjects on any antihyperglycemic regimen were eligible for enrollment (with the exception of taking an SGLT2 inhibitor). At the time of screening, the doses and frequency of all antihyperglycemic medications were to have been stable for at least 8 weeks. See
L326: APPEARS THIS WAY ON ORIGINAL
L327: Table 9 for additional information on inclusion/exclusion criteria for this trial.
L328: All eligible subjects entered a one-week single-blind, placebo run-in period to allow for optimization of compliance with diet and exercise recommendations. Subjects who were compliant in taking run-in medication were eligible for randomization. Randomization was stratified by HbA1c (7.0 to 8.5% or 8.6 to 10.5%), baseline insulin use, and eGFR (30 to 44 mL/min/1.73 m2 or 45 to 59 mL/min/1.73 m2) at the screening visit.
L329: Out of 490 screened subjects, 312 were randomized to either the bexagliflozin arm (n=157) or the placebo arm (n=155). All randomized subjects (ITT) took at least one dose of investigational product (safety population), and thus the ITT and safety analysis populations were the same. As shown in Table 11, subjects enrolled in C-448 had a mean age of 69.6 (39 to 88) years, a mean diabetes duration of 15.9 (0 to 50.2) years, and a mean baseline HbA1c of 8.0% (SD =0.8). Mean baseline eGFR was 45.1 mL/min/1.73 m2. The majority of subjects were male (63%), White (55%), and non-Hispanic/Latino (92%). Approximately 56% of subjects used insulin as part of their regimen for glycemic control.
L330: The results of the primary efficacy analysis (i.e., placebo-subtracted change in HbA1c from baseline to Week 24), are presented in Table 159 and reproduced in Table 16 below.
L331: Bexagliflozin demonstrated a modest, but statistically and clinically significant reduction in HbA1c as compared to placebo (LS mean difference: -0.27%; 95% CI: -0.44%, -0.09%). In accordance with these results, fewer subjects received rescue treatment for uncontrolled hyperglycemia in the bexagliflozin group (9 subjects (5.7%)) as compared to the placebo group (17 subjects (11.0%)), and rescue medication was prescribed to subjects in the bexagliflozin group at a later mean date in the treatment period as compared to subjects in the placebo group (mean time-to-first rescue medication of 84.3 versus 72.3 days in the bexagliflozin and placebo groups, respectively; Applicant's analysis). As demonstrated in Figure 9, the bexagliflozin group consistently had a larger mean change in HbA1c over time as compared to placebo.
L332: More modest glycemic efficacy of SGLT2 inhibitor products in patients with moderate renal impairment is expected based on the mechanism of action of the drug class and has been characterized with other approved products. As discussed above (Section 6.2.3.2.1), it is difficult to draw meaningful conclusions from cross-trial comparisons as differences in study designs and analysis methods may impact trial results. However, the reduction in HbA1c with bexagliflozin treatment in C-448 is generally consistent with data available from other members of class. For example, in a double-blind, 26-week, placebo-controlled trial enrolling 269 subjects with T2DM and moderate renal impairment (eGFR 30 to 50 mL/min/1.73 m2), canagliflozin 100 mg and 300 mg demonstrated placebo-adjusted changes in HbA1c of -0.30% (95% CI: -0.53%; -0.07%) and -0.40% (95% CI: -0.64%; -0.17%), respectively (Janssen 2020). In VERTIS CV enrolling subjects with T2DM and CVD, ertugliflozin demonstrated a placebo-adjusted change in HbA1c of -0.28% (95% CI: -0.4, -0.15) in a subgroup of subjects with baseline eGFR of 45 to 59 mL/min/1.73 m2 (see clinical review in DARRTS dated September 16, 2021).

L359: ## **Trial C-476 in Patients With Increased CV Risk**
L360: Subjects with eGFR \ge45 mL/min/1.73 m2 were eligible for enrollment in C-476, allowing for an efficacy evaluation in a subgroup of subjects with stage 3a CKD in this trial. Unlike C-448, an historical eGFR measurement was not utilized to confirm stability of renal function over time,
L361: and some patients with baseline eGFR &lt;45 \text{ mL/min}/1.73 \text{ m}^2 were enrolled in C-476 due to variability between screening and baseline eGFR measurements (this also occurred in C-448, albeit to a lesser extent; Table 11). For the subgroup analysis presented in this review, a cutoff of eGFR &lt;60 \text{ mL/min}/1.73 \text{ m}^2 was utilized to identify subjects with renal impairment in C-476. Of the subjects in C-476 with baseline eGFR &lt;60 \text{ mL/min}/1.73 \text{ m}^2, approximately 15% of subjects in each treatment group had baseline eGFR &lt;45 \text{ mL/min}/1.73 \text{ m}^2. The mean (SD) eGFR value in subjects with eGFR &lt;45 \text{ mL/min}/1.73 \text{ m}^2 was 41 (4) \text{mL/min}/1.73 \text{ m}^2.
L362: Although efficacy in subjects with renal impairment was a prespecified subgroup, the Applicant did not include this subgroup in their hierarchical testing plan, and therefore the analyses below are presented descriptively. As shown in Table 18, glycemic efficacy was not observed in subjects with eGFR &lt;60 \text{ mL/min}/1.73 \text{ m}^2 in C-476, with bexagliflozin demonstrating a mean treatment difference (vs. placebo) in HbA1c of 0.0% (95% CI: -0.23, 0.23). Change from baseline in HbA1c over time by treatment group and baseline renal function is shown in Figure 12. In subjects with eGFR &lt;60 \text{ mL/min}/1.73 \text{ m}^2 maximal glycemic reduction in the bexagliflozin occurred at week 12, followed by a decline if efficacy at week 24.
L363: The Applicant proposes several reasons that may account for this finding. The Applicant notes that, although the mean change from baseline of HbA1c in the bexagliflozin arm of this subgroup was more modest (-0.50%) compared to the mean change for bexagliflozin arm with normal renal function or mild renal impairment (-0.87%), the mean change from baseline in the placebo arm was larger in the subgroup with eGFR &lt;60 \text{ mL/min}/1.73 \text{ m}^2 (-0.50%) as compared to the subgroup with eGFR \ge 60 \text{ mL/min}/1.73 \text{ m}^2 (-0.32%). Furthermore, in subjects with eGFR &lt;60 \text{ mL/min}/1.73 \text{ m}^2, over twice as many subjects in the placebo arm required treatment intensification as compared to the bexagliflozin group, and over twice as many subjects in the bexagliflozin group had documented relaxation of concomitantly prescribed antihyperglycemic agents as compared to the placebo group (Table 19). The Applicant states that these factors indicate a degree of investigator intervention that did not occur in C-448, thereby explaining the discrepant results between trials.
L364: The rationales proposed by the Applicant do not provide compelling justification for the lack of treatment effect in subjects with eGFR &lt;60 \text{ mL/min}/1.73 \text{ m}^2 in C-476. For example, while more subjects in the placebo group received treatment intensification as compared to the bexagliflozin group, this occurred to approximately equal extents in both subgroups (Table 19). In addition, these data are difficult to interpret since the degree of treatment intensification/relaxation is unclear. The Applicant also posits that differences in placebo effect between subgroup accounts, at least in part, for the lack of glycemic efficacy in subjects with eGFR &lt;60 \text{ mL/min}/1.73 \text{ m}^2. This argument is not very compelling because in a randomized, controlled trial, the placebo arm should reflect what would have happened in the drug arm absent the drug.
