L385: ## Conclusion
L386: A dedicated renal impairment trial (C-448) demonstrated statistically significant and clinically meaningful reductions in HbA1c in subjects with T2DM and moderate renal impairment. Despite this, efficacy was not observed in a subgroup analysis of subjects with baseline eGFR &lt;60 mL/min/1.73 m2 in C-476. While the Applicant has proposed explanations for these results, the underlying reason for the data observed is ultimately unclear. Trial C-476 was not designed to assess glycemic efficacy in subjects with renal impairment. Hence, all of the descriptive findings presented herein are for exploratory purposes only. In contrast, C-448 was an adequate and well-controlled study designed to assess glycemic efficacy in subjects with renal impairment, thus providing more conclusive evidence of the glycemic lowering effect of bexagliflozin in this patient population. In addition, while modest, the efficacy observed in C-448 was generally in accordance with the efficacy observed with other SGLT2 inhibitors, which also demonstrate more modest efficacy in this patient population.
L387: As discussed in detail in Section 7.7.2, the safety of bexagliflozin in subjects with moderate renal impairment is generally similar to the overall population, and no safety findings were observed that significantly impact the benefit-risk assessment. Subjects enrolled in C-448 (i.e., subjects with T2DM failing standard of care therapy with renal impairment) represent a patient population who could benefit from therapies that could further improve glycemic control. Taken together, the data presented support the efficacy of bexagliflozin in this patient population. Labeling in “8.6 Renal Impairment” and “14 Clinical Studies” is proposed to describe the results obtained in the bexagliflozin clinical development program.
L388: ## Dissent
L389: Not applicable.
L390: ## 7. Risk and Risk Management
L391: ## 7.1. Potential Risks or Safety Concerns Based on Nonclinical Data
L392: Bexagliflozin was evaluated in a comprehensive program of nonclinical safety studies that included secondary (off-target) pharmacology studies, in vitro and in vivo (rats and monkeys) safety pharmacology studies, general toxicology studies (up to 6 months in rats and 9 months in monkeys), genetic toxicology studies (Ames, in vitro chromosomal aberration, and in vivo rat micronucleus assays), a full battery of reproductive toxicity studies in rats and rabbits, a juvenile animal study in rats, and 2-year (lifetime) carcinogenicity studies in mice and rats.
L393: In the chronic (39-week) monkey study, minimal to slight kidney cortical tubular cell vacuolation, characterized by cytoplasmic microvacuoles adjacent to the basement membrane, was observed at all bexagliflozin dose levels. This finding is considered secondary to bexagliflozin-induced glucosuria but was not considered toxicologically significant based on the absence of significant adverse effects on renal function. In the chronic (26-week) rat study, a low incidence of minimal to slight stomach erosion/ulcer was observed in all treated male groups, without dose dependency, and in high dose females. These findings might be treatment related
L394: because similar findings were also reported in rats with other SGLT2 inhibitors. However, the clinical importance of stomach erosion is limited considering the low incidence and severity in rats and absence of similar findings in nonrodent species as well as in humans based on the extensive clinical experience with the drug class. In both monkeys and rats, the no observed adverse effect level (NOAEL) was the highest dose tested, which corresponded to 78 and 89 times the clinical dose of 20 mg, respectively, based on AUC.
L395: Bexagliflozin produced no adverse effects on fertility in rats, on embryofetal toxicity in rats or rabbits, or on pre- and postnatal development in rats at clinically relevant exposures. In juvenile rats administered bexagliflozin during a period of renal development corresponding to the late second and third trimesters of human pregnancy, adverse renal pelvic and tubular dilatation was observed at the end of dosing and throughout the 4-week recovery period at exposures \ge 11 times the MRHD. These findings are secondary to bexagliflozin's pharmacodynamic activity (see details in Section 5.1) and have been seen with all the drugs in the class. Based on the juvenile animal data, bexagliflozin is not recommended for use during the second and third trimester of pregnancy.
L396: Bexagliflozin produced no evidence of carcinogenic potential in mice or rats when administered for a lifetime. The duration of the male rat study was inadequate to allow rigorous statistical evaluation of carcinogenic potential, due to early mortality that resulted in premature study termination at Week 88. However, the available information, including the absence of imbalances for preneoplastic findings and tumors in male rats, suggests that repeating the carcinogenicity study in male rats at lower doses would be unlikely to provide additional useful information. See details in Sections 13.1.1.4.2 and 13.1.1.4.3.

L408: ## 7.4. FDA Approach to the Safety Review
L409: ## 7.4.1. Data Pooling
L410: The FDA's safety evaluation for this application was based on the review of pooled safety data from three placebo-controlled trials enrolling subjects, who were either treatment naïve or inadequately controlled on metformin (C-419, C-449, and C-450), termed the placebo-controlled pool, and the review of individual phase 3 trial data from active-controlled trials (C-423 and C-480) and trials enrolling specific populations (C-448 and C-476). The Applicant's approach to the safety review is discussed in Section 17.2.
L411: The placebo-controlled pool was utilized to evaluate the safety and tolerability of 20 mg bexagliflozin relative to placebo across multiple trials in a similar patient population. This pool excluded the uncontrolled, high-glycemic group (i.e., baseline HbA1c &gt;10.5%) from C-419, as well as the 5 and 10 mg bexagliflozin dosage strengths evaluated in C-449 that are not proposed for marketing. This pool was used to inform common adverse reaction information presented in Section 6 of the labeling.
L412: Not all of the placebo-controlled trials were included in the placebo-controlled pool, as C-448 (enrolling subjects with moderate renal impairment) and C-476 (enrolling subjects with increased CV risk) evaluated distinct patient populations as compared to trials C-419, C-449, and C-450. In addition, trial C-476 was by far the largest (1,699 subjects in the safety population) and longest (median duration of 2.4 years) trial in the safety program, and therefore pooling of this trial with other trials in the clinical development program would have skewed the results of the safety analysis towards this trial. Additional reasons to exclude C-476 from pooled analyses also include higher background rates of AEs in C-476 compared to other trials that may dilute imbalances observed in other trials, potential attenuation of imbalances due to the long observation period, and potential introduction of bias such as ascertainment bias due to differential dropout rates between treatment groups over time. For these reasons, safety data from C-448 and C-476 are presented independently where appropriate. Active-controlled trials were also reviewed and presented where appropriate, but not pooled with other placebo-
L413: controlled trials to inform product labeling. Lastly, a “broad pool,” which pooled all phase 2b/3 trials (C-418, C-419, C-423, C-449, C-450, C-476, C-480, C-603A), was used to assess more infrequent adverse events and inform overall exposure. As the broad pool consisted of trials of significantly different study designs, patient populations, and drug formulation, safety analyses with this pool were used for exploratory purposes only. See Section 17.2 for additional information regarding this pool, including data handling considerations.
L414: Safety data from phase 1/2a trials were excluded from the safety review conducted to inform product labeling as trials were generally short (e.g., 1 to 14 day) PK/PD studies that did not utilize the to-be-marketed formulation of bexagliflozin and/or did not enroll subjects with T2DM. Relevant phase 1 trials to this safety review, including C-428 conducted to assess the impact of bexagliflozin on cardiac repolarization, are discussed where relevant.
L415: ## 7.4.2. Categorization of Adverse Events
L416: This section summarizes relevant information and methods utilized for the definition, categorization, assessment, and adjudication of safety data.
L417: - **Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities (MedDRA) coding and mapping:** All adverse events were coded according to MedDRA using the current version at the time of trial reporting. For the purposes of the integrated safety analysis, the Applicant mapped adverse events (AEs) from all trials to MedDRA version 22.0. The CoreDF Report was utilized to ensure adequate mapping of verbatim terms to preferred terms (PTs).
- **AE:** The Applicant defined an AE as any untoward medical occurrence in a subject administered a pharmaceutical product that does not necessarily have a causal relationship with the treatment. An AE could therefore be any unfavorable and unintended sign (including an abnormal laboratory finding), symptom, or disease temporally associated with the use of a medicinal product, whether or not it is considered related to the medicinal product use.
- **Serious adverse event (SAE):** A serious AE was defined as any untoward medical occurrence that at any dose resulted in the following: death, a life-threatening experience, in-patient hospitalization, or prolongation of existing hospitalization, persistent or significant disability/incapacity, or a congenital anomaly. Important medical events would also be considered an SAE when (based on appropriate medical judgement) the event may jeopardize the subject and may require medical or surgical intervention to prevent one of the outcomes listed in the definition of SAE.
- **Safety population and treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs):** The safety population was defined as all randomized subjects who received at least one dose of investigational product. A TEAE was defined as an AE that begins after the first dose date or an existing AE that worsens after the first dose date. The Applicant's TEAE definition was deemed adequate, and only TEAEs were considered in this review.2
- **MACE and fatal events:** An independent clinical endpoint committee (CEC), based out of the Clinical Endpoint Center at Brigham and Women's Hospital (Boston, MA),
L418: 2 The Applicant's ISS SAP defines a TEAE as an event occurring within 28 days of the last dose taken; however, a 28-day window was not applied in the Applicant's analysis. The Applicant confirmed (SD0018) that this was an error in their ISS SAP, and that their analysis did not utilize a 28-day window.
L419: performed blinded adjudication of CV events that contributed to the MACE+ meta-analysis. The CEC members included medical experts in the field of cardiovascular disease. The CEC received and reviewed the following events for adjudication: all deaths, suspected nonfatal myocardial infarction (MI), suspected hospitalization for unstable angina, suspected transient ischemic attack and stroke, suspected hospitalization for heart failure, and coronary revascularization procedures. The CEC also reviewed a listing of SAEs on a monthly basis to identify MACE events potentially not identified/reported by the investigator. The CEC's manual of operations (i.e., adjudication charter) was reviewed and deemed adequate to classify events appropriately, consistently, and in an unbiased manner. Deaths were classified as CV death, non-CV death, or death of unknown cause. CV deaths were subclassified as either fatal MI, pump failure, sudden death, presumed sudden death, presumed CV death, fatal stroke, fatal pulmonary embolism (PE), death related to CV procedure, or other CV death. There was no classification or judgement by adjudicators on the investigator-reported PT for any event type.
L420: - **Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA):** DKA events were adjudicated by an endocrinologist according to the Applicant's DKA adjudication charter. See Section 17.3.6 for additional information on the DKA monitoring plan and case definitions used in the clinical program.
L421: ## 7.4.3. Data Querying
L422: Several methods to query the data were employed in this safety review, including the use of FDA Medical Queries (FMQs), custom MedDRA queries (CMQs) developed by the Applicant, and grouped queries (GQs) developed by the clinical reviewer. All FMQ analyses utilized the "narrow" queries from FMQ release Version 2.0. Additional information on the PTs considered for each GQ is provided in the caption of the associated table.
L423: ## 7.5. Adequacy of Clinical Safety Database
L424: ## 7.5.1. Exposure

There were 1,294 subjects exposed to bexagliflozin for \ge 1 year, and 791 patients exposed for \ge 2 years, with longer duration exposure primarily occurring in C-476. Given that all trials included a follow-up period, on-trial exposure was longer, with 3,824 patient-years of on-trial exposure in the broad pool. See Section 7.5.3 for a discussion on how the total exposure met current divisional guidance recommendations.

L436: ## 7.5.2. Characteristics of the Safety Population
L437: Baseline characteristics of subjects from trials that comprise the placebo-controlled pool, C-448, and C-476, are presented in Table 23. The placebo-controlled pool consisted of 672 subjects with T2DM. The mean age of the population was 56 years and 5% were older than 75 years of age.
L438: Fifty-seven percent (57%) of the population was male and 45% were Caucasian, 38% were Asian, and 15% were Black or African American. Baseline renal function was normal or mildly impaired in 98% of subjects and moderately impaired in 2% of subjects (mean eGFR of 92.2 mL/min/1.73 m2). Baseline characteristics of active-controlled trials C-423 and C-480 were generally similar to the placebo-controlled pool (data not shown).
L439: C-448 (renal impairment trial) and C-476 (increased CV risk trial) enrolled distinct populations, with subjects in these trials being generally older, having a longer duration of diabetes, and worse renal function as compared to subjects in the placebo-controlled pool and active-controlled trials (Table 23). For example, the mean age of subjects enrolled in C-448 and C-476 was 64 and 69 years old, respectively, compared to a mean of 56 years in the placebo-controlled pool. Over half of subjects in C-476 and C-448 used insulin as a part of their diabetes management at baseline, indicating more advanced disease, as compared to no subject using insulin at baseline in the placebo-controlled pool.

L446: ## 7.5.3. Exposure per FDA's Draft Guidance Recommendations
L447: The extent to which the clinical program meets the recommendations set forth in the draft guidance document *Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus: Evaluating the Safety of New Drugs for Improving*
L448: *Glycemic Control Guidance for Industry* (March 2020) is shown in Table 24 and discussed below:
L449: **Total Exposure and Exposure Duration:** There were 3,482 patient-years of on-treatment exposure and 3,824 patient-years of on-trial exposure in the broad pool. On-trial exposure was longer due to follow-up periods in each trial (AEs that occurred during the follow-up period were considered treatment-emergent and thus considered in this safety review). Therefore, the guidance recommendation to have at least 4,000 patient-years of exposure was not met. In addition, while the program did not meet the guidance recommendations for 1-year exposure duration, it exceeded the recommendations for 2-year exposure durations.
L450: **Older adults:** The clinical program exceeded the recommendation to evaluate at least 600 subjects &gt;65 years of age.
L451: **Established CV Disease:** The clinical program exceeded the recommendation to evaluate at least 600 subjects with established CV disease. In C-476, there were 703 subjects assigned to bexagliflozin in group 1 (consisting of subjects with a history of atherosclerotic vascular disease) and 166 patients assigned to bexagliflozin in group 2 (consisting of subjects with a history New York Heart Association [NYHA] class II/III HF), for a total of 869 subjects with established CV disease exposed to bexagliflozin. As exposure in C-476 exceeded the guidance recommendation, the Applicant did not undertake a program-wide evaluation of exposure for this category.
L452: **Renal Impairment:** The clinical program did not meet the recommendation to evaluate at least 500 subjects with stage 3/4 CKD exposed to drug. There were 375 subjects in C-448 and C-476 with baseline eGFR &lt;60 mL/min/1.73 m^2 exposed to bexagliflozin (Table 11). While all other trials excluded subjects with eGFR &lt;60 mL/min/1.73 m^2, a small number of subjects in these trials were enrolled with baseline eGFR &lt;60 mL/min/1.73 m^2 due to variability in measurements between screening and baseline. Given that baseline eGFR was variable between screening and baseline, these subjects were not considered in the evaluation of exposure for this population.
L453: With the new guidance, the Division has moved away “from a narrow focus on evaluating cardiovascular safety” and toward an approach that would yield a robust evaluation for a broad range of safety concerns (Chong et al. 2020). In lieu of a requisite minimum number of events and a degree of risk to be excluded, adequate enrollment of a broad population with enough exposure to generate a robust safety database was sought. The bexagliflozin clinical program was completed prior to issuance of the draft guidance in March 2020. Furthermore, at the time the clinical program was under development, a prior draft guidance document (Guidance for Industry: Diabetes Mellitus – Evaluating Cardiovascular Risk in New Antidiabetic Therapies to Treat Type 2 Diabetes dated December 2008; now withdrawn (December 2008)) was in effect, and the Applicant’s clinical program was completed in accordance with the recommendations in the 2008 guidance. Despite not meeting all criteria recommended in the 2020 draft guidance for each category, the total exposure and exposure durations observed in the clinical program for bexagliflozin are adequate given that 1) they are sufficient to characterize commonly occurring AEs, 2) the additional exposure needed to meet the guidance recommendations is not of sufficient quantity such that it is likely to characterize safety signals that may occur at a low frequency, and 3) the safety profile of SGLT2 inhibitors is generally well established, and the safety review supports a similar safety profile to other SGLT2 inhibitor products. On balance, given that the program enrolled higher numbers for older adults and those with established CV
L454: disease (see below) and exceeded the recommended number of patients with exposure greater than 2 years, the total exposure was deemed adequate.
L455: The amount of exposure in subjects with renal impairment is considered adequate as bexagliflozin will not be recommended for use in patients with eGFR &lt;30 mL/min/1.73 m^2. In addition, the amount of exposure in C-448 is generally comparable to renal impairment trials that have been used to inform the safety and efficacy of other SGLT2 inhibitors in this patient population (e.g., dapagliflozin/DERIVE N=160 exposed subjects, empagliflozin/1245.36 N=188 exposed subjects, canagliflozin/DIA3004 N=179 exposed subjects).

L464: ## 7.6. Safety Findings and Concerns Based on Review of Clinical Safety Database
L465: ## 7.6.1. Safety Findings and Concerns
L466: ## 7.6.1.1. Overall Treatment-Emergent Adverse Event Summary
L467: There were no clinically meaningful imbalances in the overall incidence of subjects experiencing AEs in the placebo-controlled pool, C-476, or C-448 (Table 25), nor in active-controlled trials (data not shown). While some event categories shown in Table 25 demonstrated imbalances unfavorable to bexagliflozin (e.g., AEs leading to discontinuation in the placebo-controlled pool, SAEs in Trial C-448), limited data in these categories impedes interpretability. No meaningful imbalances were observed for AEs leading to discontinuation, AEs leading to drug interruption, or SAEs in C-476, which had the most data to support meaningful conclusions. Overall, there do not appear to be concerning trends.

L473: ## 7.6.1.2. Deaths
L474: There were 69 deaths across all phase 2b/3 trials (broad pool). The majority of deaths in the bexagliflozin clinical program occurred in C-476 (65 deaths), which enrolled patients with either established cardiovascular disease or multiple risk factors for cardiovascular morbidity (Table 26 and Table 27). Deaths were limited in other phase 2/3 trials, with no deaths occurring in C-419, C-448, C-449, or C-603. Single events of fatal cardiac arrest and sigmoid adenocarcinoma occurred in the bexagliflozin groups of C-418 and C-423, respectively, and events of fatal cardiomyopathy and small cell undifferentiated lung carcinoma occurred in the placebo and glimepiride groups of C-450 and C-480, respectively.
L475: In C-476 there were proportionally fewer deaths in the bexagliflozin group (3.4%) as compared to the placebo group (4.6%) (Table 26). As expected, the majority of deaths were related to cardiac events. As discussed in Section 7.4.2, an independent CEC reviewed all deaths that occurred in the clinical program regardless of whether they were indicated as CV-related or not by the investigator, and classified the event as either a CV death, non-CV death, or death of unknown cause. Deaths of unknown cause were considered CV deaths for the purpose of the MACE analysis and are presented in accordance with this practice in Table 26. In line with conclusions from the MACE+ meta-analysis, there were proportionally fewer adjudicated CV deaths in the bexagliflozin group (26 events, 2.3%) as compared to the placebo group (18 events, 3.2%). In addition, there were no meaningful imbalances in subcategories of CV death (e.g., sudden deaths, deaths of unknown cause, pump failure, etc.); although events in each category were limited.
L476: An imbalance unfavorable to bexagliflozin in the PT of “cardiac arrest” was observed (1.0% versus 0.2% in the bexagliflozin and placebo groups, respectively), as shown in Table 26. Narratives for the cardiac arrest events were reviewed and no apparent trend was observed, although some events contained incomplete information limiting interpretability. The majority of adjudicated CV deaths were classified as sudden deaths in both treatment groups, with more
L477: sudden deaths occurring in the placebo group (Table 26). The CEC did not comment on the PT associated with the event, and several events with the PT of “cardiac arrest” were adjudicated not to be CV related by the CEC. Overall, the reason for the noted imbalance in investigator-assigned PT is unclear; however, the overall favorable drug effect on CV death in C-476 and the MACE+ meta-analysis is reassuring.
L478: There were proportionally fewer deaths that were adjudicated to be non-CV deaths in the bexagliflozin group (13 events (1.1%)) versus the placebo groups (8 events (1.4%)) (Table 26). There were also no meaningful imbalances in any PTs for noncardiac deaths or concerning trends at the system organ class (SOC) level (Table 27), although data were limited.
L479: Lastly, to assess deaths that may have occurred after subjects were lost to follow-up or withdrew consent, the Applicant attempted to determine the vital status (i.e., living or deceased) for all subjects randomized in C-476. Vital status was obtained for all but four subjects. Results from this analysis show that there were 82 deaths in C-476, 48 (4.2%) occurring in subjects randomized to receive bexagliflozin and 34 (6.0%) occurring in subjects randomized to receive placebo.
L480: Overall, death data from the bexagliflozin clinical program indicate trends favorable to bexagliflozin; however, it is acknowledged that death events, and particularly noncardiac death events, were limited.

L492: ## 7.6.1.3. Serious Adverse Events
L493: The incidence of SAEs was similar between treatment arms in the placebo-controlled pool, occurring in six (1.7%) and five (1.6%) subjects in the bexagliflozin and placebo groups, respectively (Table 25). No events by PT occurred in more than one subject and there were no apparent trends between treatment groups by SOC (data not shown). Notable SAEs in bexagliflozin-exposed subjects in this pool include single events of urinary tract infection (UTI) and DKA, which are discussed in additional detail in Sections 17.3.6 and 17.3.9.
L494: Similarly, limited SAE data were obtained in C-448 and active-controlled trials (C-423, C-480), with no meaningful imbalances in the incidence of SAEs or events by SOC between treatment groups (data not shown). Significant SAEs in bexagliflozin-exposed subjects in these trials include single events of pyelonephritis and phimosis with subsequent radial circumcision in C-480 and a single event of gangrene in C-423. The event of gangrene occurred on Day 16 subsequent to a trauma event (subject stepping on a nail), and therefore the event may not be related to bexagliflozin use.
L495: Of note, UTI, including serious events of urosepsis/pyelonephritis, DKA, and genital mycotic infection (GMI) are considered class effects proposed for labeling. SAE data from these trials therefore do not raise new safety concerns.
L496: Most SAEs were observed in C-476. In this trial, there was a lower incidence of SAEs in the bexagliflozin group compared to the placebo group (33% versus 37%, respectively) (Table 25). SAEs reported in at least two subjects in the bexagliflozin group with risk difference (RD) \ge 0.1 are shown in Table 28. In line with the enrolled patient population, various cardiac SAEs were observed. Imbalances unfavorable to drug were observed for various PTs including coronary artery disease, cardiac failure, and myocardial ischemia.
L497: As this trial enrolled patients with increased CV risk, cardiac events are expected in the enrolled population and some imbalances in individual PTs due to chance may be expected. The MACE+ meta-analysis did not identify a risk for MACE with bexagliflozin and provided reassuring evidence of cardiac safety.
L498: Several imbalances unfavorable to bexagliflozin involving infection-related events were observed in C-476, including sepsis/septic shock, osteomyelitis, localized infection, and cellulitis. These are discussed individually below.
L499: ## Sepsis/Septic Shock
L500: Twelve subjects (1.1%) in the bexagliflozin group and one subject (0.2%) in the placebo group had an SAE of sepsis and/or septic shock in C-476. The imbalance persisted upon evaluation of all events (i.e., SAEs and nonserious AEs), with 14 (1.2%) and 2 (0.4%) subjects experiencing an event of sepsis/septic shock in the bexagliflozin and placebo groups, respectively. Four subjects in the bexagliflozin group with serious events of sepsis died during the trial. Subject 476-(b)(6) died during hospitalization for infective endocarditis with the primary causes of death listed on the death certificate attributed to acute respiratory failure, septic shock, and endocarditis. Subject 476-(b)(6) died after hospitalization for sepsis, gangrene, and severe end-stage peripheral artery disease (PAD). The subject refused below-the-knee (BTK) amputation, and the reported cause of death was gangrene. Subject 476-(b)(6) died of acute respiratory failure in the setting of metabolic acidosis secondary to septic shock that was
L501: presumed to have been caused by a nonhealing sacral ulcer. Subject 476-(b) (6) was hospitalized with an event of sepsis on Day 495 and later died on Day 518 due to acute left ventricular failure. Of the remaining nonfatal SAEs, three events in the bexagliflozin group and the single sepsis event in the placebo group appeared secondary to UTI. Urosepsis will be included as a Warning and Precaution in the labeling.
L502: The potential drug-relatedness of the sepsis events is unclear. While some events appeared to be urosepsis events, which could be drug-related, other sepsis events appeared associated with endocarditis, pneumonia, appendicitis, and cellulitis events. In cases where death occurred, there were multiple contributing factors that lead to the event of death. Laboratory parameter assessments in C-476 did not indicate clinically meaningful changes in relevant hematology parameters (e.g., decreases in WBCs with bexagliflozin treatment) between treatment groups, nor were there significant imbalances in the SOC for “Infections and Infestations” (data not shown). As shown in Table 29, there was no significant imbalance between groups in serious bacterial infections as identified by the “Bacterial Infections” FMQ (4.1% versus 3.9% in the bexagliflozin and placebo groups, respectively). Associations between drug exposure and increased risk of sepsis have not been characterized with approved SGLT2 inhibitors. Despite unclear drug relatedness, labeling is recommended to inform providers on the potential increased risk of sepsis events with bexagliflozin treatment as they are serious and potentially life-threatening. Based on the available information, standard postmarket surveillance appears reasonable to monitor the risk of serious sepsis events. Postmarketing reports related to serious infections should be monitored.
L503: ## Osteomyelitis
L504: Serious osteomyelitis events occurred in 10 (0.9%) subjects in the bexagliflozin group versus 1 (0.2%) subject in the placebo group. The imbalance persisted when evaluating events of all severity, with 12 (1.1%) and 3 (0.5%) subjects in the bexagliflozin and placebo groups experiencing an event of osteomyelitis, respectively. Seven subjects (six in the bexagliflozin group and one in the placebo group) underwent amputations prompted, at least in part, by osteomyelitis. See Section 7.7.1 for additional discussion regarding increased risk of amputation with bexagliflozin exposure, which is proposed for labeling.
L505: ## Localized Infection
L506: Serious events of localized infection occurred in five subjects assigned to the bexagliflozin group as compared to none in the placebo group. This imbalance persisted when evaluating events of all severity (12 (1.1%) and 2 (0.4%) subjects with an event in the bexagliflozin and placebo groups, respectively). Narrative review of the serious events revealed that four of the five subjects had toe/foot infections, of which one subject had a subsequent amputation event.
L507: ## Cellulitis
L508: Serious events of cellulitis occurred in nine (0.8%) and two (0.4%) subject in the bexagliflozin and placebo groups, respectively. However, an imbalance in these events was not observed when assessing cellulitis events of all severity, with 34 (3.0%) and 16 (2.8%) of subjects in the bexagliflozin and placebo groups having an event. Five of the nine subjects with a cellulitis event had concurrent osteomyelitis and/or sepsis events. Eight of the nine serious cellulitis events were located on a lower limb.
L509: Amputation is a serious and clinically meaningful consequence of osteomyelitis and skin infections, including cellulitis. As discussed in Section 7.7.1, the labeling for bexagliflozin should advise prescribers to consider risk factors that may increase a patient's risk of amputation before initiating treatment and monitor for infections or ulcers of the lower limbs and discontinue treatment should these events occur. Labeling that describes predisposing factors (e.g., osteomyelitis, diabetic foot ulcers, etc.) is also recommended.

L524: ## 7.6.1.4. Dropouts and/or Discontinuations Due to Adverse Events
L525: Data to characterize AEs leading to discontinuation were limited in all trials except C-476. Discontinuations due to AEs in the placebo-controlled pool are shown in Table 30 and include isolated events of frequent urination (polyurea, pollakiuria), DKA, and potential UTI (dysuria). In active-controlled Trials C-480 and C-423, there was a higher incidence of GMI events leading to discontinuation of treatment in the bexagliflozin group as compared to the active comparator groups (data not shown).

The data presented herein supports that commonly occurring AEs may lead to treatment discontinuation. Information regarding these important tolerability related events will be included in labeling.

L539: ## 7.6.1.5. Treatment-Emergent Adverse Events
L540: AEs reported in ≥2% of subjects treated with bexagliflozin and greater than placebo in the placebo-controlled pool are shown in Table 32 and include female GMI, increased urination,
L541: vaginal pruritus, UTI, thirst, hypoglycemia, and male GMI. Grouped queries (GQs) were utilized to identify events that represented a similar medical concept (e.g., terms of polyuria, pollakiuria, micturition urgency, and nocturia were grouped for increased urination events). The events resultant from this analysis are considered class effects that are described in the labeling of currently marketed SGLT2 inhibitor products. Aside from the events utilized in the GQ analysis shown in Table 32, there were no other PTs that occurred in \ge 2\% of subjects and more frequently with drug than placebo.

L549: FMQs were used to investigate potential safety signals in the placebo-controlled pool (Table 33). Similar to the GQ analysis presented above, FMQs for fungal infection, renal and urinary tract infection, and hypoglycemia demonstrated RDs &gt;0.5\%. The FMQ for “Pruritus” contained both events of genital pruritus identified in the above noted grouped queries, as well as additional nonspecific/generalized pruritus events. FMQs for hepatic injury, study abuse potential, and palpitations also demonstrated a risk difference of 0.5; however, the low number of events limits
L550: interpretability. Events of rash and hepatic injury are further discussed in Sections 17.3.4 and 17.3.5, respectively.
L551: There was a higher incidence in the FMQ for “Tendinopathy” with exposure to drug (1.3% versus 0% of subjects in the bexagliflozin and placebo groups, respectively). PTs included tenosynovitis and trigger finger, and a review of the verbatim terms for the tenosynovitis events indicated events generally involved fingers. Imbalances unfavorable to drug in tenosynovitis events were also observed in FMQ analyses completed with C-448 (3 (1.9%) and 1 (0.6%) subject in the bexagliflozin and placebo groups, respectively), and C-476 (35 (3.1%) and 13 (2.3%) subjects in the bexagliflozin and placebo groups, respectively; Table 34). These events were generally not serious, nor did they lead to treatment discontinuation. In C-476, the majority of events identified by the FMQ in both treatment groups were events of rotator cuff syndrome (1.0% versus 0.9%, bexagliflozin versus placebo), tendonitis (0.8% v 0.5%, bexagliflozin versus placebo), and trigger finger (0.6% versus 0.2%, bexagliflozin versus placebo) (Table 34). Events of tendon rupture were balanced between treatment groups (0.2% in each treatment group).
L552: The clinical meaningfulness of the imbalance in events captured by the tendinopathy FMQ is unclear. Drug-induced tendinitis and tendon rupture is associated with quinolones, statins, aromatase inhibitors, and glucocorticoids, but has not been previously characterized with SGLT2 inhibitors (Kirchgesner et al. 2014; Knobloch 2016; Bolon 2017). Drug-induced tendinitis typically affects lower limb tendons, most commonly the Achilles tendon. The pathophysiology of drug-induced tendinopathy is incompletely understood but proposed mechanisms include apoptosis and structural disintegration of tenoblasts and tenocytes in the absence of inflammation. Time to onset varies from days to years and any tendon can be affected. The anatomical location of tendinopathy events in the clinical program is unclear as this information was not systematically collected; however, where information exists, the events appear to occur in the upper extremities (i.e., rotator cuff, trigger finger, etc.). Overall, the clinical meaningfulness of this imbalance in unclear and events were not generally serious or severe. Based on these considerations, specific product labeling is not warranted.

L561: To further investigate for important imbalances in AEs, additional analyses were completed with C-476. **Table 35** shows the results from an FMQ analysis of FMQs with RD \ge 0.5 and **Table 36** shows AEs by PT with an RD \ge 0.5. In addition, no differences in mean platelet count over time were observed in the placebo-controlled pool (Section 17.4, Figure 76), nor are changes in platelet count labeled for other approved SGLT2 inhibitor products.

L572: Lastly, an analysis utilizing Applicant-derived custom MedDRA query (CMQs) for the evaluation of AESIs was performed for C-476 (Table 37). For example, the FMQ for “Fungal Infection” is not specific to genital infections. In addition, the “Fungal Infection” FMQ does not contain all PTs that are typically assessed in SGLT2 inhibitor programs (e.g., PTs for phimosis and balanoposthitis events are not included in the query). To provide another example, the “Volume Depletion” FMQ does not include events that have previously been utilized to identify potential volume depletion events such as events of dizziness and hypotension, which have dedicated FMQs. Therefore, the Applicant’s CMQs are informative as they are more tailored to SGLT2 inhibitor programs. CMQs were reviewed and they appeared appropriate to identify events for each AESI category. Labeling of results from Applicant-derived CMQs appears appropriate when informative.

L579: ## 7.6.1.6. Laboratory Findings
L580: The following changes in laboratory parameters are proposed for labeling: increases in serum creatinine and decreases in eGFR, increases in hemoglobin/hematocrit, and increase in low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C). See Section 17.4 for a detailed review of laboratory findings.
L581: ## 7.7. Key Review Issues Relevant to Evaluation of Risk
L582: ## 7.7.1. Increased Risk of Nontraumatic Amputation With Bexagliflozin Treatment
L583: ## Issue
L584: An increased incidence of nontraumatic amputation was identified in the bexagliflozin group compared to the placebo group in C-476.
L585: ## Background
L586: Lower limb amputation is a recognized complication of diabetes mellitus. An excess risk of lower limb amputation beyond background risk has been previously identified with canagliflozin and ertugliflozin, but not dapagliflozin and empagliflozin (Janssen 2020; AstraZeneca 2021; Merck 2021; Ingelheim 2022). The risk of amputation with SGLT2 inhibitor treatment has been assessed in the postmarketing CVOTs for SGLT2 inhibitors, enrolling patients with T2DM and increased CV risk, which were conducted to rule out 30% excess CV risk per the 2008 diabetes CV safety guidance (now withdrawn) (December 2008). In the CANVAS Program, which was
L587: comprised of two nearly identically designed trials (CANVAS and CANVAS-R), an increased risk of lower limb amputations associated with canagliflozin use versus placebo was observed in CANVAS (5.9 versus 2.8 events per 1,000 patient-years) and CANVAS-R (7.5 versus 4.2 events per 1,000 patient-years) (Janssen 2020). Amputations of the toe and midfoot (99 out of 140 patients with amputations receiving canagliflozin in the two trials) were the most frequent; however, amputations involving the leg, below and above the knee, were also observed (41 out of 140 patients with amputations receiving canagliflozin in the two trials). Some patients had multiple amputations, some involving both lower limbs. Lower limb infections, gangrene, and diabetic foot ulcers were the most common precipitating medical events leading to the need for an amputation. The risk of amputation was highest in patients with a baseline history of prior amputation, peripheral vascular disease, and neuropathy. Increased risk of amputation was also observed in a CVOT conducted with ertugliflozin (VERTIS CV), where the occurrence of nontraumatic lower limb amputation was 4.7, 5.7, and 6.0 events per 1,000 patient-years in the placebo, ertugliflozin 5 mg, and ertugliflozin 15 mg treatment arms, respectively (Merck 2021). Similar to the CANVAS Program, amputations of the toe and midfoot were most frequent (81 out of 109 patients) with the most common precipitating events being infection, gangrene, and diabetic foot ulcers.
L588: An underlying mechanism for an increased risk of lower limb amputation has not been clearly identified. It has been hypothesized that volume depletion with SGLT2 inhibitors may lead to hypoperfusion of extremities in patients at risk for an amputation event, which can slow wound healing, make any existing infection become irreparable, and cause tissue damage or necrosis. However, it is unclear how this hypothesis can support a different degree of risk of amputation among SGLT2 inhibitors because volume depletion events can occur with all SGLT2 inhibitors. Overall, given conflicting data from several large, postmarketing clinical programs, it is unclear at this time whether SGLT2 inhibitor treatment increases amputation risk.
L589: ## Assessment
L590: All nontraumatic amputations that occurred in the bexagliflozin clinical development program were observed in C-476 (one traumatic amputation event occurred in C-448). The potential association with SGLT2 inhibitor treatment and amputation risk became known while the clinical development program, including C-476, was ongoing. Amputation and revascularization procedures were included as AESIs via protocol amendment (protocol Version 8, dated October 28, 2016). In addition, a dedicated case report form (CRF) was introduced in protocol Version 8 to capture additional information regarding amputation and revascularization events including the anatomical location of amputation and the condition leading to the amputation. Eighty-two percent of total study follow-up time occurred under a consent or reconsent to protocol Version 8.
L591: Despite inclusion of a dedicated CRF and specification of amputation as an AESI in protocol Version 8, the Applicant states that failures to record procedures occurred that were not detected until after database lock (integrated summary of safety [ISS], page 165). While the reason for underreporting of these procedures is unclear, the Applicant notes that investigators may have considered amputation events planned treatments/responses to medical conditions as opposed to AEs. To address this, the Applicant performed a review of CRF and SAE narratives for unreported procedures. The information submitted by the Applicant in the ADaM adverse events
L592: analysis (ADAE) and ADaM procedures analysis (ADPR) datasets incorporates their thorough review of the available safety data.
L593: Given that underreporting of amputation events was a concern in this program, exploratory analyses were conducted to identify potentially missed amputation events. A list3 of amputation-related PTs and PTs for events that may precede an amputation event was generated. A search of the terms was conducted in the ADAE and ADPR datasets to identify potential missed amputations. A review of the findings of this search indicated that all additional events identified through this process were not amputation events. Therefore, the Applicant's search of procedures and AEs appears to have adequately captured amputation events in C-476.
L594: Time-to-event data were derived for time-to-first nontraumatic amputation based on the procedure and AE datasets. Post hoc analyses were conducted using the derived data. The results of an on-study analysis are presented in Table 38, while the results of an on-treatment +14-day analysis are presented in Table 39. Both analyses used a Cox proportional hazards model with treatment as the only fixed effect. Estimated 95% confidence intervals for the hazard ratios for both analyses include the null value 1. However, the time-to-event analyses showed a numerical increase in the incidence of amputations associated with bexagliflozin and the point estimates of the hazard ratios (HRs) are both greater than 1.6 (on-study: 1.64; on-treatment: 1.71).

L619: As noted above, the dedicated CRF was also designed to capture information on revascularization procedures. There was a minor imbalance unfavorable to bexagliflozin in the number of revascularization procedures for PAD (2.5% and 2.1% of subjects having a procedure in the bexagliflozin and placebo groups, respectively). Other revascularization procedures (e.g., coronary artery bypass grafting [CABG], percutaneous coronary intervention [PCI], etc.) are discussed in additional detail in Section 17.3.14.
L620: ## Conclusion
L621: As detailed above, data from C-476 indicated an increased risk of amputation with bexagliflozin treatment as compared to placebo (HR: 1.64 (0.70, 3.82)). Although the findings above on amputations do not necessarily raise new concerns about the risk of amputation due to treatment with SGLT2 inhibitors, the concern about the potential for excess risk of amputations on the bexagliflozin arm has not been alleviated, especially given the existing concern about increased risk of amputations for this class of drug. Labeling should state that before initiating treatment with bexagliflozin, providers should consider factors that may increase the risk of amputation, such as a history of prior amputation, peripheral vascular disease, neuropathy, and diabetic foot ulcers. In addition, labeling will advise providers to monitor patients receiving bexagliflozin for infection, new pain or tenderness, sores or ulcers involving the lower limbs, and discontinue treatment if these complications occur. Labeling is appropriate to inform providers about increased risk of amputation associated with bexagliflozin treatment.
L622: ## Dissent
L623: Not applicable.
L624: ## 7.7.2. Safety of Bexagliflozin in Subjects With Moderate Renal Impairment
L625: ## Issue
L626: The safety of bexagliflozin in patients with stage 3 CKD.
L627: ## Background
L628: The efficacy of bexagliflozin in subjects with moderate renal impairment was a key efficacy review issue. As detailed in Section 6.3.1, the efficacy of bexagliflozin in subjects with stage 3 CKD is considered acceptable for approval in the population in the absence of safety findings that could impact the overall benefit-risk assessment in this population.
L629: ## Assessment
L630: ## Approach to Review
L631: This key risk review issue was assessed using safety data from the dedicated renal impairment trial (C-448) in addition to supportive information from the subpopulation of subjects with renal impairment in C-476. The subpopulation assessed from C-476 was based on baseline eGFR values (i.e., having a baseline eGFR &lt;60 mL/min/1.73 m^2). Protocol synopses for these trials are provided in Section 15 and key trial design features, including inclusion/exclusion criteria, are presented in Section 6.2. In C-476, treatment was stratified by eGFR category (eGFR &lt;60 or \ge 60 mL/min/1.73 m^2), and approximately 20% of subjects in each treatment arm had eGFR &lt;60 mL/min/1.73 m^2. Baseline demographics for C-448 and C-476 are presented in Table 11.
L632: ## Overview of AEs
L633: The frequency of AEs between treatment arms in C-448 were generally balanced, with 69.4% and 67.7% of subjects experiencing at least one AE in the bexagliflozin and placebo groups, respectively (Table 42). Events by severity were also generally balanced between treatment arms. There were few events of AEs leading to permanent discontinuation or dose interruption of the study drug, limiting interpretability of the data. No deaths occurred in this trial.

L643: ## SAEs and Discontinuations

L645: group experienced two events of severe hypoglycemia. A Warnings and Precautions statement is proposed for the labeling regarding the risk of hypoglycemia when bexagliflozin is used in combination with insulin or an insulin secretagogue.

L666: ## **Commonly Occurring AEs**
L667: AEs reported in \ge 2\% of subjects treated with bexagliflozin and greater than placebo in C-448 are shown in Table 48. GQs were utilized to group PTs of similar medical concept. Commonly occurring AEs were generally similar in C-448 as compared to the placebo-controlled pool, with more subjects experiencing events of female GMI, increased urination, UTI, and thirst in the bexagliflozin group compared to the placebo group. Approximately 25% of subjects in this trial experienced at least one hypoglycemia event, which is likely attributable to over 50% of subjects using insulin at baseline in this trial (as compared to no subjects using baseline insulin in the placebo-controlled pool; Table 11). Other AEs reported in \ge 2\% of subjects treated with bexagliflozin and greater than placebo in C-448 that were not observed in the placebo-controlled pool include AKI, blood creatinine increased, bronchitis, hypertension, hypotension, sinusitis, back pain, fall, and arthralgia. Higher incidence of these events may be, at least in part, due to differing patient populations between C-448 and the placebo-controlled pool (e.g., an older patient population with more comorbidities, more advanced disease, and poorer renal function in C-448 as compared to the placebo-controlled pool).

L678: ## **Significant AEs**
L679: To investigate potential safety signals in C-448, a FMQ analysis was performed, and queries occurring at an RD &gt; 0\% are shown in Table 49. As anticipated, “Renal and Urinary Tract Infection” and “Fungal Infection” queries had a higher incidence with drug than placebo, reflecting higher rates of UTI and GMI with bexagliflozin treatment. A higher incidence of hypertension (as a reported AE) was observed in the bexagliflozin group (3.2%) compared to the
L680: placebo (0%) group. Analysis of mean changes in SBP demonstrated a mean decrease in SBP over time, with a mean decrease of 8 mm Hg versus 4 mm Hg in the bexagliflozin and placebo groups at Week 24, respectively. There were also more events of hypotension in the bexagliflozin group (3.8%) versus the placebo group (3.2%). The meaningfulness of these findings is unclear, although it is noteworthy that events were not serious and did not lead to treatment discontinuation. Moreover, adverse event reporting for hypotension/hypertension is subjective and investigator dependent, limiting interpretation of reported events. In addition, objective systolic and diastolic blood pressure measurements revealed slight decreases in mean values in the placebo-controlled pool (see Section 17.5, Figure 80).
L681: An imbalance unfavorable to drug occurred for “Dizziness” (4.5% versus 1.3%). While the events of dizziness are nonspecific, these events could potentially indicate mild volume depletion events. There was no imbalance in fracture events as identified by FMQ, with three patients experiencing a nonserious fracture event in each treatment group, although the incidence of falls was slightly higher in the bexagliflozin group (3.2%) compared to the placebo group (1.9%).
L682: Regarding AKI events, the protocol-specified definitions specified changes of serum creatinine from baseline levels as opposed to acute serum creatinine changes as recommended in the Kidney Disease Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) Guidelines (Khwaja 2012). It is possible that AKI events may be overreported in this trial, as decreases in renal function over time are expected in this patient population; however, this would not be expected to bias the data (i.e., potential AKI overreporting should occur equally in both treatment arms). As shown in Table 49, there was no meaningful imbalance in AKI events in C-448.
L683: Approved SGLT2 inhibitors report volume depletion events in subjects with renal impairment in Section 6 of the labeling, with events reported including events dehydration, dizziness postural, presyncope, syncope, hypotension, and orthostatic hypotension. The FMQ analysis completed in this review differs from previous SGLT2 inhibitor reviews. For example, a single event of “dehydration” was captured by the “Volume Depletion” FMQ, and events considered potential volume depletion events in other SGLT2 inhibitor reviews (e.g., hypotension, dizziness, syncope) were not identified by this query. For the purposes of Section 6 of the labeling, the FMQs for “Volume Depletion,” “Syncope,” “Hypotension,” and “Dizziness” are pooled to characterize potential volume depletion events. There were 14 (8.9%) and 6 (3.9%) subjects having at least one event of volume depletion as assessed by the noted queries in the bexagliflozin and placebo groups, respectively.

L690: An FMQ analysis of the subpopulation of subjects with baseline eGFR &lt;60 mL/min/1.73 m2 in C-476 was performed, and FMQs with a RD ≥0.5 are shown are Table 50. An imbalance in the “Lipid Disorder” FMQ was observed. PTs that occurred in the bexagliflozin group identified by the FMQ included the following: dyslipidemia, hypertriglyceridemia, hyperlipidemia, blood cholesterol increased, low density lipoprotein increased, blood triglyceride increased, and hypercholesterolemia. As discussed in Section 17.4, SGLT2 inhibitor treatment is associated with modest increases in LDL-C which may, at least in part, support the results observed here. Important clinical consequences of elevated lipid parameters include increased risk of MACE. As presented in Section 17.1, the subgroup analysis by renal function group did not show an increased risk for MACE+ events in subjects with baseline eGFR &lt;60 mL/min/1.73 m2 (HR: 0.56 (0.29, 1.1)) as compared to subjects with baseline eGFR &gt;60 mL/min/1.73 m2 (HR: 0.88 (0.61, 1.26)). Changes in lipid parameters from laboratory assessments in subjects with renal impairment are further discussed in the next section.

L695: ## **Laboratory Parameters**
L696: Changes in laboratory parameters over time in C-448 were generally in line with data observed in other trials, including modest mean increases in serum magnesium, serum phosphate, hemoglobin/hematocrit, and transient decreases in serum bicarbonate (see Section 17.4 for detailed analyses of changes in laboratory parameters over time). Transient increases in serum creatinine and decreases in eGFR are known class effects. The magnitude of change in these parameters was greater in C-448 as compared to the placebo-controlled pool, with a mean increase in serum creatinine of 0.14 mg/dL (10.8%) and a mean decrease in eGFR of -4.6 mL/min/1.73 m^2 (9.0%) from baseline to Week 6 (Figure 16). In contrast, in the placebo-controlled pool, serum creatinine increased 0.03 mg/dL (3.8%) and eGFR decreased -2.3 mL/min/1.73 m^2 in the bexagliflozin group from baseline to Week 6. These results appear in line with data from other SGLT2 inhibitor programs.

L700: There were no significant mean changes over time in lipid parameters between the bexagliflozin and placebo groups in C-448 (data not shown); however, there were more subjects with level 3 elevations in serum cholesterol (&gt;225 mg/dL), LDL-C (&gt;190 mg/dL), and triglycerides (500 mg/dL) in the bexagliflozin group as compared to the placebo group (Table 51). Supportive data from the subpopulation of subjects with baseline eGFR &lt;60 mL/min/1.73 m2 also indicated a higher incidence of lipid disorders in this population. As discussed above, subgroup analyses
L701: from the MACE+ meta-analyses provide reassurance that the noted changes in lipid parameters do not increase the risk of MACE; however, labeling is proposed in Section 6 to inform providers on potential changes in lipid parameters in this patient population.

L706: ## Conclusion
L707: Overall, considering the safety data from C-448 and C-476, no new safety issues were identified in subjects with stage 3 CKD, although data to characterize certain events (e.g., SAEs, events leading to discontinuation, etc.) were limited. Labeling to inform prescribers regarding changes in certain laboratory parameters (i.e., eGFR/creatinine and lipid parameters) is warranted. The available safety data do not raise new safety concerns and support labeling of bexagliflozin in patients with eGFR &gt;30 mL/min/1.72 m2.
L708: ## Dissent
L709: Not applicable.
L710: ## 7.7.3. Safety Database Quality Concerns
L711: ## Issue
L712: Safety database quality concerns.
L713: ## Background
L714: Concerns regarding the quality of the safety database were raised when multiple events of falls and AKI were found in subject narratives that did not have a corresponding PT in the ISS ADAE dataset. For illustrative purposes, the following excerpts have been reproduced from subject narratives where there was no PT of “fall” or “AKI” in the ISS ADAE dataset:
L715: ## Fall:
L716: - Subject 476-(b) (6): “On 1(b) (6) (Day 247), the subject had a mechanical fall at home, suffered abrasion of the left shin and subsequently developed cellulitis.”
- Subject 476-(b) (6): “On (b) (6) (Day 577), the subject sustained left hip fracture due to accidental fall at home.”
- Subject: 476-(b) (6): “On (b) (6) (Day 639), the subject sustained a right hip fracture and complained of neuropathic symptoms on the right sole after he had a fall.”
L717: ## AKI:
L718: - Subject 476-(b) (6): “Hypotension was likely due to over diuresis, which also caused prerenal acute kidney injury.”
- Subject: 476-(b) (6): “The site reported that elevated lipase was due to acute kidney injury secondary to bilateral obstructing ureteral stones.”
L719: In addition, as previously discussed in Section 7.7.1, the Applicant acknowledged in their application that amputation events were underreported by investigators, and that additional querying of the safety database was needed to adequately identify all amputation events.
L720: Falls, AKI, and amputation were AESIs in all phase 3 protocols, and robust methods for identifying, reporting, and analyzing these events are expected. As underreporting of AEs, including AESIs, could ultimately impact labeling and the overall benefit-risk assessment, data integrity and quality were examined.
L721: ## Assessment
L722: Several approaches were taken to investigate the quality of the safety database. First, FDA requested that the Applicant perform additional analyses to investigate whether AESIs may have been underreported in the bexagliflozin clinical program. Second, FDA asked the Applicant to provide detailed information on the processes and procedures used for the collection of clinical safety data, starting from the clinical encounter, and extending to the preparation of the safety database, to provide assurance that the submitted data were of sufficient quality for review. Third, Office of Scientific Investigations (OSI) inspection information was reviewed to inform potential data integrity issues. These approaches are discussed individually below.
L723: ## Natural Language Processing-Based Data Querying
L724: To investigate whether potential under-coding of safety data occurred in the bexagliflozin clinical program, the Applicant utilized a natural language processing (NLP)-based approach to query available free-text safety data (e.g., subject narratives, verbatim terms, the Argus safety database (the database used to track, review and process individual safety events, including SAEs), etc.). In accordance with the findings observed by the review team, a significant number of additional fall events were identified by the Applicant utilizing the NLP-based approach. For
L725: example, the Applicant states that 69 fall events occurring in 64 subjects were considered to potentially represent distinct fall or fall-like occurrences based on free-text search of narrative sources, 57 of which affected subjects without recorded events of fall in the ADAE database, 6 of which were fall events present in the ADAE database, and 6 of which were additional events in subjects with existing events in the ISS ADAE database (SD0031). In other words, approximately 90% of subjects who experienced a fall event were not included in the ISS ADAE dataset submitted with this application.
L726: The Applicant submitted a modified ISS ADAE dataset that included AEs identified by the NLP-based search for additional events. FMQ analyses were used to assess the original ISS ADAE dataset (adae.xpt) and the NLP-modified ADAE dataset (tadae.xpt). As the majority of additional adverse events found were identified from hospitalization records and/or narrative information for SAEs, C-476 was utilized for this analysis as it contained the majority of SAEs observed in the bexagliflozin clinical development program. In accordance with observations of the review team, there were an additional 40 and 19 subjects who experienced a fall event in the bexagliflozin and placebo groups, respectively, reported in the NLP-modified dataset as compared to the original ISS dataset. A number of additional AKI events were also reported in the NLP-modified dataset. However, the identification of these events appeared primarily based on elevations in creatinine that did not appear to represent events that necessitated coding based on a random review of corresponding subject narratives. There was no significant difference in the FMQs for “Fungal Infection,” “Dizziness,” “Rash,” “Renal and Urinary Tract Infections,” “Hypersensitivity,” “Malignancy,” or “Fracture” between datasets (Table 52).
L727: For FMQs where additional events were coded in the NLP-modified dataset, there was no evidence of systemic bias towards underreporting in the bexagliflozin treatment group. For example, in the original ISS dataset, there were 2.7% and 3.0% of subjects who had at least one fall (as identified by the FMQ for “Fall”) in the bexagliflozin and placebo group of C-476, respectively. In the NLP-modified dataset, there were 6.3% and 6.3% of events in the bexagliflozin and placebo groups, respectively.

L733: Abbreviations: ADAE, ADaM adverse events analysis dataset; Bexa, bexagliflozin; FMQ, Food and Drug Administration Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities query; ISS, integrated summary of safety; NLP, natural language process; RD, risk difference.
L734: A root cause analysis for why fall events were underreported was requested by the Agency. The Applicant states that there was no single explanation for the underreporting of fall events but explained that contributing factors could include lack of guidance to investigators regarding the collection of falls as AEs and the ability for a fall event to be viewed as a symptom of event by investigators as opposed to a stand-alone event requiring independent reporting. In addition, the Applicant also clarified that although “Falls and Fractures” were identified as AESIs in study protocols, beginning with Version 3 of their AESI definitions (March 09, 2018), the PT of fall was no longer included as an AESI. The Applicant provided the following response to FDA’s information request:
L735: *There were several reasons for discontinuing fall as a component of the “Falls and Fractures” AESI. Falls in of themselves do not contribute to an understanding of potential adverse effects of bexagliflozin on bone, except as a kind of denominator over which traumatic events leading to fracture could be assessed (e.g., to calculate fractures per fall). Because few falls were expected to lead to fractures, (as was the case), inclusion of falls could reduce the discriminating power of the event category. In addition, fractures could originate from a variety of forms of trauma, not simply falls. Enumerating traumatic events in general is one possible response, but subcategories of trauma have poor support in MedDRA and their inclusion would also likely be dilutive. Fall and related events associated with loss of postural control can have diverse etiologies, such as hypoglycemia, hypotension, seizure, syncope, trauma or vestibular events.*
L736: Thus, falls were not considered AESIs for the purposes of the integrated summary of safety. Note, we do not agree with the Applicant’s rationale for removing falls from the AESI category and all AEs related to falls should have been included.
L737: ## Processes-Based Quality Review
L738: In addition to efforts to uncover evidence of potential under-coding and differential coding (i.e., the same adverse event coded differently) of adverse events, the review team also examined whether the bexagliflozin development program was designed with important data quality and processes in place. We reviewed the Applicant’s data collection, management, and data quality processes and procedures employed during the trial with reference to International Conference on Harmonisation (ICH) E6(R2) Guidance entitled *Good Clinical Practice: Integrated Addendum to ICH E6(R1)* (March 2018), as summarized below.
L739: - Confirmed that investigators were qualified by education, training, and experience to assume responsibility for the proper conduct of the trial.
- Confirmed that electronic CRFs (eCRFs) were generated in a structured process following the standard operating procedures by the contracted clinical research organizations (CROs), [REDACTED] (b) (4) (C-476) or [REDACTED] (b) (4) (C-419, C-423, C-448, C-450, C-480). The eCRF captured relevant clinical, demographic, and safety information on both designated medical events (e.g., hypoglycemia, DKA) and unsuspected adverse events. All CRFs were generated using a Medidata RAVE electronic data capture (EDC) system, which provided a standalone database instance with appropriate middleware to facilitate the secure and auditable entry of clinical data in a manner conforming to FDA Guidance for Industry *Computerized Systems Used in Clinical Investigations* (May 2007) for each study. The design of the eCRF and the incorporated edit checks were a joint
L740: undertaking of the CRO and the Applicant's medical oversight vendor, the [REDACTED](b) (4). Investigators were introduced to each study through investigator meetings where training in the process of data entry into the eCRF was conducted. Each study had an eCRF completion requirements manual that provided guidance for the entry of data and appropriate responses to real-time validation checking initiated by form-control logic incorporated in the system.
L741: - Confirmed that the two primary CROs who conducted all studies in the drug development program have been inspected by FDA's OSI on multiple prior occasions ([REDACTED](b) (4) in [REDACTED](b) (4) and [REDACTED](b) (4) inspected twice in [REDACTED](b) (4)) and had no significant prior citations.
- Clinical sites were routinely audited, wherein CRF entries were verified against source documents (e.g., medical records, medical notes, laboratory results, electrocardiogram traces etc.). Audit certificates were provided by the Applicant.
- Adverse event terminology and reporting standards conformed to the definitions and principles outlined in the ICH E2A Guidance on *Clinical Safety Data Management: Definitions and Standards for Expedited Reporting* (March 1995).
- The standard procedures for coding of AEs in the clinical trials appears to have followed MedDRA principles to ensure complete and accurate coding of events. This included instructions pertaining to term selection to guard against missed concepts.
- The establishment and maintenance of a safety database was undertaken through a contract with the pharmacovigilance provider, [REDACTED](b) (4), doing business as [REDACTED](b) (4). The datastore was an instance of an Oracle Argus Cloud relational database administered by [REDACTED](b) (4) data managers.
- Clinical laboratory data were imported into the RAVE database by direct electronic transfer from the central laboratory sites.
- The Argus safety database was maintained under a safety management plan that was established for all TheracosBio, LLC bexagliflozin clinical studies. The plan was an integral part of an oversight architecture that included a medical responsibility plan, an unblinding plan and a clinical and safety database reconciliation plan, all of which were provided by the Applicant for review.
L742: ## OSI Review
L743: As detailed in OSI's review (see DARRTS consult dated July 13, 2022), eight domestic clinical investigators were inspected. Investigators/study sites were selected based on the ability of data from their site to potentially impact the overall benefit-risk assessment. Amongst other activities, site inspections reviewed subject source documents including AE and SAE reports, and source records were compared to the Applicant's data line listings in the NDA submission. OSI concludes that no significant regulatory violations were found upon inspection and that, based on the results of inspections and regulatory assessments, Trials C-419, C-423, C-448, C-450, C-476 and C-480 appear to have been conducted adequately.
L744: ## Conclusion
L745: Results from analyses conducted with the Applicant's NLP-modified dataset (tadae.xpt) were in line with the review teams observations that certain events (i.e., falls, AKI, amputation),
L746: appeared under-coded in the safety database; however, a systematic under-coding of other important events (e.g., fungal infections, fractures, malignancies) does not appear to have occurred. In addition, no evidence of biased underreporting was observed (i.e., under coded events impacted both treatment groups generally equally). The Applicant provided information to support that the trials were designed with appropriate measures to ensure the collection of high-quality data. Lastly, as detailed in OSI's review, pivotal studies appear to have been conducted adequately based on inspectional findings. Overall, the data generated and submitted by the Applicant appear of acceptable quality for review.

L749: ## 8. Therapeutic Individualization
L750: ## 8.1. Intrinsic Factors
L751: ## Renal Impairment
L752: In patients with mild, moderate, and severe renal impairment, bexagliflozin AUC increased by 6.8%, 33.8% and 53.9% compared to patients with normal renal function. The maximum plasma concentration (C_{max}) was not affected. Consistent with the mechanism of action, the 24-hour UGE declined with decreased eGFR, from 100 g without impairment to 83, 40, and 17 g in the setting of mild, moderate, and severe impairment, respectively.
L753: The effects of moderate renal impairment (stage 3 CKD, 30 \le eGFR &lt; 60 mL/min/1.73 m^2) were evaluated in two phase 3 studies (C-448 and C-476). Based on the efficacy and safety observed in these studies, bexagliflozin can be used in patients with mild and moderate renal impairment without dose adjustment (see Section 6.3 for detailed information).
L754: The safety and efficacy of bexagliflozin have not been established in patients with severe renal impairment, with end stage renal disease, or receiving dialysis. However, bexagliflozin is not expected to be effective in these patient populations based on its mechanism of action.
L755: ## Hepatic Impairment
L756: The use of bexagliflozin has not been studied in patients with severe hepatic impairment. In subjects with moderate hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh class B), bexagliflozin AUC increased by 28.3%, and C_{max} increased by 6.2% compared to subjects with normal hepatic function. The extent of exposure increase is less than that from moderate renal impairment and is not considered clinically relevant and therefore dose adjustment is not needed in patients with mild and moderate hepatic impairment.
L757: ## UGT1A9 Polymorphism
L758: Bexagliflozin is mainly metabolized by UGT1A9, which is polymorphic. Although the Applicant didn't collect information on UGT1A9 allelic variants in clinical studies, the impact of UGT1A9 genotype on the PK of bexagliflozin may be less than or similar to that observed in the clinical
L759: study with UGT1A9 inhibition. Based on a &lt;40% increase in bexagliflozin AUC in the presence of UGT1A9 inhibitor probenecid, UGT1A9 polymorphism is unlikely to contribute a sufficiently substantial effect to warrant a change in the dosing regimen.
L760: ## Other Intrinsic Factors
L761: The impact of intrinsic factors on bexagliflozin PK exposure was evaluated. Intrinsic factors included in the population PK analysis (i.e., creatinine clearance, body weight, Asian race, healthy status) were not considered to have a clinically meaningful effect on bexagliflozin PK. Refer to the covariate effect assessment in the Pharmacometrics Review Appendix (Section 14.3.4).
L762: ## 8.2. Food Effect
L763: Administration of bexagliflozin after consumption of a high-fat, high-caloric meal delayed bexagliflozin time to maximum concentration (T_{max}) by about 1.5 hours and increased its C_{max} and AUC values by 31% (90% CI: 17%, 48%) and 10% (90% CI: 3.9%, 17%), respectively, compared to the values observed following dosing in the fasted state (Trial C-481). The observed exposure increases are not considered clinically meaningful and bexagliflozin can be administered with or without food.
L764: ## 8.3. Drug Interactions
L765: In vitro studies indicated that bexagliflozin is mainly metabolized by UGT1A9 with minor contribution from the cytochrome (CYP)3A enzyme. In addition, bexagliflozin is a substrate and inhibitor of P-gp at clinically relevant concentrations. Based on the in vitro findings, the Applicant conducted several clinical drug-drug interaction (DDI) studies to further evaluate the effect of UGT1A9 inhibition (probenecid), CYP3A/uridine diphosphate-glucuronosyltransferase (UGT) induction (rifampin), and p-gp inhibition (verapamil) on the PK of bexagliflozin, as well as the effect of bexagliflozin on the PK of a sensitive P-gp substrate (digoxin). The Applicant also evaluated the potential interactions between bexagliflozin and commonly prescribed antidiabetic agents including exenatide, glimepiride, sitagliptin, and metformin.
L766: Based on the results of these studies (Figure 17 and Figure 18), clinically meaningful DDI is not expected when bexagliflozin is taken with 1) antihyperglycemic agents including exenatide, glimepiride, sitagliptin, metformin, 2) drugs that are substrates of P-gp, and 3) drugs that inhibit P-gp or UGT1A9, (see Section 8.3.3 for further details). UGT enzyme inducers may significantly reduce bexagliflozin exposure and decrease its efficacy. Therefore, adding another antihyperglycemic agent may be considered in patients who require additional glycemic control.
