L771: ## 8.3.1. DDI Potential as a Victim
L772: ## Effect of UGT Inhibition on the PK/PD of Bexagliflozin
L773: Effect of UGT inhibition on bexagliflozin PK/PD was assessed in 16 healthy subjects using a nonspecific UGT inhibitor probenecid. During the study, subjects took a single dose of bexagliflozin 20 mg on Day 1 and Day 5. Probenecid 500 mg twice a day was administered from Day 3 to Day 6. Coadministration with probenecid increased bexagliflozin AUC0-t and Cmax by 38.8% [29.5%, 48.8%] and 18.7% [11.1%, 26.7%], respectively, compared to bexagliflozin alone. Bexagliflozin Tmax and t1/2 were similar between treatments. Postdose UGE for each 12-hour collection interval was similar for both treatments, indicating no impact on UGE. Based on the safety profile of bexagliflozin, the magnitude of exposure increase observed in this study was not considered clinically significant. Therefore, bexagliflozin can be taken with drugs that inhibit UGT.
L774: ## Effect of CYP3A/UGT Induction on the PK/PD of Bexagliflozin
L775: Effect of CYP3A/UGT induction on bexagliflozin PK/PD was assessed in 16 healthy subjects using a strong CYP3A/UGT inducer (rifampin). During the study, subjects took a single dose of bexagliflozin 20 mg on Day 1 and Day 6. Rifampin 600 mg once daily was administered from Day 3 to Day 7. The point estimate of geometric mean ratio (GMR) (90% CI) for treatments bexagliflozin + rifampin vs. bexagliflozin alone was 86.1% (70.2%, 105.6%) for AUC0-t and 119.6% (94.4%, 151.6%) for Cmax. The half-life of bexagliflozin was decreased from 12.9 hours to 5.9 hours when co-administered with rifampin. Postdose UGE for each 12-hour collection interval was similar for both treatments.
L776: The review team is concerned that a 3-day pretreatment with rifampin is too short to achieve the full potential of CYP3A/UGT induction. The induction effect-time profile of rifampin on CYP3A has been demonstrated by several publications. In general, at least 5 days of treatment with rifampin (600 mg per day) is needed to approach the plateau of CYP3A induction. Based on the shared activation pathway of Pregnane X Receptor between CYP3A and UGT, it's anticipated that a 3-day pretreatment duration may not fully reach the peak of UGT1A9 induction as well.
L777: Overall, the current study may not capture the worst-case scenario on the impact of CYP3A/UGT induction on bexagliflozin PK. This speculation is further supported by the smaller extent of exposure decrease with bexagliflozin compared to other SGLT2 inhibitors, all of which are also mainly metabolized by UGT1A9. Specifically, DDI studies with rifampin showed AUC reductions of 51%, 22%, and 39%, respectively, for canagliflozin, dapagliflozin, and ertugliflozin.
L778: Overall, the current study result may not reflect the maximum effect of CYP3A/UGT induction on the PK of bexagliflozin. It is expected that strong CYP/UGT inducers may lead to significantly decreased bexagliflozin exposures and may potentially result in compromised efficacy in glycemic control. Therefore, adding another antihyperglycemic agent may be considered in patients who require additional glycemic control. The impact of UGT enzyme inducers on bexagliflozin and the potential requirement for additional antihyperglycemic agents will be included in the prescribing information.
L779: ## Effect of P-gp Inhibition the PK of Bexagliflozin
L780: When bexagliflozin (20 mg) was administered one hour after the intake of a P-gp inhibitor verapamil (120 mg), the mean GMR (90% CI) was 96.6% (88.1%, 105.9%) and 106.0% (88.1%, 126.7%) for bexagliflozin AUC0-t and Cmax, respectively. Therefore, concomitant drugs that are P-gp inhibitors are unlikely to affect bexagliflozin PK.
L781: ## 8.3.2. DDI Potential as a Perpetrator
L782: In vitro studies indicate that bexagliflozin may be a P-gp inhibitor at the clinically relevant dose. Therefore, a clinical DDI study with a sensitive P-gp substrate digoxin was conducted. The results show no significant changes in the systemic exposures of digoxin when coadministered with bexagliflozin (20 mg one daily for 8 days). Therefore, bexagliflozin administered as 20 mg daily is unlikely to affect the PK of concomitant drugs that are substrates of P-gp.
L783: ## 8.3.3. DDI Potential With Commonly Prescribed Antidiabetic Agents
L784: ## DDIs With Exenatide
L785: Following injection of 10 µg of exenatide, the GMR (90% CI) for AUC0-t, and Cmax of bexagliflozin with exenatide compared to bexagliflozin alone were 1.47 (1.30, 1.67), and 1.25 (1.04, 1.50), respectively, and the median Tmax increased from 2 hours to 5 hours. Per the Applicant, the effects of exenatide, a glucagon-like peptide (GLP)-1 receptor agonist, were consistent with the known delay of gastric emptying by GLP-1 receptor agonists and mimicked the effects of prior consumption of food (Trial C-481). However, it should be noted that the impact on the PK of bexagliflozin was much larger with exenatide compared to the food effect (47% versus 10% increase in AUC). The exact mechanism of interaction is not clear. The PD response of 24-hour UGE was lower in the bexagliflozin plus exenatide group (~55 g) compared to the bexagliflozin alone group (~65 g). Nonetheless, the decreased UGE is unlikely to translate to diminished efficacy, given the 24-hour UGE value of 55 g is still on the plateau of the bexagliflozin dose-UGE response curve (Figure 5). In addition, the observed 47% exposure increase in bexagliflozin is not considered clinically relevant as no major safety concerns were identified when bexagliflozin was given to patients with T2DM for 28 days at the dose of 50 mg. Therefore, no dose adjustment is needed when bexagliflozin is taken with a GLP-1 receptor agonist.
L786: ## DDIs With Metformin, Glimipiride and Sitagliptin
L787: DDI potential of bexagliflozin with commonly prescribed antidiabetic agents including metformin, glimepiride, and sitagliptin was assessed in 54 healthy subjects (N=18 per group). For each group, subjects received a single dose of bexagliflozin 20 mg alone, a single dose of an oral hypoglycemic agent (1000 mg metformin, 2 mg glimepiride, or 100 mg sitagliptin) alone, and the combination of both (bexagliflozin and antidiabetic agents) alternately in a crossover fashion, with three treatment periods separated by a washout period of at least 7 days.
L788: The results show that bexagliflozin had no significant effect on the PK of metformin, glimepiride, and sitagliptin. Similarly, there was no clinically relevant impact on the PK of bexagliflozin. UGE values of bexagliflozin were slightly lower when administered with other antidiabetic agents but the differences were not statistically significant. Overall, no dose adjustment is needed for bexagliflozin when administered with metformin, glimepiride, and sitagliptin.
L789: ## Other Drug Interactions
L790: A few drug interaction warnings have been added to the product labeling, but they were not reviewed in the current submission. These drug interactions are related to the class effects of SGLT2 inhibitors including increased risk of hypoglycemia when used combination with insulin and/or insulin secretagogues, interference with the 1,5-anhydroglucitol (1,5-AG) assay, a positive urine glucose test and potential reduction in serum lithium levels during the treatment with SGLT2 inhibitors.
L791: ## 8.4. Plans for Pediatric Drug Development
L792: The initial approval of bexagliflozin will be limited to adults as the trials included in this application did not enroll pediatric subjects. The Division agrees to waive the pediatric study requirement for ages 0 through 9 years (inclusive) because necessary studies are impossible or highly impracticable. This is because there are too few children in this age range with T2DM to study. Furthermore, the Division agrees to defer submission of the Applicant's pediatric study for ages 10 to 17 years (inclusive) for this application because this product is ready for approval for use in adults and the pediatric studies have not been completed.
L793: The Applicant's deferred pediatric study is required under section 505B(a) of the FDCA as a required postmarketing study. The status of this postmarketing study must be reported annually according to 21 CFR 314.81 and section 505B(a)(3)(C) of the FDCA. The required pediatric study is listed below:
L794: - A 24-week, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel group study of the safety, efficacy, pharmacokinetics (PK), and pharmacodynamics (PD) of bexagliflozin for the treatment of type 2 diabetes mellitus in pediatric patients ages 10 to 17 years (inclusive), followed by a 28-week double-blind, controlled extension. The bexagliflozin dose will be determined based on the initial PK/PD lead-in portion of the study.

L799: ## 8.5. Pregnancy and Lactation
L800: There are no available data on bexagliflozin use in pregnant women to evaluate a drug-associated risk of major birth defects, miscarriage, or adverse maternal or fetal outcomes, or information regarding the presence of bexagliflozin in human milk. A standard battery of reproductive
L801: toxicology studies and a juvenile toxicology study with relevance to pregnancy were conducted with bexagliflozin. No treatment-related adverse effects on fertility, embryo-fetal development, or pre- and postnatal development were observed at clinically relevant exposures. Based on adverse renal effects (adverse renal pelvic and tubular dilatation) in juvenile rats administered bexagliflozin during periods of renal development corresponding to the late second and third trimester of human renal development, bexagliflozin is not recommended during pregnancy. Detailed summaries of the results of these studies are contained in Section 13 of this review.
L802: **Table 53. Nonclinical Data Supporting Labeling**
L803: Labeling Section	Nonclinical Data
8.1 Pregnancy	
Bexagliflozin dosed directly to juvenile rats at 0.3, 3, 30 mg/kg by oral gavage from postnatal day (PND) 21 to 90 caused a dose dependent increase in the incidence and severity of renal pelvic and tubular dilatation at \ge 3 mg/kg (11 times the MRHD). These effects occurred with drug exposure during periods of renal development in rats that correspond to the late second and third trimester of human renal development.
In embryofetal development studies, bexagliflozin was administered by oral gavage to rats at 0, 7, 40 or 200 mg/kg/day and to rabbits at 0, 5, 25 or 150 mg/kg/day during the period of organogenesis. No adverse developmental effects were observed in rats at doses up to 200 mg/kg/day (550 times the clinical dose of 20 mg based on AUC). Reduced maternal body weight, embryo lethality, and fetal malformations were observed in rabbits at 150 mg/kg/day (370 times the clinical dose of 20 mg based on AUC).
In a pre- and postnatal development study, bexagliflozin was administered to maternal rats by oral gavage from gestation Day 6 throughout lactation Day 20 at doses of 7, 40 or 200 mg/kg/day. Maternal mortality occurred at >40 mg/kg (79 times the clinical dose of 20 mg based on AUC), primarily following parturition. Reduced gestational body weight, increased postimplantation loss, and smaller litter size were noted at 200 mg/kg (361 times the clinical dose of 20 mg based on AUC). In the offspring, lower body weight gain and decreased survival were noted at 200 mg/kg, which occurred in the presence of significant maternal toxicity.

8.2 Lactation	
Bexagliflozin was present in rat milk at a milk: plasma ratio of approximately 2. If a drug is present in animal milk, it is likely the drug will be present in human milk. Juvenile rats directly administered dapagliflozin showed risk to the developing kidney (renal pelvic and tubular dilatations) during the period of renal development in rats corresponding to the late second and third trimester of human renal development.
L804: Labeling Section	Nonclinical Data
13.1 Carcinogenesis, mutagenesis, impairment of fertility	
Carcinogenesis: The carcinogenic potential of bexagliflozin was evaluated in 2-year studies in Sprague-Dawley (SD) rats and CD-1 mice. There were no neoplastic findings in mice and rats up to the highest doses tested (150 mg/kg/day for mice and 30 mg/kg/day for rats, representing approximately 135 and 54 times the clinical dose of 20 mg based on AUC, respectively). The male rat study was terminated prematurely at Weeks 82-88, due to excessive mortality.
Mutagenesis: Bexagliflozin was not mutagenic or clastogenic in the in vitro Ames bacterial mutagenicity assay, the in vitro mammalian chromosomal aberration assay, an in vivo micronucleus test in rats, and in vivo unscheduled hepatic DNA synthesis in rats.
Impairment of fertility: Bexagliflozin had no effects on mating, fertility, or early embryonic development in male or female rats at any dose up to the highest dose of 200 mg/kg/day, which resulted in exposures 280 times (males) and 439 times (females) the clinical dose 20 mg based on AUC.

L830: ## Opening IND 103822
L831: The Division received the opening IND 103822 for bexagliflozin on January 7, 2009. Non-hold issues were identified during the IND safety review regarding aspects of the proposed nonclinical program, and feedback was provided to the Sponsor on February 13, 2009. Additional nonclinical and clinical pharmacology feedback was provided on April 8, 2009, June 16, 2009, and September 11, 2009, to which the Sponsor provided responses on June 26, 2009, and October 19, 2009.
L832: ## Carcinogenicity SPAs
L833: A request for a carcinogenicity special protocol assessment (SPA) for the protocol “104-Week Oral Carcinogenicity Study of bexagliflozin in CD-1 Mice,” was received on March 17, 2010, and denied. It was resubmitted with the requested full report of the mouse toxicity study and received by the Agency on April 14, 2010. Another carcinogenicity SPA request for the protocol, “26-Week Oral Gavage Chronic Toxicity and Toxicokinetic Study with bexagliflozin in Rats with a 4-Week Recovery Phase,” was received on June 17, 2010. FDA recommended doses of 0 (distilled water), 0 (vehicle: 1% medium viscosity carboxymethylcellulose), 15, 50, and 150 mg/kg/day in male and female CD1 mice, 0 (distilled water), 0 (vehicle: 30% PEG400 vehicle), 2, 7, and 20 mg/kg/day in male rats, and concurred with the Sponsor’s proposed doses of 0 (distilled water), 0 (30% PEG400 vehicle), 3, 10, and 30 mg/kg/day in female rats.
L834: On February 1, 2012, the Agency received a carcinogenicity SPA amendment containing dosing and vehicle changes with which the Executive Carcinogenicity Assessment Committee (ECAC) did not concur. The Agency responded with advice on February 3, 2012. Further carcinogenicity protocol amendments and advice requests were received on February 17, 2012, and April 6, 2012. The Agency responded on February 29, and April 5, 2012, respectively. An additional amendment was received on August 14, 2012, with the Agency again responding on September 5, 2012, with ECAC reiterating their lack of concurrence with dosing and vehicle changes.
L835: On May 10, 2013, the Agency received nonclinical study reports for 104-Week Oral Carcinogenicity Studies THR-1442-T-405 and THR-1442-T-406, along with a request for comments on the carcinogenicity studies. The Agency’s reply on July 18, 2013, again reiterated ECAC’s lack of concurrence with doses and vehicle change, along with a need for a complete study review. A response from the Sponsor containing the requested study data was received on November 12, 2013.
L836: On May 20, 2017, the Agency issued feedback stating that the Division agrees that no additional assessments of the carcinogenic potential of bexagliflozin are required. However, the Division reiterated that the assessment of the carcinogenic potential of bexagliflozin in male rats was not adequate given the limited duration of exposure, due to excessive early mortality. Based on the absence of preneoplastic findings and tumors in males exposed for up to 88 weeks at 3 times the MRHD and in females exposed for 100 weeks at doses up to 68 times the MRHD, repeating the carcinogenicity study in male rats was not considered warranted.
L837: ## Thorough QT Study
L838: Protocol C-428 for a thorough QT (TQT) study was received on May 19, 2011. The Interdisciplinary Review Team for Cardiac Safety Studies (IRT-CS) reviewed the protocol (see memo in DARRTS dated July 12, 2011) and feedback was provided to the Sponsor on July 26, 2011. The Sponsor adequately incorporated feedback from the IRT-CS (see IRT-CS memo in DARRTS dated March 19, 2013). The clinical study report (CSR) was reviewed by the IRT-CS on November 4, 2013. The memo concludes that no significant QTc prolongation effect was detected in C-428.

L840: ## End-of-Phase 2 and Follow-Up Meetings
L841: An End-of-Phase 2 (EOP2) Meeting was held with the Sponsor on January 15, 2015, with final meeting minutes issued on February 12, 2015. The following topics were discussed:
L842: - **Clinical Dose Selection:** The Agency did not agree with the Sponsor's proposal to select phase 3 doses based on data from phase 1/2 studies conducted with the capsule formulation of bexagliflozin and recommended that the Sponsor perform a dose-finding study with the modified formulation prior to initiating their phase 3 program. The Agency noted that, given the lack of established bioequivalence between the capsule and tablet formulations, it is unlikely that the findings from phase 2 trials C-402 and C-418 will be relevant to the formulation they intend to evaluate in their phase 3 program.
- **Phase 3 Program:** The Sponsor stated that the efficacy and safety of bexagliflozin in the context of combination therapy will be evaluated in: Trials C-419, C-423, and C-480, in which metformin will be coadministered; Trial C-420, in which sulfonylureas will be coadministered; Trial C-470, in which insulin will be coadministered; and Trials C-448 and C-476, in which all approved antidiabetic therapies will be candidates for coadministration. In addition, Trials C-423 and C-480 will be designed to demonstrate that bexagliflozin will be as effective as sitagliptin or glimepiride. FDA indicated concurrence on the proposed phase 3 development program.
- **Adverse events of special interest (AESIs):** In addition to the AESIs proposed by the Sponsor (hypoglycemia, hypovolemia, falls, fractures, urosepsis, pyelonephritis, urinary tract infections, genital infections, hepatic adverse events, and malignancies), the Agency
L843: recommended that the Sponsor also prospectively collect and evaluate hypersensitivity reactions, hypotension episodes, acid-base disorders, and renal failure events as AESIs.

- **Studies in Older Adults:** The Sponsor proposed not to perform dedicated studies in older adults. The Agency agreed with this proposal.
- **Cardiovascular (CV) Risk Assessment:** FDA confirmed that the Sponsor's proposed major adverse cardiac event (MACE+) primary composite endpoint is acceptable for the premarketing assessment of CV safety to exclude an excess risk of over 80%. Additional feedback on the proposed inclusion criteria for C-476 and the statistical analysis plan for the proposed MACE meta-analysis was also provided.
L844: On July 8, 2016, the Agency received a request for a Type C guidance meeting to follow-up on the clinical discussions that occurred during the End-of-Phase 2 meeting. Agency feedback was provided on September 21, 2016. Feedback included the following:
L845: - **Dose Selection:** The Sponsor requested feedback regarding dose selection for their phase 3 program. The Agency encouraged the Sponsor to evaluate two bexagliflozin dosage strengths.
- **Insulin Trial:** The Sponsor requested FDA feedback on their proposal not to conduct a dedicated trial evaluating the effectiveness of bexagliflozin as an add-on to insulin therapy. The Sponsor stated that approximately 50% of the population enrolled in C-476 to date used background insulin and proposed that a substudy of C-476 could be used to inform the safety and efficacy of bexagliflozin in this population. The Agency noted that this approach is reasonable provided that the design and conduct of the glycemic efficacy portion of the trial is consistent with what would be expected if the study were conducted as a separate study.
- **Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA):** The Sponsor provided their DKA monitoring and analysis plan for the bexagliflozin clinical program and requested FDA feedback on the DKA case definitions. FDA stated that the proposed case definitions and DKA monitoring and analysis plan appear acceptable.
- **C-476:** Several aspects of C-476 were discussed. See section below (C-476 Protocol Review) for additional information
- **Amputations:** FDA recommended that amputations be included as an AESI. (Additional FDA recommendations on how amputation events should be monitored, evaluated, and analyzed was provided on October 25, 2016).
L846: ***FDA Reviewer Comment:*** *Overall, the Sponsor incorporated key FDA recommendations from this EOP2 meeting and written response only feedback dated September 21, 2016 into their clinical development program. The Sponsor did not take the Agency's recommendation to evaluate two doses of bexagliflozin in the phase 3 program.*

L856: ## 12.2. Statistical Regulatory History
L857: The Division of Metabolism and Endocrinology Products (DMEP)4 received Theracos’ IND 103822 for bexagliflozin for treatment of T2DM on January 7, 2009. Since then, the FDA statistical team has been providing review comments/statistical advice to the Sponsor regarding study design and analysis methodologies.
L858: 4 After Center for Drug Evaluation and Research (CDER)’s 2019 reorganization, Division of Diabetes, Lipid Disorders, and Obesity (DDLO).
L859: The statistical advice has been focused on aspects of missing data related to trial design and analysis methods: missing data prevention, estimand, and missing data handling strategies. Among them, advice common to all pivotal trials are summarized below.
L860: - FDA considers the treatment policy estimand critical to support effectiveness.
- Provided advice on strategies for missing data prevention
- Reiterated the importance of “off treatment” data collection
- Analysis population should include all randomized subjects regardless of treatment adherence or availability of follow-up data.
- For the primary analysis model, at different stages, the following advice has been given:Advice against the last observation carried forward (LOCF) approach in missing data handling;
- Advice against the mixed model repeated measures (MMRM) approach in missing data handling;
- Recommended addressing missing data by having the missing data from subjects who do not adhere to therapy represented by the data from those subjects on the same arm that also did not adhere to therapy but had the measurement;
- Recommended retrieved drop-out based pattern mixture modeling approach; in case the retrieved drop-out is not enough to support this analysis, recommended a return-to-baseline approach in missing data handling.
- Recommended to use sensitivity analyses to study the limitation of the missing data assumptions made in the primary analysis.Recommended the tipping point sensitivity analysis
L861: Theracos' IND phase responses to the above FDA advice is summarized below:
L862: - Implemented actions in all phase 2/3 controlled studies to minimize missing data
- The Sponsor still proposed MMRM as primary analysis for all studies, even though the Sponsor agrees that MMRM cannot be used to account for missing data entirely.
- The primary analysis will include the post-rescue data.
- Proposed a list of sensitivity analysis including the tipping point analysis method.

L882: ## Absorption Distribution, Metabolism, Excretion (ADME)/Pharmacokinetics
L883: ## Absorption
L884: Following oral administration, bexagliflozin was rapidly absorbed with a time to maximum concentration (T_{max}) ranging between 0.4 to 2.5 hours in rats, dogs, and monkeys. Exposure (maximum plasma concentration [C_{max}] and area under the concentration-time curve [AUC_{0-t}]) generally increased in a dose-proportional manner. Oral bioavailability in rats, dogs, and monkeys ranged from 46% to 82%.

L889: ## **Distribution**
L890: Bexagliflozin was 93 to 97% bound to plasma proteins across all species tested (human, rhesus monkeys, beagle dog, SD rat, and CD-1 mouse).
L891: In a distribution study in rats, the kidney medulla and cortex, liver, adrenal cortex and medulla, pancreas, harderian gland, and preputial gland showed the highest bexagliflozin concentration between 4 to 12 hours postdose.
L892: In lactating female rats, bexagliflozin distributed into maternal milk with a concentration higher than maternal plasma (1.4 to 1.8 times), which resulted in detectable plasma levels of bexagliflozin in nursing pups at levels 20 to 50 times lower than in milk. Levels in rat milk and nursing pups are not predictive of drug levels in human milk or nursing infants.
L893: ## **Metabolism**
L894: Metabolism studies were conducted in vitro using liver microsomes or recombinant cytochrome (CYP) P450 enzymes, and in vivo using radiolabeled test article. The metabolic profile was similar across the species tested and there were no unique or disproportionate human metabolites. Parent drug was the predominant drug-related component in the circulation in rats, monkeys, and humans. In humans, the majority of biotransformation appears to be by phase II metabolism and the most abundant circulating metabolite was glucose 3'-O-gluconide (32.8% in humans versus 22.8% in monkeys), which was considered qualified given the high clinical exposure multiples achieved in monkeys. An additional oxidative metabolite, EGT0001494, was also observed in monkeys. Oxidative metabolites (EGT0001301, EGT0001663, EGT0001494) were identified in incubations with animal and human liver microsomes, as well as in animal studies, with EGT0001301 (O-dealkylated metabolite) being the predominant metabolite. The metabolic enzymes CYP3A4 and UGT1A9 were responsible for the metabolism. After oral or intravenous dosing, the terminal plasma half-life of bexagliflozin in rats, dogs, and monkeys ranged between 3 to 5 hours.

L900: ## Excretion
L901: Following an oral dose of radio-labeled bexagliflozin, fecal excretion was the primary route of elimination, accounting for 86.6% and 54.1% in rats and monkeys, respectively. Urinary excretion was the secondary route, accounting for 14.4% and 29.2% in rats and monkeys, respectively. The radiolabel in excreta consisted mainly of parent drug.

L915: ## 13.1.1.4. Toxicology
L916: ## 13.1.1.4.1. General Toxicology
L917: ## 26-Week Oral Gavage Chronic Toxicity and Toxicokinetic Study With Bexagliflozin in Rats With a 4-Week Recovery Phase
L918: ## Key Study Findings
L919: - Rats were administered bexagliflozin by oral gavage at doses of 1, 3, 10, or 30 mg/kg/day for 26 weeks
- Consistent with the intended pharmacology, marked glucosuria and slightly decreased plasma glucose levels were observed in all bexagliflozin treatment groups.
- Chronic progressive nephropathy (CPN), particularly in the male treatment groups, was observed at \ge 3 mg/kg. The severity of this finding remained increased in the high dose recovery males (slight/moderate). CPN is a common background finding in aging male Sprague Dawley rats and is generally not considered to be relevant to human risk.
- A low incidence and severity (minimal to slight) of glandular stomach erosion/ulcer was observed in all male treatment groups, not dose-related, at Week 26 or after 4 weeks of recovery, and in high dose females at Week 26. Similar stomach findings have been observed with other sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors. The clinical relevance of stomach erosion is likely limited considering the low incidence and severity and due to the absence of similar findings in other species (monkeys with bexagliflozin and dogs with other drugs in this class), as well as in humans with other drugs in this class.
- The no observed adverse effect level (NOAEL) was considered 30 mg/kg (54031 and 112292 ng.h/mL, 43- and 89-fold MRHD, respectively).

L924: **Table 60. Observations and Results for 26-Week Oral Gavage Chronic Toxicity and Toxicokinetic Study in Rats**
L925: Parameters	Major Findings
Mortality	None
Clinical signs	Rough hair coat was observed for individual males in the 10 and 30 mg/kg/day male groups and for most groups including the control in the female treated animals.
Body weights	No statistically significant body weight changes
Ophthalmoscopy	No remarkable findings
ECG	Not performed
Hematology	No remarkable findings
Clinical chemistry	Relative to control, decreased serum glucose (up to -25%), increased urea nitrogen (up to 2-fold) and ALT (up to 1.6-fold) were observed in bexagliflozin treated groups. All these findings resolved after 4 weeks of recovery period.
Urinalysis	Consistent with the test article pharmacology, dose-related increases in urinary glucose concentration (up to 445-fold), glucose excretion (>1000-fold), urine volume (up to 2-fold) and specific gravity (up to 1.5-fold) were observed. All findings resolved after 4 weeks of recovery period.
Gross pathology	Bexagliflozin treatment groups showed discolored (black, ran, red or dark red) foci in the mucosa of the glandular stomach (males at \ge 3 mg/kg/day; females at 30 mg/kg/day) which correlated with microscopic findings of minimal to slight erosion/ulcer.
Organ weights	Increased organ weights in the kidney (up to 30.5%), adrenal gland (up to 20%), and liver (up to 14%), and decreased prostate gland weight (up to -28%) were observed in bexagliflozin treatment groups, in a dose-related manner. Organ weight changes in the liver, adrenal and prostate did not correlate with microscopic changes.
L926: Parameters	Major Findings
Histopathology	Bexagliflozin treatment exacerbated chronic progressive nephropathy in males and caused glandular stomach erosion/ulcer in both males and females. These findings were not resolved or only partially resolved after 4 weeks of recovery period.
Adequate battery:	
Yes	Chronic progressive nephropathy (CPN) represents a common rodent-specific finding that typically increases in incidence and severity with age in rats, with males more greatly affected than females. The CPN was characterized by dilated tubules filled with proteinaceous fluid in the inner cortical region and basophilic regenerating tubules in the cortex with aggregates of pigment-laden macrophages within the interstitium around regenerating tubules.
Minimal to slight glandular stomach erosion/ulcer, characterized by minimal to moderate degeneration of gastric epithelium associated with submucosal edema and/or submucosal inflammation in more extensive lesions, was observed in all treated male groups, not dose related, and in high dose females. This finding was still present in high dose males after the recovery period.

L936: ## 39-Week Nasogastric Intubation Toxicity and Toxicokinetics Study With Bexagliflozin in Cynomolgus Monkeys With a 4-Week Recovery Period
L937: ## Key Study Findings
L938: - Monkeys were administered bexagliflozin orally at doses of 2, 6, 20, or 60 mg/kg/day for 39 weeks.
- Consistent with the intended pharmacology, marked glucosuria and slightly decrease in blood glucose concentration were observed in all bexagliflozin treatment groups.
- Kidney tubular vacuolation (minimal to slight in severity) was observed in all bexagliflozin treatment groups at Week 39 and in one recovery male at 20 mg/kg after 4 weeks of recovery period. This kidney finding is likely glucosuria-related and not toxicologically significant.
L939: - A focal stomach erosion/ulcer of slight severity was observed in two females, one each at 2 mg/kg and 60 mg/kg. The finding is likely incidental due to the low incidence and absence of dose-relationship.
- NOAEL is 60 mg/kg (sex combined AUC0-24h of 98299 ng.h/mL, 78-fold MRHDAUC of 20 mg) based on lack of toxicologically significant findings in the study.

THR-1474-n-375
In Vitro Mammalian Chromosome Aberration Assay in Chinese Hamster Ovary Cells Challenged With EGT0001442
GLP compliant
Study is valid	Bexagliflozin concentration: 9 to 288 mcg/mL were selected based on cytotoxicity: 4h +S9, 18-144 mcg/mL; 4h-S9, 36-144 mcg/mL; 19h-S9, 9-36 mcg/mL)
Treatment duration: 4 hours \pm S9; 19 hour -S9
In the absence of S9, either 4-hour or 9-hour treatment, bexagliflozin did not produce a trend of increasing incidence of chromosomal aberrations.
In the presence of S9, bexagliflozin did cause a trend towards increasing chromosome aberrations. However, the vehicle control had an unusually low incidence of aberrant cells, bexagliflozin 36 \mug/mL had very few evaluable metaphases due to a drug-related issues on cell attachment, and bexagliflozin 144 \mug/mL had a cytotoxicity of 68%, which was outside the target range. Therefore, the positive trend observed was considered not biologically meaningful.
Bexagliflozin was negative for clastogenic potential in this study.

L972: ## 13.1.1.4.3. Carcinogenicity
L973: ## 104-Week Oral Carcinogenicity Study of Bexagliflozin in Sprague-Dawley Rats
L974: Male rats were administered bexagliflozin by oral gavage in 1% medium viscosity carboxymethylcellulose at 3, 10, and 30 mg/kg for 507 days (72.4 weeks) and then at 1, 3, and 10 mg/kg for additional 12, 5, and 2 weeks for the low dose, mid dose, and high dose group, respectively. In the male study, dosing was stopped at Week 75, 78, and 85 and the groups were terminated at Week 82, 85, and 88 at the high, mid, and low dose, respectively. Female rats were administered bexagliflozin at 3, 10 and 30 mg/kg for 100 weeks. Treatment-related findings included higher mortality in males, lower body weight (up to -14%) and higher food consumption (up to 26%) in both males and females. Treatment-related exacerbation of CPN and associated secondary findings (widespread vascular mineralization and diffuse hyperplasia of parathyroid gland), observed primarily in males, were considered to be the cause of death. There was no increase in the incidence of preneoplastic findings or tumors in any treatment group at doses up to 30 mg/kg/day.
L975: The study in males was conducted at doses that exceeded those recommended by the Executive Carcinogenicity Assessment Committee (ECAC: 2, 7, and 20 mg/kg/day), which were selected based on adverse kidney findings (increased kidney weight and chronic progressive nephropathy) in a 6-month dose ranging study. ECAC and the Division considered the study in males inadequate to assess the risk of carcinogenicity because the duration of exposure was limited. However, based on the absence of preneoplastic findings and tumors in males exposed for up to 88 weeks at 3 times the MRHD and in females exposed for 100 weeks at doses up to 68 times the MRHD, repeating the carcinogenicity study in male rats was not considered warranted.
L976: ## 104-Week Oral Carcinogenicity Study of Bexagliflozin in CD-1 Mice
L977: Mice were administered bexagliflozin by oral gavage at 0 (1% medium viscosity carboxymethylcellulose in water), 15, 50, or 150 mg/kg/day for approximately 2 years (males, 104 weeks; females, 97 weeks). The high dose of 150 mg/kg was selected based on AUC ratio and maximum tolerated dose (MTD) in males based on mortality at 120 to 160 times the clinical AUC. ECAC concurred with the Applicant's dose selection. No treatment-related non-neoplastic
L978: or neoplastic findings were observed at doses up to 150 mg/kg, corresponding to an AUC of 170550 ng.h/mL (135 times the MRHD of 20 mg/day).

L1107: ## THR-1442-T-482: A 10-Week Toxicity Study of Bexagliflozin by Oral Administration (Gavage) in Juvenile Rats With a 4-Week Recovery Period
L1108: ## Key Findings
L1109: - Bexagliflozin doses: 0, 0.3, 3, 30 mg/kg/day.
- Increased kidney weight in all treated female groups (up to 45%) and in males at \ge 3 mg/kg/day (up to 35%) correlated with increased incidence of minimal to mild renal dilatation in males at \ge 3 mg/kg/day (11 times the MRHD) and in females at 30 mg/kg/day (139 times the MRHD). There were no toxicologically significant changes in kidney injury molecule-1 (KIM-1), a biomarker of tubular injury. A longer treatment duration (~26 weeks) in adult rats (e.g., 6 weeks old) did not alter renal structures, suggesting a particularly susceptible window for renal toxicity if exposed to bexagliflozin during postnatal weeks 3 to 6. This susceptible window in the young rats is characterized by active morphological and functional development of the kidneys and is equivalent to the events in the second and third trimester of human gestation and continuing until approximately 2 years of age.
- Increased trabecular bone (femur) in the high dose groups (127 times the MRHD), associated with increased trabecular bone mineral content (BMC) and bone mineral density (BMD) at the distal metaphysis in males. No changes were observed in recovery animals. Similar findings have been observed with other approved SGLT2 inhibitors and are likely related to calorie-wasting and/or off-target inhibition of SGLT1, which is not expected at the clinical exposure.
- NOAEL was 0.3 mg/kg/day in males (1,370 ng.h/mL, at the MRHD) and 3 mg/kg/day in females (14,400 ng.h/mL, 11 times the MRHD) based on renal dilatation.

L1135: ## NDA 214373
## Brenzavvy (bexagliflozin)
L1136: Parameters	Major findings
Clinical Chemistry	No toxicological significant findings. On PND 91, there were mild increases (up to 1.8-fold) in urea nitrogen in high dose males and in females at \ge 3 mg/kg/day. No changes in creatinine were observed. Additionally, slight decreases in total protein and albumin in high dose females (6% and 7%, respectively) and slight increase in potassium levels in high dose males and females (7% and 8%, respectively) were noted. All these findings were reversible after 4 weeks of recovery period.
Urine Chemistry	Consistent with the intended pharmacology, moderate to marked increases in urine glucose excretion in all treatment groups and mild increases in renal calcium (up to 5.9 times the control group) and/or phosphorus excretion (up to 1.9 times the control group) in all treatment groups, except 0.3 mg/kg/day males, were observed. There were no toxicologically relevant bexagliflozin-related effects in urinary kidney injury molecule-1 (KIM-1), a marker of renal tubule injury.
Necropsy findings	Increased incidence of renal pelvic dilatation in males at \ge 3 mg/kg/day.

L1166: ## 14. Clinical Pharmacology: Additional Information and Assessment
L1167: ## 14.1. In Vitro Studies
L1168: ## 14.1.1. Protein Binding (Study THR-1474-N-371)
L1169: **Method:** An ultrafiltration technique was used for assessing drug binding to plasma protein. The samples were analyzed for bexagliflozin and [REDACTED](b)(4) (as a positive control) by liquid chromatography mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS).
L1170: ## **Results:**
L1171: - At concentrations of 200, 1000, and 5000 ng/mL, protein-bindings of bexagliflozin were 96.6\pm 0.7\%, 97.0\pm 0.3\%, and 93.3\pm 0.7\%, respectively, in pooled plasma samples from healthy human subjects.
- The human plasma protein binding of the positive control of [REDACTED](b)(4) was determined to be 96.7\pm 0.7\%, a value consistent with literature reports.
L1172: ## 14.1.2. Protein Binding (Study THR-1442-C-424)
L1173: **Method:** The effect of concentration on the plasma protein binding of bexagliflozin was assessed by equilibrium dialysis at 37°C for 7 hours, the experimentally determined equilibration time, in pooled plasma from subjects with T2DM and normal renal function at concentrations of 25, 50, 100, 250, and 500 ng/mL. Subsequently, in vitro experiments to assess whether or not bexagliflozin and its major metabolite EGT0002149 would interact with each other with respect to their binding to plasma proteins were performed by equilibrium dialysis at 37°C for 7 hours. Finally, the plasma protein binding of bexagliflozin was determined by equilibrium dialysis at 37°C for 7 hours in predose and 3-hour postdose plasma samples obtained from subjects enrolled in Trial C-424.
L1174: ## **Results:**
L1175: - The mean percentages of bexagliflozin bound to plasma proteins of donors with type 2 diabetes and normal renal function ranged from 90.9 to 93.0%, with no dependence on concentration over the range of 25 to 500 ng/mL.
- The mean percentages of bexagliflozin bound to plasma proteins when incubated with 0, 75, or 150 ng/mL EGT0002149 were 90.4, 90.3, and 89.3%, respectively, indicating that EGT0002149 did not affect the extent of bexagliflozin bound to plasma proteins.
- The mean or average percentages of bexagliflozin bound to plasma proteins when incubated with 0, 75, or 150 ng/mL bexagliflozin were 90.6, 88.7, and 86.3%, respectively, suggesting that bexagliflozin had a minor effect on the extent of EGT0002149 bound to plasma proteins.
- The mean or individual percentages of bexagliflozin bound to plasma proteins of 3-hour postdose plasma samples from subjects enrolled in Trial C-424 analyzed ex vitro ranged from 73.7 to 92.7%. However, with the exception of a single replicate sample at 73.7% (Subject 424-[REDACTED](b)(6)), all other postdose samples ranged from 83.7 to 92.7%.

Fraction of unbound drug substance was determined by an equilibrium dialysis method using a single sample from each study subject at 3 hours postdose (around T_{max}) and 24 hours postdose.

L1183: ## 14.1.4. In Vitro Metabolism in Human Liver Microsomes (Study THR-1474-N-341)
L1184: **Methods:** [^{14}\text{C}] bexagliflozin (100 \mu\text{M}) was incubated in the presence of human liver microsomes for 0, 15, 30, and 60 min at 37°C and a protein concentration of 1 mg/mL. Blank incubations were conducted (60 min) in the absence of microsomes and presence of an NADPH regenerating system and in the presence of microsomes and absence of an NADPH regenerating system to assess chemical degradation. Samples were analyzed with high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) using on-line ultraviolet (UV) and radiochemical detection.

L1194: ## 14.1.5. In Vitro Metabolism by Recombinant CYP3A (Study THR-1474-N-367)
L1195: **Methods:** Bexagliflozin (50 \mu\text{M} or 20 \mu\text{M}) was mixed with cell membrane preparations containing human recombinant CYP3A4 (20 pmol/mL or 10 pmol/mL) in potassium phosphate buffer (pH 7.4). An equal volume of NADPH regeneration system was added and incubated at 37°C for either 30 or 90 minutes. The reaction was terminated by the addition of acetonitrile to a final concentration of 33.33% and centrifugation at 10,000 g for 3 minutes. High performance liquid chromatography-photodiode-array mass spectrometry (HPLC-PDA/MS) was used to identify the metabolites.
L1196: ## **Results:**
L1197: - The incubation of bexagliflozin with human recombinant CYP3A4 resulted in the identification of two metabolites, EGT0001301 and EGT0001663.
L1198: - The metabolic rates for odealylation (EGT0001301) and hydroxylation (EGT0001663) increased as the amount of CYP3A4 increased (Table 79).

L1206: ## 14.1.6. In Vitro Metabolism by Human Liver Microsomes and Recombinant UGT (Study THR-1474-N-377)
L1207: **Methods:** The human liver microsome incubations were conducted at a microsomal protein concentration of 2 mg/mL and a single concentration of bexagliflozin (1mM) for 2 h; NADPH (2.0mM when present), UDPGA (2.0mM when present), magnesium chloride (10mM), and EDTA (2mM) in a total volume of 0.5 mL PBS buffer (100mM, pH 7.4) were also added to the reaction system. Reactions were terminated by adding ice-cold acetonitrile to the reaction mixtures.
L1208: Reaction mixtures containing 50mM Tris (pH 7.5), 10mM MgCl2, 5mM UDP-glucuronic acid, 0.025 mg/ml alamethicin, 0.35 \mug/\mul protein of different human recombinant UGT membrane preparations (UGT1A4, UGT1A6, UGT1A9, UGT1A10, UGT2B7), and 100\muM bexagliflozin were incubated at 37°C for 120 min in 200 \mul volume. Reactions were terminated by the addition of 100 \mul of acetonitrile, centrifuged at 10,000 g for 3 min and the supernatants were transferred to fresh tubes.
L1209: The incubation samples were analyzed by a developed HPLC-PDA/MS method.
L1210: ## Results:
L1211: - In human liver microsomes incubations containing solely UDPGA, the only glucuronide conjugate of bexagliflozin detected was metabolite M5 (EGT0002149).
- Following incubation with human liver microsomes fortified with UDPGA and NADPH, three additional metabolites M1 (EGT0001301), M2 (EGT0001494) and M4 (EGT0001663) were characterized in addition to M5. M5 was also identified following incubation with UDPGA and recombinant UGT1A9.
L1212: **Conclusion:** UGT1A9 is the major UGT isoform for glucuronidation in vitro.
L1213: ## **14.1.7. In Vitro CYP and UGT Phenotyping by Recombinant Human CYP and UGT Enzymes (Study THR-1442-N-440)**
L1214: **Methods:** For phase I metabolism, bexagliflozin (10 and 100 \muM) was incubated for 30 minutes with a panel of recombinant human CYP enzymes (rCYPs, namely rCYP1A2, rCYP2B6, rCYP2C8, rCYP2C9, rCYP2C19, rCYP2D6 and rCYP3A4, 10 pmol/incubation) and two negative controls (Bactosome control and reductase control). For phase II metabolism, bexagliflozin (10 and 100 \muM), was incubated with two recombinant human UGT enzymes (rUGTs, namely rUGT1A1 and rUGT2B7) and negative control (insect cell control). Metabolite production was monitored using an LC/MS/MS method that was transferred and modified for concentrations of the metabolites ranging from 10 to 1000 ng/mL. Positive controls were conducted in parallel using prototype substrates for each respective enzyme.
L1215: ## **Results:**
L1216: ## **Recombinant Human CYP Enzymes**
L1217: - From an initial concentration of 10 \muM bexagliflozin, CYP3A4 caused 16% depletion and CYP2D6 approximately 12% depletion. From an initial concentration of 100 \muM bexagliflozin, depletion greater than 10% was only observed in incubations with CYP3A4 (approximately 17%). Depletion by less than 10% was observed for the other recombinant CYP enzymes evaluated (data not shown).
- Bexagliflozin was metabolized in vitro by recombinant human CYP enzymes (predominantly by CYP3A4, with minor contributions from CYP2C8 and 2D6) to EGT0001301 and EGT0001685 (Table 80).

L1231: ## 14.1.8. Identification of Additional Metabolites (Study THR-1474-N-382)
L1232: **Methods:** Bioanalyses performed on plasma, urine, and fecal samples collected from subjects after administration of a single oral dose of bexagliflozin (150 mg, cohort 6) in Trial C-328. The metabolites of bexagliflozin in human urine, feces, and plasma were also identified and characterized using an ultra-high performance liquid chromatography-quadrupole time-of-flight mass spectrometry (UPLC/Q-TOF MS) via positive and negative scan modes in SCDMPK.
L1233: ## **Results:**
L1234: - In addition to the six known metabolites (three oxidative metabolites: EGT0001301, EGT0001494 and EGT0001663, and three bexagliflozin glucuronides), six additional minor metabolites were identified and partially characterized (Figure 20).In plasma, two additional metabolites were found: UM4, the product of oxidation of the bexagliflozin glucose 6' carbon to a carboxylic acid (bexagliflozin glucuronic acid) and UM6-2, a glucuronide of EGT0001301.
- In urine, six additional metabolites were found: UM4, described above, UM5-1 and -2, two glucuronides of the phenol resulting from abstraction of the bexagliflozin ethyloxycyclopropyl moiety, UM6-1 and -2, two glucuronides of EGT0001301, and UM7, a glucuronide of EGT0001494.
- In feces, UM4 was also found.
L1235: **Figure 20. Minor Metabolites of Bexagliflozin**
L1236: Chemical structures illustrating the metabolism of Bexagliflozin into minor metabolites (UM4, UM5-1, UM5-2, UM6-1, UM6-2, and UM7). Bexagliflozin is shown undergoing oxidation to form UM4 (bexagliflozin glucuronic acid) and glucuronidation to form UM6-2 (glucuronide of EGT0001301). Further oxidation of the phenol moiety leads to UM5-1 and UM5-2 (glucuronides of the phenol resulting from abstraction of the bexagliflozin ethyloxycyclopropyl moiety). Glucuronidation of EGT0001301 yields UM6-1 and UM6-2. Glucuronidation of EGT0001494 yields UM7. The distribution of these metabolites is indicated by arrows pointing to Plasma, Urine, and Feces.
L1237: Source: Figure 2.7.2-7 Summary of Clinical Pharmacology Studies
L1238: ***FDA Reviewer Comment:*** *None of the metabolites contribute to the pharmacological activity of bexagliflozin.*
L1239: ## 14.1.9. In Vivo Metabolic Profiling Study of Bexagliflozin Metabolites (Study THR-1442-N-403)
L1240: **Methods:** In this study, the major metabolites of bexagliflozin following a single oral dose of 100 mg or 17 mg in healthy subjects (Trial C-328) were profiled and quantified in plasma and urine using a developed LC/MS/MS method.
L1241: ## **Results:**
L1242: - Bexagliflozin is extensively metabolized to oxidation products and glucuronides.
- The principal metabolite is the 3'-O-glucuronide EGT0002149.

L1248: ## 14.1.10. Inhibitory Effect of Bexagliflozin on CYP450 Activities (Study THR-1474-N-346)
L1249: **Methods:** The inhibitory potential of eight concentrations (0.0229, 0.0686, 0.206, 0.617, 1.85, 5.56, 16.7, and 50.0 µM) of EGT0001474 (bexagliflozin: L-proline 1:2 cocystal) were evaluated with pooled human liver microsomes. These concentrations approximated and significantly exceeded the plasma concentrations anticipated in humans. The six CYP isoenzymes monitored in the study were CYP1A2, CYP2B6, CYP2C9, CYP2C19, CYP2D6, and CYP3A4. Control
L1250: incubations were performed for each assay with appropriate positive inhibitory controls. Time-dependent inhibition was evaluated by preincubating the test article in the presence of the microsomes and NADPH for 30 minutes prior to adding the probe substrate.
L1251: ## Results:
L1252: - EGT0001474 at concentrations up to 50 µM did not inhibit enzyme assays specific to CYP1A2, CYP2B6, CYP2C9, CYP2C19, CYP2D6, and CYP3A4 by 50% or more.
- EGT0001474 had a weak inhibitory effect on CYP2B6 as the half maximal inhibitory concentration (IC_{50}) value was more than 50 µM (Table 83).

L1259: ## 14.1.11. Induction Effect of Bexagliflozin on CYP450 Activities (Study THR-1474-N-347)
L1260: **Methods:** Plated cryopreserved human hepatocytes were separately incubated with 0.05, 0.50, and 5.0 µM solutions of EGT0001474 in supplemented William's E media for 48 hours. The selected concentrations were expected to approximate and significantly exceed the anticipated clinical exposure conditions. Controls of 1 µM 3-methylcholanthrene, 10 µM rifampicin, and 25 µM rifampicin in the same media were used to establish positive induction responses for CYP1A2, CYP2C19, and CYP3A4, respectively. The activities of CYP1A2, CYP2C19, and CYP3A4 were determined by incubating the cells with solutions of phenacetin, S-mephentytoin, and testosterone, respectively, in the same media. Samples of the media were removed, extracted, and analyzed for the metabolites of the probe substrate using HPLC in conjunction with LC/MS/MS.
L1261: ## Results:
L1262: - Exposure of human hepatocytes to 0.05, 0.5, and 5 \muM bexagliflozin did not result in notable induction of enzyme activities associated with CYP1A2, CYP2C19, or CYP3A4 isoforms in vitro (Table 84).

L1268: ## 14.1.12. Inhibitory Effect of Bexagliflozin on CYP2C8 Activity (Study THR-1442-N-439)
L1269: **Methods:** To evaluate bexagliflozin as a direct, time-dependent, and metabolism-dependent inhibitor of CYP2C8 activity, human liver microsomes from a pool of sixteen individuals were incubated with the marker substrate in the presence or absence of bexagliflozin. To distinguish between time-dependent and metabolism-dependent inhibition, bexagliflozin was preincubated with human liver microsomes for 30 minutes without and with an NADPH-generating system, respectively, prior to incubation with the marker substrate. Known direct and metabolism-dependent inhibitors of CYP2C8 were included as positive controls, and negative controls included the absence of bexagliflozin.
L1270: ## Results:
L1271: - Under the experimental conditions examined, there was little or no evidence of direct, time-dependent, or metabolism-dependent inhibition of CYP2C8 by bexagliflozin. Bexagliflozin is unlikely to inhibit CYP2C8 at the clinically relevant dose.

L1279: ## 14.1.13. In Vitro Permeation of Bexagliflozin Through Caco-2 Monolayers (Study THR-1442-N-431)
L1280: **Methods:** Bidirectional transport experiments were conducted in 21-day Caco-2 monolayer cultures. Bexagliflozin and (b) (4) (internal standard for high permeability) were dissolved in HBG buffer and added to the donor chamber of the filter at the desired concentrations (10 \muM and 100 \muM for bexagliflozin, 100 \muM for (b) (4)). The transport experiments were conducted bidirectionally in duplicate. Samples in the receiver chamber were collected at multiple time points after the addition of the test articles.
L1281: ## Results:
L1282: - An active efflux process favors basolateral to apical transport of bexagliflozin at an efflux ratio &gt;2 (mean value of 7.4). Further in vitro studies are needed to determine the efflux transporters involved in this process.

L1287: ## 14.1.14. P-gp Substrate and Inhibitory Potential (Study THR-1442-N-432)
L1288: **Methods:** For bidirectional transport assays, Caco-2 cells were grown to confluence for 14 to 21 days on 1.0 µm BD Falcon filters in 24-well plates. Monolayer integrity was confirmed by transepithelial electrical resistance values greater than 400 ohms-cm2 prior to assay initiation and monitored during the studies by Lucifer yellow transfer. The bidirectional apparent permeability coefficients (Papp) and efflux ratio were determined for 1 to 100µM bexagliflozin using 20-minute sampling intervals over 2 hours. For P-gp inhibitor assays, transport of [3H] Digoxin transport was assessed in the presence of 100µM bexagliflozin.
L1289: ## **Results:**
L1290: - The efflux ratios were 13, 6.7, and 5.4 for 1, 10, and 100 µM bexagliflozin, respectively. The inclusion of 20 µM cyclosporin A (a potent inhibitor of P-gp) with 10 µM bexagliflozin reduced the efflux ratio to 1.9, indicating that bexagliflozin is a potential P-gp substrate.
- The presence of 100 µM bexagliflozin reduced the efflux ratio for [3H]-digoxin from 10.3 to 3.5 suggesting that bexagliflozin at 100 µM is a potential inhibitor of P-gp but is not as potent as 20 µM cyclosporin A, which reduced the efflux ratio for [3H]-digoxin to 1.5. Calculation of the half-maximal inhibition constant (IC50) for this interaction based on efflux ratio yielded an estimated value of 3.7 µM (2.3 to 6 µM range).
L1291: **FDA Reviewer Comment:** The determined IC50 is much higher than the Cmax of bexagliflozin following the oral dose of 20 mg with calculated RI&lt;1.02. RI in the gut is estimated to be about 6 and is less than the cut-off value of 11 in the DDI Guidance (January 2020). Therefore, bexagliflozin is unlikely to be a significant P-gp inhibitor in the clinical setting. Nonetheless, the Applicant conducted a clinical DDI study and demonstrated the lack of significant effect of bexagliflozin on the pharmacokinetics (PK) of the sensitive P-gp substrate digoxin.
L1292: ## 14.1.15. Inhibitory Effect of Bexagliflozin on Transporters (Study THR-1442-N-441)
L1293: **Methods:** Vesicles or cells transfected with control vectors were used as negative controls and the validity of each assay was confirmed with a positive control inhibitor for each transporter. Bidirectional apparent permeability coefficients, the resulting efflux ratios (for breast cancer resistance protein [BCRP]), and the cleared volume (for BSEP, OAT1, OAT3, OATP1B1, OATP1B3, OCT1, and OCT2) were quantified using transporter specific substrates in the presence and absence of bexagliflozin at 1 and 100 µmol L-1. Each assay was conducted in duplicate and mean values were reported for each assay. For BCRP, OATP1B1, and OATP1B3, which were inhibited significantly by 100 µM bexagliflozin, IC50 values were determined.
L1294: ## **Results:**
L1295: - At concentrations up to 100µM, bexagliflozin did not inhibit BSEP, OAT1, OAT3, OCT1, and OCT2 (Table 87).
L1296: - The rank order for inhibition at 100 µM bexagliflozin was OATP1B1&gt;OATP1B3&gt;BCRP. However, the IC50 values were high multiples of the expected Cmax produced by the 20 mg bexagliflozin tablet (0.38 µM).
- Therefore, no meaningful inhibition on BCRP, BSEP, OAT1, OAT3, OATP1B1, OATP1B3, OCT1, and OCT2 is expected from the plasma levels produced by the intended dosage strength.

L1317: ## 14.2. In Vivo Studies
L1318: ## 14.2.1. Single and Multiple Dose in Healthy Subjects (Trial C-328)
L1319: ## Study Design
L1320: This was a phase 1, double-blind, placebo-controlled, dose-escalation study conducted in 78 healthy male and female subjects to assess the safety, tolerability, PK, and pharmacodynamics (PD) (24 hours urinary glucose excretion [UGE]) of rising single and multiple oral doses of bexagliflozin. In the study, bexagliflozin was administered as an L-proline: bexagliflozin 2:1 cocrystal (EGT0001474) formulated in neat-filled hypromellose capsules. Therefore, EGT0001474 doses of 2.5 mg to 150 mg listed below are cocrystal doses and are equivalent to bexagliflozin doses of 1.67 to 100 mg.
L1321: - In Part 1: subjects were randomized to receive either a single oral dose of placebo or EGT0001474 at 2.5 mg, 5 mg, 10 mg, 25 mg, 75 mg, or 150 mg in the fasted state.
L1322: Subjects in the food effect cohort received a second dose of placebo or 25 mg EGT0001474 after a standard high fat breakfast.
L1323: - In Part 2: subjects received single oral daily doses of placebo or EGT0001474 at 10 mg, 50 mg, or 150 mg in the fasted state for 14 days.
L1324: Serial PK, safety, and PD evaluations were performed at prespecified times throughout the study.
L1325: ## Results
L1326: - Following the oral administration of bexagliflozin capsules, peak plasma concentrations of bexagliflozin reached between 2 to 4 hours postdose (Figure 21).
- Based on data from the single ascending dose (SAD) portion of the study, bexagliflozin exhibits a linear PK (as assessed by C_{max} and AUC) in EGT0001474 doses ranging from 2.5 mg to 150 mg (equivalent to 1.7 mg to 100 mg bexagliflozin, Table 90).
- Food delayed T_{max} by 1 to 2 hours and decreased the mean C_{max} and AUC_{0-inf} by approximately 34% and 10%, respectively, when compared to the fasted state.
- Based on data from the multiple ascending dose (MAD) portion of the study, there is no significant accumulation after multiple doses of bexagliflozin capsules once daily for 14 days at 6.7 mg to 100 mg with accumulation ratios ranging from 1.10 to 1.17 (Table 90).
- Bexagliflozin increased UGE in healthy subjects in a dose-dependent and saturable manner with plateau between 16.7 mg and 50 mg of bexagliflozin (Figure 22).

L1335: ## Conclusion
L1336: - Bexagliflozin was well tolerated up to 100 mg per day for 14 days.
- Bexagliflozin, administered as oral capsules, was rapidly absorbed, and resulted in dose-dependent increases in systemic exposure and dose-related saturable glucosuria.
L1337: ***FDA Reviewer Comment:*** Linear PK in the dose range of 1.7 mg to 100 mg is based on C_{max} and AUC values. The terminal t_{1/2} values appear to increase with increasing bexagliflozin doses. Nonetheless, based on limited accumulation between 6.7 and 100 mg, the effective t_{1/2} may be comparable among the doses. Based on data from Part 2, after 14 days of repeat dosing, UGE declined by about 13% in the 100 mg bexagliflozin/day cohort and 26% in the 16.7 mg bexagliflozin/day cohort when compared to the UGE values measured on Day 1 in the same cohort.
L1338: ## 14.2.2. SAD Study in Patients With Type 2 Diabetes (Trial C-396)
L1339: ## Study Design
L1340: This was a phase 1, single-dose, double-blind, placebo-controlled study to assess the PK, PD (UGE), and safety tolerability of bexagliflozin following the oral administration of 25 mg, 75 mg, and 150 mg EGT0001474 (capsules; equivalent to 16.7, 50, and 100 mg bexagliflozin) in subjects with T2DM. During the study, 24 subjects (3 cohorts of 8 subjects per cohort) were randomized in a ratio of 3:1 to bexagliflozin or placebo groups. Serial PK, safety, and PD evaluations were performed at prespecified times throughout the study.
L1341: ## Results
L1342: - Upon absorption, the maximum plasma concentration (C_{max}) of bexagliflozin was reached at 2 to 3 hours postdose (range 0.5 to 8 hours) (Figure 23).
- Systemic exposures (C_{max} and AUC) of bexagliflozin showed a linear dose proportionality in the studied dose range of 16.7 mg and 100 mg (Table 91).
- Although the amount of UGE increased significantly compared to that measured in subjects taking placebo, the increase (24 hour UGE between 90 to 120 g) was comparable at the studied doses of 16.7 mg and 100 mg (Table 92).
- Single doses of bexagliflozin decreased the fasting plasma glucose (FPG) levels by 29 mg/dL, 27 mg/dL, and 26 mg/dL, respectively, 24 hours after bexagliflozin administration at the doses of 16.7 mg, 50 mg, and 100 mg (Table 93).

L1357: ## Conclusion
L1358: - A single dose of bexagliflozin up to 100 mg (or 150 mg EGT0001474) is well tolerated in subjects with T2DM.
- Bexagliflozin doses \ge16.7 mg (or 25 mg EGT0001474) produced significant glucosuria and induced significant reduction in fasting plasma glucose compared to placebo in T2DM patients.

L1367: ## Results
L1368: ## Part 1: SAD in Healthy Japanese Subjects
L1369: - Following a single dose oral administration of bexagliflozin tablets, a dose-proportional increase in C_{max} and AUC of bexagliflozin was observed in the studied dose range of 3 mg to 90 mg. The percentage of dose excreted in urine (Fe %dose) as bexagliflozin was 2.17 to 2.76% of the dose and thus, renal clearance (CL_r) was a minor component of the total clearance (Figure 24 and Table 95).
- A dose-proportional increase in C_{max} and AUC of metabolite EGT0002149 was observed. The Fe %dose as metabolite EGT0002149 was 28.4 to 34.8% of the dose and thus, CL_r was a significant component of the total clearance of the metabolite (Figure 24 and Table 96).
- For bexagliflozin, subjects dosed in the fed state exhibited a higher C_{max} compared to subjects dosed in the fasted state. The terminal elimination constant (\lambda_z) and T_{max} were unaffected by food consumption. There was no impact on the PK of the metabolite (data not shown).
- Consistent with the study results in American subjects, UGE in Japanese subjects increased in a dose-dependent manner after administration of 3 mg through 30 mg. The UGE was essentially the same in the 30 and 90-mg dose groups (Table 97)

L1387: ## Part 2: MAD in Japanese Subjects With T2DM
L1388: - The systemic exposures of bexagliflozin and its metabolite are dose-proportional at the doses ranging from 3 to 30 mg.
- Upon once daily dosing, there was no significant accumulation of bexagliflozin or its metabolite (Table 98 and Table 99).
- As shown in Table 100, although the UGE rate was greater for treated subjects than placebo subjects on Days 1 and 7, the UGE rate geometric means were comparable among 3 mg, 10 mg, and 30-mg dose groups.

L1412: ## Conclusion:
L1413: - Administration of bexagliflozin up to 90 mg to Japanese subjects was safe and well tolerated.
- Prior consumption of food was not found to markedly change the PK parameters observed following administration of the 10 and 30 mg bexagliflozin tablets.
- Bexagliflozin at the studied doses of 3 mg to 90 mg increased UGE in both healthy subjects and subjects with T2DM.
- Bexagliflozin significantly reduced FPG in Japanese subjects with T2DM at 10 mg and 30-mg doses.
L1414: ## 14.2.4. Mass Balance Study (Trial C-410)
L1415: ## Study Design
L1416: This was an open-label, radiolabeled mass balance study conducted in six healthy male subjects to determine absorption, routes of elimination, and circulatory and excretory metabolites of bexagliflozin. During the study, subjects received a single oral dose of 50 mg of bexagliflozin (with approximately 100 µCi of [14C]-bexagliflozin) in an aqueous solution. Plasma and whole blood samples were collected for at least 48 hours after dosing. Urine and feces samples were collected for up to 9 days or to when the total excreted radioactivity levels had exceeded 90% of the administered radioactivity, whichever occurred first.
L1417: ## Results
L1418: ## Plasma:
L1419: - Mean C_{max} and AUC_{inf} values for total radioactivity in plasma were approximately 2-fold higher than those for total radioactivity in whole blood, indicating that most of the total radioactivity resides in the plasma compartment of blood and is not highly associated with blood cells.
- The t_{1/2} of unchanged parent drug in plasma from humans was 5.6 hours after oral dosing.
- In plasma, 55% of the circulating radioactivity was associated with unchanged bexagliflozin. EGT0002149, an O-glucuronide, was the major circulating metabolite in plasma contributing to 32% of parent AUC and 18% of total radioactivity AUC. Other metabolites identified in plasma were the O-glucuronide conjugates EGT0002147 and EGT0002148; and the phase 1 metabolites EGT0001301 (M1), EGT0001494 (M2), and EGT0001684. All other metabolites were &lt;10% of parent AUC and total radioactivity AUC (Table 102). A metabolism diagram is provided in Figure 25.

L1426: ## Urine and Feces:
L1427: - Total recovery of radioactivity in urine and feces combined was approximately 91.6% over the 192-hour postdose assessment period, representing 51.1% mean recovery in feces and 40.5% mean recovery in urine.
- Most of the radioactivity excreted in urine was associated with EGT0002149, accounting for 30.1% of the administered dose through 96 hours post dosing, of which the majority was excreted within the first 12 hours.
L1428: - For minor metabolites, 1.69% EGT0001301 (M1), 3.88% EGT0001494 (M2), 1.63% EGT0002147, and 0.45% EGT0002148 were also identified in urine.
- Unchanged parent drug in urine accounted for 1.50% of the dose through 96 hours postdose.
- Most of the radioactivity in feces was associated with the unchanged parent drug, accounting for 28.7% of the administered dose through 144 hours postdose.
- In feces, EGT0001301 (M1) and EGT0001494 (M2) were the major metabolites and accounted for 8.03 and 10.1% of the dose, respectively, through 144 hours postdose. EGT0001684 was also identified in feces.
L1429: ## Conclusions
L1430: - Most of the total radioactivity was in plasma and was not highly associated with blood cells.
- Bexagliflozin was metabolized in humans via oxidation and glucuronidation with 55.3% of the circulating radioactivity associated with the parent drug.
- EGT0002149 (glucuronide metabolite) was the major circulating metabolite in plasma.
- Mean total recovery of radioactivity was 91.6%, with a mean of 51.1% of the dose excreted in feces and 40.5% excreted in urine through 192 hours postdose.
- In urine, most of the radioactivity (30.1% of the dose) was associated with EGT0002149.
- In feces, most of the radioactivity (28.7% of the dose) was associated with unchanged parent drug.
- Bexagliflozin was safe and well tolerated in this group of healthy male subjects.
L1431: ## 14.2.5. Food Effect Study (Trial C-481)
L1432: ## Study Design
L1433: This was a phase 1, open-label, two-treatment, two-period crossover study designed to assess the effects of a high-fat meal on the PK of orally administered bexagliflozin tablets in 18 healthy adults. Subjects were randomized 1:1 to receive bexagliflozin tablets with a high-fat meal on Day 1 and without a meal on Day 8 after an overnight fast or to receive bexagliflozin tablets without a meal on Day 1 after an overnight fast and with a high-fat meal on Day 8. Blood and urine samples were collected at prespecified time points up to 48 hours postdose.
L1434: ## Results
L1435: - High fat, high calorie meal did not affect the extent of bexagliflozin absorption with both AUC parameters entirely contained within the 80% to 125% margins (Table 103).
- Intake of a high-fat, high-calorie meal increased bexagliflozin Cmax by approximately 30% and delayed the median Tmax by 1.5 hours (5.0 and 3.5 hours for fed and fasted states, respectively).
- Intrasubject variability was low (&lt;30%) for the primary PK parameters AUC0-t, AUC0-∞, and Cmax.
L1436: - The elimination half-life is 11.7 h or 10.1 h following dosing in the fasted or fed states, respectively.
- Administration of bexagliflozin was well tolerated under both fasted and fed conditions.

L1446: ## 14.2.6. Formulation Development (Trial CLR-002)
L1447: ## Study Design:
L1448: This was a phase 1, open-labeled, crossover (Part 1) and parallel (Part 2) study to assess the PK and PD of multiple oral doses of bexagliflozin sustained release (SR) tablets in healthy male subjects.
L1449: - In Part 1, a crossover design was used. Twenty eligible subjects were dosed in a randomized sequence with each of 4 formulations of bexagliflozin in 15-mg formulations of bexagliflozin SR tablets (SR11, SR8, and SR5) and 20 mg bexagliflozin capsule.
- In Part 2, three bexagliflozin formulations (SR5 and additional formulations of 10 and 30 mg) were administered orally under fasting condition on Day 1 and 2 and 30 minutes after a standard meal on Day 3.
L1450: Serial PK, safety, and PD evaluations were performed at prespecified times up to 48 hours postdose.
L1451: ## Results:
L1452: - Median Tmax values were 1 hour for the capsule formulation and 3 hours for all SR tablet formulations (Figure 26). Administration of the SR formulations in the fed state resulted
L1453: in an increase in exposure of 17% to 45% and 71% to 97%, for AUC_{0-\infty} and C_{max}, respectively, compared to administration in the fasted state (Table 104).

- SR5 formulation showed the largest systemic exposures of the SR formulations and was selected to be studied in Part 2.
- In Part 2, bexagliflozin exposures (AUC_{0-24} and C_{max}) generally increased in a dose-proportional manner over the dose range of 10 to 30 mg of the SR5 formulation (Figure 27 and Table 105).
- There was no apparent difference in UGE between formulations in Part 1 (data not shown). In Part 2 (SR5 formulation), UGE_{0-24} values were comparable between 10 and 15-mg dose groups, both of which were slightly lower than that from the 30-mg dose group (Table 106).

L1473: ## Conclusions
L1474: - Administration of 10 to 30 mg of bexagliflozin from SR5 formulation was safe and well tolerated in this group of healthy male subjects.
- Based on the PK and PD data from this study, SR5 formulation was selected as the formulation for further clinical trials.
L1475: ***FDA Reviewer Comment:*** Per the Applicant, the prolonged release profile of bexagliflozin from the SR5 formulation is mediated by (b) (4) excipients that promote gastric retention. In Part 1 of the study, PK exposure of bexagliflozin was compared between 20 mg prolonged release tablet formulation (SR5) and 15 mg immediate release capsule formulation in a crossover manner. Based on the demonstrated dose proportionality of bexagliflozin in the range of 1.67 to 100 mg, bexagliflozin exposures were normalized by the studied doses to assess the relative bioavailability between capsule and tablet (SR5) formulations. The results showed that the prolonged release tablet formulation (SR5) had about 16% lower AUC and 55% lower Cmax compared to the immediate release capsule formulation.

- Seven phase 3 clinical trials and six clinical pharmacology studies were conducted using the modified SR5 formulation.
- The PD (UGE) activities of bexagliflozin are comparable between the capsule and tablet formulations (Figure 28). PK and PD information was used to support the dosage form designation as immediate release tablet by the biopharmaceutical reviewer (See. Dr. Joan Zhao's review for details).

L1480: ## 14.2.7. Effect of Hepatic Impairment (Trial C-455)
L1481: ## Study Design
L1482: This was a phase 1, open-label, parallel-group study to assess the effect of moderate hepatic impairment on the PK and PD of orally administered bexagliflozin tablets. A total of 16 subjects comprising 8 with moderate hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh total score 7 to 9) and 8 healthy, matched controls, were enrolled and received a single oral dose of bexagliflozin tablets, 20 mg, after an overnight fast. Blood samples were collected prior to dosing, and at multiple time points for up to 48 hours postdose. The unbound fraction of bexagliflozin at 24 hours postdose and at the maximum plasma concentration for each subject was determined by equilibrium dialysis. Urine samples for PD analysis were collected for the 12 hour interval preceding dosing and 48 hours following dosing. Plasma concentrations of bexagliflozin were determined by a validated LC-MS/MS assay.
L1483: ## Results
L1484: - Bexagliflozin AUC_{0-\infty} and C_{max} were about 28 to 32% and 6 to 10% higher, respectively, in subjects with moderate hepatic dysfunction compared to subjects with normal function. (Table 107 and Table 108).
- Plasma protein binding were minimally affected by moderate hepatic impairment.
- T_{1/2} values were comparable between subjects with moderate hepatic impairment (11.2\pm4.16 hrs) and subjects with normal hepatic function (12.3\pm6.56 hrs).
- Urinary glucose excretion was lower in the group with reduced hepatic function, with 24 hour collection values of 58.5 and 46.8 g for subjects with normal and moderately diminished function, respectively. The corresponding values for the creatinine normalized urinary glucose excretion over the 24 hours postdose was 67.38 (19.0) and 74.69 (35.2) g for subjects with normal or moderately diminished function, respectively, and were consistent with the substantially lower creatinine excretion displayed by the impaired cohort.
L1485: - Bexagliflozin was well tolerated, treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs) were mild in severity and no subject experienced a death, serious TEAE, or TEAE leading to withdrawal from the study.

L1500: ## Conclusions
L1501: - Moderate hepatic impairment slightly increased bexagliflozin exposures (~30% for AUC). No significant impact on UGE was observed after correcting by the renal function.
- An adjustment of dosage for patients with mild to moderate hepatic impairment is not considered necessary in light of the wide safety margins observed in the bexagliflozin development program.
L1502: ## 14.2.8. Effect of Renal Impairment (Trial C-424)
L1503: ## Study Design
L1504: This was a phase 1, open-label, parallel-group study to assess the effect of mild, moderate, and severe renal impairment on the PK and PD of orally administered bexagliflozin capsules in subjects with T2DM. During the study, subjects received a single dose of 20 mg bexagliflozin
L1505: capsules, administered orally after overnight fast. Four cohorts of 6 to 9 subjects were enrolled, representing individuals with normal (GFR \ge 90 mL min^{-1} per 1.73 m^2, n=8), mildly impaired (60 \le GFR &lt; 90, n=8), moderately impaired (30 \le GFR &lt; 60, n=9) or severely impaired (GFR &lt; 30, n=6) renal function. Timed blood and urine specimens for PK and PD analysis were collected.
L1506: ## Results
L1507: ## Parent Drug PK
L1508: - Systemic exposure (AUC_{0-\infty}) of bexagliflozin was significantly increased in subjects with moderate and severe renal impairment, with a mean ratio of 1.34 and 1.54, respectively, as compared to subjects with normal renal function. AUC_{0-inf} was similar between the groups with normal renal function and mild renal impairment (Figure 29 and Table 109).
- The percent of plasma protein binding was not affected by declining renal function, with mean values of 88.23%, 87.99%, 89.38%, and 85.97% in the normal renal function, mildly, moderately, and severely impaired groups, respectively.
- Elimination half-life was slightly increased in subjects with renal impairment (7.3 to 7.9 hours) but was not significantly different from the group with normal renal function (6.7 hours).
- The percent of parent drug excreted in urine gradually decreased with declining renal function: 1.25% was excreted in urine in the group with mild impairment, 0.91% in the group with moderate impairment, and 0.51% in the group with severe impairment.
L1509: ## Metabolite PK
L1510: - For metabolite EGT0002149, its systemic exposures increased with increasing kidney disease severity suggesting reduced renal clearance. Compared to subjects with normal renal function, AUC_{0-24h} was comparable in subjects with mild renal impairment, 1.6-fold, and 2.2-fold higher in subjects with moderate and severe renal impairment, respectively (Figure 29).
- As renal clearance is a significant route of elimination for the glucuronide, renal excretion was incrementally reduced with increasing kidney disease severity, from 32.9% to 21.5%, 15.6%, and 6.3% of dose in normal renal function and mild, moderate, and severe impairment, respectively.
- As a result of decreased renal elimination of the glucuronide, metabolite to parent AUC ratios were incrementally higher with increasing severity of renal impairment (geometric means 69.4%, 76.2%, and 98.2% in mild, moderate, and severe renal impairment, respectively).
L1511: ## PD (UGE)
L1512: - Consistent with the mechanism of action of bexagliflozin, the urinary excretion of glucose highly depends on the renal function. In patients with moderate and severe renal impairment, UGE values were reduced by 60% and 80% compared to patients with normal renal function (Table 110).
