L2055: **Statistical Methods:** The primary hypothesis is that bexagliflozin is noninferior to glimepiride by evaluating the treatment effect on HbA1c reduction at Week 60 in combination with metformin. The noninferiority margin for mean change from baseline at Week 60 in HbA1c comparing bexagliflozin group with glimepiride group will be 0.35%. Superiority will be declared without additional statistical testing when the upper bound of the 95% CI for difference in change from baseline at Week 60 in HbA1c comparing bexagliflozin group with glimepiride group is less than 0. The treatment difference will be examined by using an MMRM ANCOVA. The model will include treatment, visit, treatment-by-visit interaction, and randomization stratification factors as the fixed effects terms and the baseline HbA1c value as a fixed effect covariate. Least squares mean treatment differences between the bexagliflozin group and the comparator group at Week 60 in change from baseline will be estimated from the model. An unstructured covariance will be used to model the within-subject correlation. If the model with the unstructured covariance structure does not converge, an autoregressive (1) covariance structure will be used. HbA1c values obtained after the start of rescue medication will not be excluded from this primary analysis. Primary endpoint will be analyzed on both ITT and PP analysis sets.
L2056: The MMRM model is one approach to obtain treatment effect estimates in the presence of missing data. As sensitivity analyses for missing data, the following will be performed on both ITT and PP analysis sets:
L2057: - Missing data will be imputed via multiple imputations, following which the MMRM will be repeated on the complete datasets with results combined across complete datasets using standard multiple imputation techniques; HbA1c values collected after the start of rescue medication will not be excluded.
- Missing data will be imputed via LOCF, following which the MMRM will be repeated; HbA1c values collected after the start of rescue medication will be considered missing.
- HbA1c values collected after the start of rescue medication will be considered missing, and the MMRM analyses will be reperformed.
L2058: The effects of bexagliflozin on the changes from baseline at Week 60 in body weight and systolic blood pressure, the difference in the proportion of subjects with \ge 1 severe or documented symptomatic hypoglycemia events over 96 weeks and the change in HbA1c from baseline at Week 60 will be tested as key secondary endpoints and will be analyzed in a hierarchical testing strategy and only if the primary objective is met. Similar to the primary endpoint, ANCOVA models will be used for the continuous secondary endpoints and logistic regression model will be used for the binary endpoint. A hierarchical testing strategy will be followed to preserve experiment-wide alpha at 0.05:
L2059: - Superiority test of the change in body weight in subjects with baseline BMI \ge 25 kg/m^2 in the bexagliflozin group versus the glimepiride group at Week 60
- Superiority test of the change in SBP in subjects with baseline SBP \ge 140 mm Hg in the bexagliflozin group versus the glimepiride group at Week 60
- Superiority test of the difference in proportion of subjects with \ge 1 severe or documented symptomatic hypoglycemia event in the bexagliflozin group versus the glimepiride group over 96 weeks
L2060: Additional effects of bexagliflozin versus glimepiride on the changes in HbA1c, FPG, SBP, body weight, the proportion of subjects who reach an HbA1c &lt;7\%, and the proportion of subjects with \ge 1 severe or documented symptomatic hypoglycemia events over time, as well as the general safety in subjects with T2DM, will be analyzed as exploratory efficacy endpoints. These endpoints are considered exploratory and will not be adjusted for multiplicity.
L2061: For the primary efficacy endpoint, a minimum of 172 subjects are needed in each treatment arm to detect noninferiority of bexagliflozin to glimepiride with respect to the change in HbA1c from baseline at Week 60 by a margin of 0.35%, assuming an estimated pooled standard deviation of 1.0%. This estimation is based on a one-sided t-test with 90% power at a 0.025 level of significance. To allow for an estimated 18.0% dropout rate, 210 patients will be randomized in each treatment arm, and the total sample size will be 420 subjects for this study.
L2062: Statistical analyses and summaries will be performed using SAS software (SAS Institute, Cary, NC).
L2063: ***FDA Reviewer Comment:*** *This trial aimed to demonstrate that bexagliflozin is noninferior to the sulfonylurea glimepiride as add-on therapy in subjects with T2DM not adequately controlled by metformin treatment. Sulfonylureas may be prescribed with metformin as a combination therapy for treating T2DM. As such, clinical programs for other SGLT2 inhibitors have evaluated noninferiority of the candidate drug to glimepiride. Glimepiride is an appropriate comparator for the evaluation of noninferiority of bexagliflozin to another oral agent prescribed for the treatment of T2DM.*
L2064: *The trial enrolled subjects with T2DM taking stable doses of metformin monotherapy, or subjects taking metformin and one other antihyperglycemic agent willing to undergo a 6-week washout period. The trial also included a two-week run-in period, such that subjects requiring washout were on metformin monotherapy for a minimum of 8 weeks prior to randomization. In addition, randomization was stratified by background treatment status (metformin only versus metformin plus an additional oral agent), HbA1c (\le 8.5\% versus &gt;8.5\%), and eGFR (\ge 90 mL/min/1.73 m^2 versus &lt;90 mL/min/1.73 m^2). These procedures appear reasonable to mitigate the possibility that oral antihyperglycemic agents other than metformin taken prior to study enrollment impacted study outcomes.*
L2065: *Sulfonylureas are known to increase the risk of hypoglycemia. To control hyperglycemia and minimize hypoglycemia, subjects were initiated on glimepiride (or placebo glimepiride) at 2 mg and underwent dose up-titration based on protocol-specified criteria during the first 6 weeks of the study. Although the maximum approved dose in the US is 8 mg, titration of glimepiride only occurred up to 6 mg, potentially due to differences among countries in maximum approved doses in this global trial. The procedures for glimepiride titration in this trial appear generally reasonable. Similar to active controlled Trial C-423, the NI margin was larger than what is has been used in other SGLT2 inhibitor development programs (i.e., 0.35% as opposed to 0.3%). At the IND stage, FDA reviewed agreed with the margin selection and accepted the Applicant's justification for the proposed margin.*
L2066: *Minor changes occurred from Protocol Version 1 to Version 3, including the addition of amputation and revascularization procedures as AESIs. Protocol deviations were captured during clinical monitoring visits and recorded in the CRF. Review of the above major protocol deviations did not reveal any obvious/important trends or treatment differences across treatment groups.*
L2067: ## 16. Efficacy: Additional Information and Assessment
L2068: ## 16.1. Bexagliflozin for T2DM Clinical Program
L2069: The Applicant, Theracos, submitted eight efficacy studies for supporting the efficacy of bexagliflozin as an adjunct to diet and exercise to improve glycemic control in adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus. The bexagliflozin clinical program was designed in accordance with the recommendations set forth in FDA's draft guidance for industry *Diabetes Mellitus: Developing Drugs and Therapeutic Biologics for Treatment and Prevention* (March 2008). The guidance states, "Efficacy and safety of new products for the treatment of type 2 diabetes can be evaluated in placebo-controlled monotherapy trials, placebo-controlled add-on therapy trials, and active-controlled trials."
L2070: Based on consultation with the medical team, the statistical efficacy review will be focused on the six phase 3 HbA1c studies: Trial C-450, a placebo-controlled monotherapy study in T2DM patients who are treatment-naïve or previously treated with one OHA; Trial C-419, a placebo-controlled add-on to metformin study in T2DM patients who are not adequately controlled by metformin alone; Trials C-423 and C-480, two active-controlled add-on to metformin studies in T2DM patients who have inadequate glycemic control by metformin with sitagliptin (C-423) or glimepiride (C-480) as an active control; Trial C-448, a placebo-controlled study in T2DM patients with moderate renal impairment (eGFR 30 to 60 mL/min/1.73 m2); and Trial C-476, a placebo-controlled study in T2DM patients with increased risk of cardiovascular adverse events.
L2071: Based on consultation with the medical team, results from Trials C-450 and C-419 serve as the key basis of the benefit evaluation.
L2072: ## 16.2. Trial Design Overview
L2073: See Trial Design Overview in Section 6.2.1.
L2074: ## 16.3. Statistical Analysis Plan Overview
L2075: ## 16.3.1. Primary Efficacy Endpoint
L2076: The primary efficacy endpoint in all the six studies was change from baseline in HbA1c. Except for the glimepiride-controlled study, which used a 60-week endpoint, the primary endpoint was evaluated at 24 weeks. The primary endpoint point selection was also in accordance with the above-mentioned FDA 2008 Draft Guidance. The draft guidance states "For purposes of drug approval and labeling, final demonstration of efficacy should be based on reduction in HbA1c (i.e., HbA1c is the primary endpoint of choice, albeit a surrogate), which will support an indication of glycemic control" (March 2008).
L2077: ## 16.3.2. Key Secondary Efficacy Endpoints
L2078: The key secondary efficacy endpoints (mainly, change from baseline in weight, FPG, and SBP) varied little across the six trials. However, in each trial the endpoints were ranked in different orders (see Table 136), as each order was reflected in the corresponding study specific prespecified sequential testing procedures for multiplicity control. The study designs were similar, but the study populations varied across trials; neither the individual study protocols nor the NDA Clinical Overview offers reasons why the secondary endpoints should differ across trials and be prioritized in different orders. Hence, in this review, the same set of secondary efficacy endpoints were evaluated across trials when data were available.
L2079: Of note, in C-419, no formal hypothesis testing was planned for the secondary efficacy endpoints.
L2080: In addition, the Applicant's statistical analysis plan (SAP) prespecified that efficacy in terms of weight and SBP were to be evaluated in subgroups of subjects:
L2081: - In all six studies, efficacy on change from baseline in weight was to be evaluated in the subgroup of subjects with baseline BMI \ge 25 kg/m^2
- In C-448, efficacy on change from baseline in SBP was to be evaluated in the subgroup of subjects with baseline SBP \ge 130 mm Hg; and, in Trials C-476 and C-480, in the subgroup of subjects with baseline SBP \ge 140 mm Hg.
L2082: Of note, in C-476, the Applicant added HbA1c changes from baseline to Week 24 in subjects who have been prescribed sulfonylurea as an exploratory endpoint in the late stage of the trial, one day before the database lock (see Section 12). The Applicant proposed to include the results for this exploratory endpoint in labeling.
L2083: ## 16.3.2.1. Labeling Considerations on the Key Secondary Efficacy Endpoints
L2084: From an individual study perspective, at the judgement of the review team, when the results for a specific key secondary endpoint are statistically significant based on the prespecified sequential testing procedure and also deemed clinically meaningful, these data could be included in the labeling Clinical Studies section as it could be used to support distinct claims of effectiveness.
L2085: Since multiple studies are included in the bexagliflozin for T2DM development program, some key secondary endpoints did not meet the criteria for statistical significance in all studies. In such cases, the review team should determine whether the totality of evidence supports inclusion of the endpoint in labeling. For body weight and SBP endpoints that were prespecified in the subset, the results should be indicated clearly with the number of subjects used in the analysis and described in the text instead of a table format in the Clinical Studies section of the labeling.
L2086: ## 16.3.2.2. Other Secondary Efficacy Endpoint: Proportion of Subject Reaching HbA1c &lt;7% at Week 24/60
L2087: The primary efficacy endpoint of change from baseline in HbA1c (%) was established by rigorous statistical methods. However, the binary measure of HbA1c (%) levels, *proportion of subjects reaching* &lt;7%, is an important endpoint for understanding the treatment effects in
L2088: HbA1c (%) and a measure useful to prescribers and patients. Since the binary version HbA1c endpoint was not included in any of study-specific sequential multiplicity testing procedures for multiplicity protection, a descriptive statistic, the responder proportional information, was considered for inclusion in the labeling. The statistical reviewer has also verified the Applicant's analysis results for this endpoint.
L2089: ## 16.3.3. Analysis Set
L2090: The screened analysis set included all subjects screened for eligibility prior to randomization. The screened population will include screen failures. This population was used for subject listings and for summaries of subject disposition.
L2091: All subjects who were randomized and had taken at least one dose of double-blind study medication were included in the safety analysis set. Safety analyses were based on the first medication kit that was dispensed to a subject. The safety analysis set is the primary analysis set for safety evaluation.
L2092: All subjects who were randomized were included in the ITT analysis set. All analyses of the ITT analysis set were based on the randomization schedule. The ITT analysis set was preplanned to serve as the primary set for the efficacy analyses.
L2093: ## 16.3.4. Analysis Method
L2094: ## 16.3.4.1. Primary Analysis Method – Regulatory Interaction History
L2095: During the IND stage, the Applicant first proposed an LOCF analysis, and then an MMRM method for the primary analysis of the primary or secondary endpoints with missing data. We advised against the LOCF first, and then advised that the MMRM approach likely does not appropriately address missing data, as it treats the behavior of missing data for those subjects who are off-treatment to be the same as that of observed data for those subjects who are on-treatment in the same treatment group. We clarified that the preferred estimand is the treatment policy (de facto) estimand. To estimate the treatment policy estimand, efficacy data should be collected and utilized in analyses on all randomized treated subjects regardless of treatment adherence, rescue status, or other post baseline status (e.g., post bariatric surgery status). Missing data should be imputed in a fashion consistent with what the measurement would have been, had it been measured.
L2096: Disagreeing with the proposed MMRM approach in the Applicant's preNDA meeting package (meeting date December 5, 2019), we recommended that where there are a sufficient number of retrieved dropouts (subjects who discontinued treatment before the final assessment window but still had an efficacy measurement in the final assessment window), we prefers a multiple imputation approach that models the missing final assessment of nonretrieved dropouts (subjects who discontinued treatment before the final assessment window and did not have a measurement in this assessment window) based on known measurements from the retrieved dropouts. We suggested that, for the nonretrieved dropouts, the Sponsor should multiply impute the change from the last measurement before treatment discontinuation to the final assessment, using this
L2097: information from the retrieved dropouts. Where there are not enough retrieved dropouts to do a retrieved dropout analysis, we recommended a return-to-baseline analysis. In this analysis a subject's final assessment is multiply imputed based on the subject's baseline value. Variance for the multiple imputation can be based on residual variance from an ANCOVA model, using the nonmissing final assessments as the response variable. Henceforth, we refer to this approach as the return-to-baseline coupled ANCOVA.
L2098: In the Applicant's final SAP, the primary efficacy endpoint was to be tested based on the ITT analysis set using all observed data and the MMRM approach. The MMRM model included terms for stratification factors as a fixed effect covariate. HbA1c values obtained after the start of rescue medication were not excluded from the analysis.

L2106: ## 16.3.4.2. Primary Analysis Method – A Return-to-Baseline Coupled ANCOVA
L2107: As lack of enough retrieved dropouts rendered the pattern mixture multiple imputation approach analysis not feasible, we used the three-step return-to-baseline coupled ANCOVA in this NDA review.
L2108: ## Missing Data Handling Approach
L2109: Across the six pivotal studies, there were not enough retrieved dropouts to do a retrieved dropout analysis. The Applicant's return-to-baseline multiple imputation method is based on the baseline data of an endpoint for the subject, with variance adjustment for the baseline data estimated from an ANCOVA model of nonmissing Week 24 (Week 60 for Trial C-480) HbA1c for the treatment arms. The ANCOVA model will include the same variables. The variance, \sigma^2, for the Week 24 (Week 60 for Trial C-480) data for each treatment arm will be used as the variance in an imputation model X_{\text{Week 24 or 60}} \sim N(X_{\text{baseline}}, \sigma^2) to impute the missing Week 24 (Week 60 for Trial C-480) data.
L2110: ***FDA Reviewer Comment:*** *The predictor/covariate variables used in the imputation variance estimation ANCOVA model were the same treatment and stratification factors and the corresponding baseline variable as prespecified in the MMRM model (shown in Table 135).*
L2111: **Table 135. ANCOVA Model Covariates in Return-to-Baseline Variance Estimation by Study**

L2115: ## ANCOVA Model Analysis
L2116: Then, for continuous endpoints, for each iteration of the multiply imputed full dataset, the primary and secondary endpoints were analyzed using an ANCOVA model with treatment and stratification factors as fixed effects and the corresponding baseline value as a covariate. Based on this model, the least squares (LS) mean differences between bexagliflozin 20 mg and control, and the associated two-sided 95% CIs were estimated.
L2117: For the categorical secondary efficacy endpoint (proportion of subjects reaching HbA1c &lt;7.0\%), the imputation results from the corresponding HbA1c (%) values were used to derive the responder status. For descriptive analysis, the Applicant chose to present the crude by arm proportion of subjects reaching HbA1c &lt;7.0\%. We also carried out a logistic model analysis with treatment and stratification factors as fixed effects and baseline HbA1c as a covariate to estimate the by arm responder rates.
L2118: ## Rubin's Rule to Combine the Results
L2119: Lastly, Rubin's rule was applied to combine the analysis results from the multiply imputed datasets for both the continuous endpoints and the binary HbA1c responder proportion endpoint.
L2120: ## 16.3.4.3. Primary Endpoint – Subgroup Analysis Methods
L2121: ## 16.3.4.3.1. Sample Estimates of Subgroup Treatment Effects
L2122: Following the primary analysis method change that was finalized during our NDA review, the analysis method for the SAP preplanned subgroup analyses of the primary endpoint was also updated. For each subgrouping factor level, an LS mean difference versus placebo at Week 24/60 was assessed using the same return-to-baseline coupled ANCOVA model as described for the primary endpoint. When carrying out subgroup analyses, the corresponding subgroup factor was removed from the primary analysis model. Forest plots were used to display subgroup level LS mean differences together with the associated 95% CI.
L2123: When a subgroup analysis interaction test was necessary, we took a three-step approach in deriving the interaction test p-value. First, for each imputation, the difference (double-delta) between the two subgroup-level placebo-adjusted treatment effects was derived by running a full analysis model including the interaction term; second, we used Rubin's Rule to summarize the double-deltas across iterations; lastly, we output the t-test p-value associated with the iteration mean double-delta as the treatment by subgroup interaction test p-value.
L2124: ## 16.3.4.3.2. "Shrinkage" Estimates of Subgroup Treatment Effects
L2125: There were likely some random highs and random lows in sample estimates of subgroup treatment effects due to small sample size and large variability for some subgroups. Therefore, we also derived shrinkage estimates of subgroup treatment effects using a Bayesian hierarchical model based on summary sample estimates. The total variability in the sample estimates is the sum of the within subgroup variability of the sample estimator and the across subgroups variability in underlying/true parameter values. A shrinkage estimate of the subgroup treatment effect, which borrows information from the other subgroups while estimating the treatment effect for a specific subgroup, is a "weighted" average of the sample estimate and overall estimate. The weights are based on the ratio of the between subgroup variability to the within subgroup variability. The greater the ratio the smaller the weight on the overall estimate (the less the shrinkage). We used the same flat prior to derive shrinkage estimates for all subgroups. The
L2126: Bayesian hierarchical model assumptions for change in HbA1c (%) from baseline at Week 24/60 are:
L2127: For i = 1, 2, \dots, Y_i represents the observed sample estimate of treatment effect in a subgroup level i, assume Y_i \sim N(\mu_i, \sigma_i^2) where
L2128: - \sigma_i^2 are the observed variance for sample estimates
- \mu_i \sim N(\mu, \tau^2)
- \mu \sim N(0, 9), 1/\tau^2 \sim \text{Gamma}(0.001, 0.001)
L2129: A flat prior with mean 0 and variance of 9 was chosen. The results of the sample estimates and the shrinkage estimates of treatment effects in the same subgroups, are presented in Forest plots respectively. Some of the sample subgroup analyses are indicative of certain subgroups having no treatment benefit. However, after shrinkage, the subgroup treatment effects are, in general, consistent across subgroups and with the overall treatment effect.
L2130: ## 16.3.4.4. Exploration of Potential Modulation Effect of Baseline HbA1c Levels
L2131: To investigate the potential modulation effect of baseline HbA1c levels, aside from the Applicant's preplanned subgroup analysis on the dichotomized baseline HbA1c levels (\le 8.5\%, or &gt; 8.5\%), an additional "subgroup" analysis was carried out for the four placebo-controlled studies by treating baseline HbA1c as a continuous variable. For each of the four studies, a simple linear regression model based on the completers data was used for this exploratory analysis. The response variable was still change from baseline in HbA1c at Week 24, the predictor variables include treatment, baseline HbA1c levels, and a treatment by baseline HbA1c levels interaction. The size and significance level of the interaction term (difference in by-arm baseline HbA1c slopes) from this model fitting is an indicator of the potential modulation effect.
L2132: ## 16.3.4.5. Primary Endpoint – Tipping Point Sensitivity Analysis Method
L2133: ## 16.3.4.5.1. Placebo-Controlled Studies
L2134: To conduct analyses that systematically and comprehensively explore the space of plausible missing data assumptions, at the IND stage, we recommended the inclusion of tipping point analyses that vary assumptions about the missing outcomes on the two treatment arms. The tipping point analyses should target the de facto estimand and therefore include all observed data regardless of treatment adherence. The analyses should be two-dimensional, i.e., should allow assumptions about the missing outcomes on the two arms to vary independently, and should include scenarios where dropouts on bexagliflozin have worse outcomes than dropouts on control. The goal is to explore the plausibility of missing data assumptions under which the conclusions change, i.e., under which there is no longer evidence of a treatment effect.
L2135: The Applicant's preplanned tipping point sensitivity analysis method consists of three steps:
L2136: - Nonmonotone (intermediate visits) missing data were to be imputed first using the Monte Carlo Markov Chain (MCMC) method under the missing at random (MAR) assumption
L2137: in all treatment arms (using the MCMC statement in PROC MI). Multiple chains option (CHAIN = MULTIPLE option in the MCMC statement of PROC MI) was to be used. For the nonmonotone imputation of the HbA1c missing data, a multivariate normal model was to be used including variables for the HbA1c at baseline and all postbaseline visits within each treatment group. The Applicant preplanned to generate five hundred imputed datasets.
L2138: (2) After the nonmonotone missing data have been imputed, the remaining monotone missing data were to be imputed within each treatment arm and subgroup, using a regression approach. The predictors for the regression imputation model at any time point were the stratification factors, and HbA1c at all previous time points, including baseline. Imputations were performed using a sequence of regression-based imputations (using PROC MI statement MONOTONE REG) at each postbaseline time point.

(3) The first imputed values were to be penalized or rewarded based on the treatment the subject received:

- Subjects in the bexagliflozin group: missing value will be analyzed assuming the treatment effect is worsened by \delta_1 (where \delta = 0.1 to 0.5, in step of 0.1) compared to the subjects who have no missing value in the reduction of HbA1c;
- Subjects in the placebo group: missing value was to be analyzed assuming the treatment effect is better by \delta_2 (where the range and step of change \delta_2 also depends on the observed study effect size) compared to the subjects who have no missing value in the reduction of HbA1c.
L2139: ***FDA Reviewer Comment:*** *The Applicant's preplanning only included a range of \delta_1 and by \delta_2 from 0.1 to 0.5 with a fixed step. In this review, depending on the observed study effect sizes, we adjusted the range of the deltas by increasing the size of the steps (size tailored for each study) to reach the tipping points.*
L2140: ## 16.3.4.5.2. Active-Controlled Studies
L2141: For each of the two active-controlled studies, we performed a one-dimensional tipping point analysis: based on the return-to-baseline multiple imputation, we penalized the missing outcomes on the bexagliflozin arm by the null hypothesis of the noninferiority test (i.e., the margin) while multiply imputing the active-control arm missing outcomes with the return-to-baseline method. The goal was to determine if the null margin penalty applied to the bexagliflozin changes the primary analysis conclusion, and if not, under what level of penalty there is no longer evidence of a treatment effect.
L2142: ## 16.3.4.6. Secondary Endpoint – Primary Analysis Method
L2143: All the key secondary efficacy endpoints were continuous change from baseline endpoints. The above-described return-to-baseline coupled ANCOVA approach was also used for the key secondary endpoint analyses.

L2146: statistical test was to be conducted at the 5.0% significance level. Table 136 summarizes, for each study, the ranks of the primary and key secondary endpoints within the study specific testing sequence.

L2159: ## 16.4.1. Trial C-450
L2160: ## 16.4.1.1. Design, Trial C-450
L2161: Trial C-450 was a phase 3, multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group study. C-450 was designed to compare the efficacy and safety of once daily oral administration of bexagliflozin tablets, 20 mg, to placebo in treatment-naïve T2DM subjects or subjects previously treated with no more than one OHA.
L2162: ## Run-In Procedures for OHA Treatment Naïve or Not
L2163: Potential subjects were screened within three weeks of the start of the wash-out or run-in period. The study included both treatment-naïve T2DM subjects with inadequate control on diet and exercise and subjects on an OHA, who underwent a washout of the OHA. Subjects not on an OHA directly entered a 2-week, single-blind, placebo run-in period, while subjects on an OHA underwent a 6-week OHA washout period followed by a 2-week single-blind placebo run-in period. After the placebo run-in period, all subjects were randomized into a 24-week, double-blind, placebo-controlled period, followed by a 2-week follow-up period.
L2164: Treatment assignment randomization was stratified by HbA1c level at the start of the run-in period (\le 8.5 or &gt;8.5\%), country (Canada or United States), and background antidiabetic treatment status (treatment-naïve or not). The study design is depicted in Figure 47.

L2192: Analysis population and subject disposition information for Trial C-450 are summarized in Table 139. Overall, about 90% of the subjects completed study treatment, the bexagliflozin group had a numerically lower treatment completion rate (88%) than the placebo arm (93%). The most frequent reasons for treatment discontinuation were “subjects withdrew consent” and “subjects lost to follow-up” for the bexagliflozin arm.
L2193: This disposition table reveals two issues with trial disposition data collection and consolidation. First, a “withdrawal of consent” is a broad umbrella term that covers potentially multiple specific reasons why subjects opt to withdraw consent and participation in the trial. Withdrawal of consent is the result of these potential reasons, the term itself gives no deliberate reason as to which caused the subject to opt out (e.g., efficacy, safety, or administrative reasons). More specific reasons such as adverse drug effects and tolerability issues, lack of efficacy, subject relocation, and others could be handled differently in a missing data imputation algorithm. Second, in analysis dataset derivation, the more than one entry in the form of “adverse event: specific reason” should be consolidated under one category “adverse event” so unnecessary details could be omitted from crowding a summary level table. The overall study completion rate (90.3%) is very close to the treatment completion rate (89.4%).

L2226: ## 16.4.1.3.3. Subgroup Analyses of the Primary Endpoint
L2227: Subgroup analyses showed that the HbA1c lowering effect was consistent across subgroup levels (Figure 49). There are trends that HbA1c reductions with bexagliflozin were greater in males, in the subgroup of subjects who had higher baseline HbA1c (&gt;8.5%), and in the subgroup of subjects who were on an OHA at screening.
L2228: To further investigate the potential modulation effect of baseline HbA1c level, a linear regression “subgroup” analysis using the continuous baseline HbA1c level based on the completers data was carried out. Figure 50 shows a scatter plot of change from baseline in HbA1c at Week 24 versus baseline HbA1c data, overlaid with the estimated by-arm group regression lines. In general, in both bexagliflozin-treated subjects and in placebo subjects, higher baseline HbA1c level is associated with a bigger change from baseline HbA1c levels at Week 24. The two by-arm regression lines are nearly parallel, the difference in slope (slope in bexagliflozin arm - slope in placebo arm) is -0.042 (standard error [SE]=0.167, p-value=0.80). The small size of the difference and the p-value of 0.80 suggest that baseline HbA1c level is less likely to have any modulating effect on the action of this SGLT2 inhibitor drug in this study population.

L2235: ## 16.4.2. Trial C-419
L2236: ## 16.4.2.1. Design, Trial C-419
L2237: Trial C-419 was a phase 3, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study conducted to determine the effect of bexagliflozin as add-on to metformin on the placebo-corrected change in HbA1c from baseline to Week 24 in adults with T2DM whose disease is inadequately controlled by metformin alone.
L2238: The trial consisted of a double-blinded main part of the study and an open-label single-arm high glycemic arm of the study. Figure 51 illustrates the schematic of the overall study plan. The high glycemic arm recruited 37 subjects with HbA1c &gt;10.5\% and \le 12.0\% into an open-label arm, to receive bexagliflozin tablets, 20 mg, for 24 weeks. The endpoint for the open-label arm was the
L2239: change from baseline to Week 24 of the HbA1c (%). For this efficacy review, we focus on the main part (placebo-controlled) of the study.
L2240: In the placebo-controlled part of the study, subjects who successfully completed a 1-week run-in and who remained eligible were randomized 1:1 to receive bexagliflozin 20 mg or placebo, in addition to their customary metformin dosage for 24 weeks in an outpatient setting. The randomization was stratified by HbA1c (\le 8.5\% or &gt; 8.5\%) and country (United States or Japan). Study subjects were not to change their metformin dosage unless adjustment was medically necessary to manage hypoglycemia.

L2290: ## 16.4.2.3.3. Subgroup Analyses of the Primary Endpoint
L2291: Preplanned subgroup analyses showed that the HbA1c lowering effect was consistent across subgroup levels (Figure 53). There is a trend that HbA1c reductions with bexagliflozin were less effective in subjects 65 years of age and older in this study population.
L2292: Figure 54 shows a scatter plot of change from baseline in HbA1c at Week 24 versus baseline HbA1c data, overlaid with the estimated by-arm group regression lines. In general, in both bexagliflozin treated subjects and in placebo subjects, a higher baseline HbA1c level is associated with bigger change from baseline HbA1c levels at Week 24. Compared with placebo, bexagliflozin treatment is associated with a slightly flatter slope, the difference in slope (slope in bexagliflozin arm - slope in placebo arm) is 0.074 (standard error [SE]=0.127, p-value=0.56). The small size of the difference and the p-value of 0.56 suggest that baseline HbA1c level is less likely to have any modulating effect on the action of this SGLT2 inhibitor drug in this study population.

L2300: ## 16.4.3. Trial C-423
L2301: ## 16.4.3.1. Design, Trial C-423
L2302: Study 423 is a phase 3, randomized, double-blind, active-controlled study to demonstrate that bexagliflozin is noninferior to sitagliptin by evaluating the treatment effect on HbA1c reduction in subjects with T2DM who have inadequate glycemic control by metformin.
L2303: ## Noninferiority Margin Selection and Justification
L2304: The Applicant's proposed noninferiority margin of 0.35% was based on a published clinical trial that demonstrated the effectiveness of sitagliptin, 100 mg, on HbA1c reduction in subjects with T2DM (Charbonnel et al. 2006). The Applicant further reasoned that: the sitagliptin study included male and female adult subjects with T2DM diagnosis and inadequate glycemic control
L2305: defined by an HbA1c \ge 7.0\% and \le 10\% while taking metformin monotherapy at a stable dose of \ge 1500 mg per day. Trial C-423 recruited the same patient population except that the HbA1c range was between 7.0% to 11%. Baseline HbA1c values in the sitagliptin study (Charbonnel et al. 2006) were 8.03\pm 0.82\% in the placebo arm and 7.96\pm 0.81\% in the active arm, respectively. This is close to the baseline mean HbA1c of 7.99\pm 0.87\% in the C-423 subject population. In the published sitagliptin study, a placebo-adjusted least-squares mean (95% CI) treatment effect of reduction from baseline in HbA1c was -0.65\% (-0.77, -0.53). The clinical meaningful margin is selected to be approximately half of sitagliptin effect, i.e., 0.35% reduction.
L2306: At the IND stage, FDA reviewed agreed with the margin selection and accepted the justification.

L2340: ## Primary Endpoint – Primary Analysis
L2341: Table 149 summarizes the primary analysis results for C-423. At Week 24, 11 (5.8%) and 3 (1.6%) subjects in bexagliflozin 20 mg group and sitagliptin 100 mg group, respectively, had missing data. A return-to-baseline approach multiple imputation analysis method was used for missing data handling. L2342: Also based on the multiply imputed HbA1c (%) values at Week 24, a responder defined as reaching the treatment goal of glycemic control (HbA1c (%) &lt;7%) was derived. Seventy-seven (40.3%) subjects reached the treatment goal of glycemic control in the bexagliflozin 20 mg group versus 87 (45.1%) subjects in the sitagliptin 100 mg group. Logistic regression model adjusted proportions of responders were 36.4% and 44.5% for bexagliflozin 20 mg group and the sitagliptin 100 mg group, respectively.

L2369: ## 16.4.4. Trial C-480
L2370: ## 16.4.4.1. Design, Trial C-480
L2371: Trial C-480 was a phase 3, multicenter, randomized, double-blind, parallel-group study. It was designed to evaluate the hypothesis that bexagliflozin would be noninferior to glimepiride as a therapy added to metformin in subjects with disease inadequately controlled by metformin alone or by metformin plus one other OHA (see Figure 57 for study design).
L2372: Figure 57. Study Plan, Trial C-480
L2373: Source: Applicant's Trial C-480 Clinical Study Report, Figure 1.
Abbreviations: met: metformin, OHA: oral hypoglycemic agent, Glim: glimepiride, FU: follow-up, SCN: screening, Rand: randomization
L2374: ## Treatment Duration
L2375: Different from the other five pivotal trials, both the primary endpoint and key secondary efficacy endpoints were assessed at Week 60.
L2376: ## Noninferiority Margin Selection
L2377: The Applicant provided the following justifications for this noninferiority margin selection:
L2378: According to FDA Guidance for Industry *Non-Inferiority Clinical Trials to Establish Effectiveness* (November 2016), the noninferiority margin, M2, reflects the largest loss of effect that would be clinical acceptable (Section III.C.). M2 is generally accepted to be 50% of M1, or the entire effect of the active control versus placebo as seen in historical placebo-controlled trials and is assumed to be present in the noninferiority study. A double-blind, double-dummy, parallel group study with a similar study design as Trial C-480 showed subjects taking 6 mg glimepiride as an add-on to metformin for 8 weeks after a 12 week up-titration period had HbA1c values - 0.81% compared to placebo (Charpentier et al. 2001). Fifty percent of the total effect size of the placebo-controlled study is 0.41%. Based on these historical data, a noninferiority margin of 0.41 could be justified. The proposed 0.35% is a conservative and reasonable M2 noninferiority margin that represents a clinically acceptable loss of effect to demonstrate noninferiority.
L2379: Also, in justification for the noninferiority margin selection in C-423, the Applicant referred to FDA's Draft Guidance for Industry *Diabetes Mellitus: Developing Drugs and Therapeutic Biologics for Treatment and Prevention* (March 2008). The guidance states, "Typically, we accept a noninferiority margin of 0.3 or 0.4 HbA1c percentage units provided this is no greater than a suitably conservative estimate of the magnitude of the treatment effect of the active control in previous placebo-controlled trials."
L2380: While the reviewer considers the noninferiority margin selection of 0.35% to be in accordance with FDA Guidance, the reviewer has one concern with the accuracy of the Applicant's quoted M1 estimate, 0.81%. In Charpentier 2001, the description was:
L2381: *...Combination treatment was significantly more efficient in reducing HbA1c levels than either glimepiride alone (difference in mean change 1.04%, 95% CI*
L2382: 0.81 to 1.27%; P&lt;0.001) or metformin alone (difference in mean change 0.92%, 95% CI 0.63 to 1.21%; P&lt;0.001). ...
L2383: Since the primary comparison in C-480 is between bexagliflozin + metformin and glimepiride + metformin, this reviewer considers a proper reference effect size estimate should be the lower bound 0.63% of the 95% CI for the treatment effect of (glimepiride + metformin) versus metformin from the reference paper (Charpentier et al. 2001). Since 50% of 0.63% is 0.315%, while slightly lower than the selected 0.35%, it is still a reasonable choice. So, we have no further concern on this issue.

L2512: To further investigate the potential modulation effect of baseline HbA1c level, a linear regression “subgroup” analysis using the continuous baseline HbA1c level based on the completers data was carried out. Figure 62 shows a scatter plot of change from baseline in HbA1c at Week 24 versus baseline HbA1c data, overlaid with the estimated by-arm group regression lines. In general, in both bexagliflozin-treated subjects and in placebo subjects, higher baseline HbA1c level is associated with a bigger change from baseline HbA1c levels at Week 24. The two by-arm regression lines are near parallel, the difference in slope (slope in bexagliflozin arm - slope in placebo arm) is -0.004 (standard error=0.113, p-value=0.97). The small size of the difference and the p-value of 0.97 suggest that baseline HbA1c level is less likely to have any modulating effect on the action of this SGLT2 inhibitor drug in this study population.

L2517: ## 16.4.6. Trial C-476
L2518: ## 16.4.6.1. Design, Trial C-476
L2519: Trial C-476 was a double-blind, placebo-controlled study to evaluate the placebo-adjusted change in HbA1c from baseline after 24 weeks of exposure to bexagliflozin in type 2 diabetic subjects with increased risk of cardiovascular adverse events. The cardiovascular outcome trial (CVOT) data are reviewed by OB/DBVII and are covered in Section 17.1 of this review.

L2576: ## Exploratory Secondary Endpoint – Primary Analysis
L2577: There were 313 subjects in the bexagliflozin group and 163 subjects in the placebo group who had been prescribed a sulfonylurea. There were 7% missing data in each arm (22 subjects in bexagliflozin and 12 subjects in placebo) imputed for Week 24. L2578: ## 16.4.6.3.3. Subgroup Analyses of the Primary Endpoint
L2579: Subgroup analyses showed that the HbA1c lowering effect was generally consistent across subgroup levels (Figure 64). However, the subgroup level treatment effect associated with impaired baseline renal function (eGFR &lt;60 mL/min/1.73m2) has an estimated size of 0. This lack of treatment effect in a subgroup of the population is discussed as a review issue in Section 6.3.1.
L2580: To further investigate the potential modulation effect of baseline HbA1c level, a linear regression “subgroup” analysis using the continuous baseline HbA1c level based on the completers data was carried out. Figure 65 shows a scatter plot of change from baseline in HbA1c at Week 24 versus baseline HbA1c data, overlaid with the estimated by-arm group regression lines. In general, in both bexagliflozin-treated subjects and in placebo subjects, higher baseline HbA1c level is associated with bigger change from baseline HbA1c levels at Week 24. Compared with placebo, bexagliflozin treatment is associated with a steeper slope, the difference in slope (slope in bexagliflozin arm – slope in placebo) is -0.21 (standard error=0.05, p-value&lt;0.001). Both the effect size and the significant p-value indicate that baseline HbA1c level may have a strong modulation effect on the action of this SGLT2 inhibitor drug in subjects at risk of cardiovascular adverse events, the higher the baseline HbA1c level, the larger the expected treatment effect at Week 24.
L2581: Figure 64. Preplanned Subgroup Analysis Results, ITT, Trial C-476
L2582: Figure 65. Exploration of the Modulation Effect of Baseline HbA1c Levels, Regression Analysis, ITT, Completer Data at Week 24, Trial C-476
L2583: Source: FDA statistical reviewer

L2719: ## 17.1.2. Data Quality
L2720: The format, content, and documentation of the submitted data were adequate to conduct a statistical evaluation of the CV risk associated with bexagliflozin based on the prespecified meta-analysis plan. Data from individual trials were integrated into single datasets. The data define file of the integrated datasets, in combination with the submitted Analysis Data Reviewer's Guide, provides sufficient information about the variables included in each dataset. Using the submitted data, the reviewer was able to reproduce the findings included in the CV meta-analysis study report, and perform other key analyses conducted as part of this statistical review. There were no notable data quality or analysis issues discovered in this electronic submission that would impact the evaluation and conclusions regarding CV safety of bexagliflozin.
L2721: ## 17.1.3. Summary of Study Design
L2722: During the clinical development of bexagliflozin, the CV meta-analysis was planned in accordance with the FDA Guidance for Industry: *Diabetes Mellitus – Evaluating Cardiovascular*
L2723: *Risk in New Antidiabetic Therapies to Treat Type 2 Diabetes* (December 2008), for a premarket CV risk assessment. The primary objective of this meta-analysis was to exclude a hazard ratio of MACE+ greater than 1.8 for subjects exposed to bexagliflozin compared to subjects exposed to comparators. MACE+ was defined as a 4-component composite endpoint with the following components: CV death (including deaths of unknown cause), nonfatal MI, nonfatal stroke, or hospitalization for unstable angina.
L2724: The meta-analysis includes all phase 2 and phase 3 randomized controlled clinical trials in which bexagliflozin tablets 20 mg once daily, or bexagliflozin capsules 20 mg once daily, were administered for a treatment period of at least 12 weeks. As a result, the meta-analysis synthesized nine phase 2 and phase 3 trials designed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of bexagliflozin. Seven of these trials included a randomized placebo control arm and two trials included an active control arm (glimepiride in Trial C-480, sitagliptin in Trial C-423). One placebo-controlled trial, Trial C-476, recruited subjects with elevated CV risk and was expected to contribute a preponderance of events for the meta-analysis.
L2725: In the clinical development program of bexagliflozin, CV events were prospectively defined, collected, and adjudicated in a consistent manner. All suspected CV events were adjudicated by an independent and blinded CEC, according to a prespecified adjudication plan.
L2726: A summary of design characteristics of these phase 2 and phase 3 trials is presented in Table 192.

L2740: As Trial C-476 was expected to provide the majority of CV events for the meta-analysis, the study design of the trial is described below in more detail. Please refer to Sections 6.2 and 15.1 of the integrated review for study design details of the other phase 2/3 trials included in the meta-analysis.
L2741: ## CVOT: Trial C-476
L2742: C-476 was a multicenter, multinational, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group trial conducted to evaluate the effect of bexagliflozin on hemoglobin A1c in T2DM subjects with increased risk for CV adverse events. The primary safety objective of this study was to contribute at least 134 MACE+ to be pooled with CV events data from other phase 2/3 studies in the prespecified CV meta-analysis to exclude a hazard ratio of 1.8 or greater for subjects exposed to bexagliflozin compared to subjects exposed to comparators.
L2743: Trial C-476 planned to randomize approximately 1650 male and female subjects aged 40 years or older with T2DM and elevated CV risk from any of the following three groups: (1) a history of atherosclerotic vascular disease, (2) a history of the NYHA class II or class III heart failure, or (3) an age of \ge 55 years plus at least two additional risk factors including: diabetes of long duration, hypertension, smoking, renal impairment, or dyslipidemia. If a subject qualified for more than one risk group, she or he was to be assigned to the group with the anticipated highest risk. To ensure that subjects with diverse CV risks were adequately represented, at least 352 subjects (21%) from each of the three risk groups were to be enrolled and at most 400 subjects with a history of class II or III heart failure were to be randomized. The definition of group 2 was modified to include subjects with preserved ejection fraction in Protocol Amendment 8 dated October 28, 2016, due to difficulties recruiting the desired numbers of participants in the heart failure group. The definitions of CV risk groups are presented in Figure 66 below.
L2744: Figure 66. Cardiovascular Risk Eligibility Criteria for the Study Population, Trial C-476
L2745: ## (A) CV Risk Group Definition in Protocol Version 5
L2746: ## (B) CV Risk Group Definition in Protocol Version 8
L2747: Source: Figure 1, page 17, Bexagliflozin Cardiovascular Risk Assessment Statistical Report.
Abbreviations: AF, atrial fibrillation/flutter; CABG, coronary artery bypass grafting; CV, cardiovascular; eGFR, estimated glomerular filtration rate; HbA1c, hemoglobin A1c; HDL, high density lipoprotein-associated cholesterol concentration; HF, heart failure; LVEF, left ventricular ejection fraction; MI, myocardial infarction; NYHA, New York Heart Association; NT-proBNP, N-terminal probrain natriuretic peptide; SBP, systolic blood pressure; T2DM, type 2 diabetes mellitus; UACR, urinary albumin/creatinine ratio.
L2748: During a two-week run-in period, subjects were to self-administer placebo run-in product once daily. Adjustments of treatment for hypertension or dyslipidemia were not permitted during the screening and run-in periods. Eligible subjects were randomly assigned in a 2:1 ratio to take either bexagliflozin tablets 20 mg/day or placebo as an add-on therapy to other antidiabetic medications. Randomization was stratified by HbA1c (&gt; or \le 9.5\%), eGFR (&lt; or \ge 60 mL/min/1.73 \text{ m}^2), BMI (&lt; or \ge 25 \text{ kg/m}^2), and history of heart failure.
L2749: The study subjects were to be contacted by the site at Weeks 2 and 18 by phone. At Weeks 6, 12, 24, 36 and 48 postrandomization, clinic visits were to be scheduled. After Week 48, clinic visits were to be scheduled every 24 weeks followed by a phone interview 12 weeks after each visit until the last randomized subject had completed at least 52 weeks of treatment and a total of 134 subjects had experienced an adjudicated MACE+ event. A follow-up visit was to be conducted 4 weeks after the conclusion of treatment.
L2750: During the first 24 weeks of the treatment period, hyperglycemia was to be managed with diet and exercise counseling and only with changes in antidiabetic therapy if clinically indicated.
L2751: After 24 weeks, the investigators were to prescribe adjustment of the antidiabetic therapies if deemed necessary. Any approved antidiabetic medications were allowed except an SGLT2 inhibitor.
L2752: At every visit, including the phone interviews, participants were queried regarding adverse events. Information on all events that potentially represented MACE+ was to be adjudicated by an independent CV CEC. All potential MACE+ were to be captured as serious adverse events (SAEs). The SAE listing was reviewed periodically by the CEC members to identify potential unreported MACE+. All subjects were to be followed by investigators for CV events assessment during the study, including during the post-treatment follow-up period after permanent cessation of randomized treatment.
L2753: ## **Sample Size Calculation of Trial C-476**
L2754: The sample size of Trial C-476 was determined based on the required number of MACE+ for the program-wide meta-analysis of CV safety, where nonexcess risk of bexagliflozin versus combined control was to be formally assessed based on a 1.8 risk margin for the hazard ratio of MACE+.
L2755: To ensure the meta-analysis would be adequately powered, it was assumed that no MACE+ events would be contributed by other studies. Assuming a true underlying hazard ratio of 1.0 between bexagliflozin and control, 134 positively adjudicated MACE+ events would be required to provide 87% power to demonstrate nonexcess risk using a 1.8 risk margin, at a 2-sided \alpha level of 0.05.
L2756: Approximately 1650 randomized subjects would be needed in Trial C-476, based on the following assumptions:
L2757: - An enrollment period of 1 year
- A follow-up period of 1 to 3 years, except for premature withdrawals
- An annual premature withdrawal rate of 6.5%
- A randomization ratio of 2:1 (bexagliflozin versus placebo)
- A true underlying hazard ratio of 1.0 and a monthly event rate of 0.308% in placebo arm
L2758: ## **17.1.4. Statistical Methodology**
L2759: ## **17.1.4.1. Analysis Populations and Cardiovascular Events Ascertainment**
L2760: The prespecified primary analysis population used in the CV meta-analysis was the full analysis set (FAS) which included all subjects who were randomized in the phase 2 and phase 3 studies (Table 192) and received at least one dose of investigational product. Subjects were analyzed according to their randomized treatment.
L2761: Per the SAP of the CV meta-analysis, the prespecified primary endpoint was the time-to-first confirmed occurrence of a 4-component composite MACE+: CV death (including deaths of unknown cause), nonfatal MI, nonfatal stroke, or hospitalization for unstable angina.
L2762: The SAP also lists the following key secondary endpoints for the assessment of CV safety:
L2763: - Time-to-first confirmed occurrence of any event in a 3-component composite endpoint of MACE: CV death (including deaths of unknown cause), nonfatal MI, or nonfatal stroke;
- Time-to-first confirmed occurrence of hospitalization for heart failure or CV death.
L2764: Additional exploratory endpoints included the time-to-first 6-component MACE consisting of CV death (including deaths of unknown cause), nonfatal MI, nonfatal stroke, hospitalization for unstable angina, unplanned coronary revascularization, and hospitalization for nonfatal heart failure. Time-to-first occurrence of each component of the 6-component MACE were considered exploratory endpoints and analyzed individually.
L2765: All CV events listed above were defined, identified, and adjudicated consistently across the phase 2 and phase 3 clinical development program of bexagliflozin. Suspected CV events occurring subsequent to randomization were reported by investigators and sent for adjudication by the independent CEC. Additionally, serious adverse event listings were reviewed monthly for any unreported potential events by the CEC members. If such events were identified, the information required for adjudication was provided by the clinical investigators and assembled by the Applicant for delivery to the CEC. The CEC was responsible for reviewing and adjudicating suspected CV endpoints in a blinded manner, according to a prespecified adjudication process outlined in the CEC Manual of Operation (Appendix 1 of the CV-meta-analysis study report).
L2766: The following censoring schemes were used for CV event ascertainment in time-to-event analyses:
L2767: - On-study: Events that occurred during the course of the study from the date of first dose following randomization (including both on- and off-treatment periods) were captured. Subjects who had not experienced such an event were censored on their last date of observation;
- On-treatment +7 days: Events that occurred while a subject was on the study treatment or within 7 days after the last date of treatment were captured; those who had not experienced such an event were censored on the last date of treatment +7 days, or their last date of observation, whichever was earlier;
- On-treatment +30 days: Events that occurred while a subject was on the study treatment or within 30 days after the last date of treatment were captured; those who had not experienced such an event were censored on the last date of treatment +30 days, or their last date of observation, whichever was earlier.
L2768: ## 17.1.4.2. Analysis Methods for Cardiovascular Endpoints
L2769: ## Meta-Analysis Treatment Group
L2770: In the CV meta-analysis, all bexagliflozin dose levels were combined to form the bexagliflozin treatment group (referred to as “bexagliflozin”), and all the comparators were combined into the pooled comparator group (referred to as “control”). The analyses of the primary and secondary CV endpoints were based on the comparison of these two combined groups. Note that all trials in the meta-analysis included a single bexagliflozin treatment arm, bexagliflozin 20 mg once daily,
L2771: expect for Trial C-449, which randomized subjects to bexagliflozin 5 mg (n=72), 10 mg (n=72), and 20 mg once daily (n=76).
L2772: ## Meta-Analysis Study Group
L2773: The meta-analysis was not stratified by individual study. It was stratified by a dichotomous study group variable: C-476 versus other phase 2 and phase 3 studies combined, since a majority of the primary cardiovascular events were anticipated to occur in Trial C-476, which enrolled a population with elevated CV risk. The other eight studies were combined as only a few MACE events in total were anticipated to occur in these studies of a shorter duration and a population of low CV risk.
L2774: ## 17.1.4.2.1. Analysis Methods for Primary Endpoint
L2775: The prespecified primary analysis was based upon time-to-event methods for MACE+, using the FAS and on-study censoring, which included positively adjudicated events that occurred during study participation. The following hypothesis was to be tested on MACE+:
L2776: H_0: hazard ratio (HR) \ge 1.8; versus
L2777: H_a: HR &lt; 1.8.
L2778: A stratified Cox proportional hazards regression model that included the meta-analysis treatment group (bexagliflozin or control) as a fixed effect and the meta-analysis study group (C-476 or other phase 2/3 studies) as the stratification factor was to be used. The between-treatment difference in time-to-first MACE+ was assessed by the hazard ratio estimate of bexagliflozin versus control. The two-sided 95% confidence interval for the hazard ratio was calculated using the Cox model and its upper bound was compared with the 1.8 risk margin. If the upper bound is below 1.8, nonexcess risk of bexagliflozin versus control would be met for MACE+.
L2779: A Cox regression model with the meta-analysis treatment group as the only independent variable was fitted to the time-to-first on-study adjudicated MACE+ for Trial C-476 and for the combined phase 2/3 studies excluding Trial C-476, separately. Kaplan-Meier (K-M) estimates and plots of time-to-first MACE+ would be presented by meta-analysis treatment groups for Trial C-476 and for other studies combined, respectively.
L2780: ***FDA Reviewer Comment:*** *Kaplan-Meier curves were provided in the Bexagliflozin Cardiovascular Risk Assessment Statistical Report submitted by the Applicant to visually compare the observed survival functions of the primary and secondary endpoints between the two meta-analysis treatment groups. However, due to the varying randomization ratios and baseline CV risks across trials included in the meta-analysis, the overall K-M plot may be subject to Simpson's Paradox and may be confounded by imbalance of baseline characteristics of the two combined groups for comparison. Therefore, while the K-M plots for CVOT C-476 are presented by treatment arms, the overall K-M plots of the CV meta-analysis are not included in this review.*
L2781: For the primary endpoint MACE+, sensitivity analyses were done on the FAS using “on-treatment +7 days” and “on-treatment +30 days” censorings, respectively. The same Cox model as that used for the primary analysis was applied in these sensitivity analyses to compare the two groups.
L2782: Other sensitivity analyses included:
L2783: - MACE+ censored upon other SGLT2 inhibitor initiation
- MACE+ before and after Trial C-476 amendment
- MACE+ tipping point analysis using multiple imputations for early withdrawal subjects who had not experienced an event prior to study withdrawal
- MACE+ with unknown death from control group excluded
L2784: ## 17.1.4.2.2. Analysis Methods for Secondary Endpoints
L2785: Per the meta-analysis SAP, a hierarchical testing procedure was to be used for the primary and key secondary endpoints to preserve the family-wise type I error at a two-sided significance level of 0.05.
L2786: If the null hypothesis was rejected for the primary endpoint MACE+, nonexcess risk for the first key secondary endpoint time-to-first 3-component MACE was to be evaluated against a preset risk margin for the hazard ratio of 1.3. If the risk margin was met for MACE, superiority for the time-to-first occurrence of hospitalization for heart failure or CV death was to be tested.
L2787: All secondary and exploratory CV outcomes described in Section 17.1.4.1, including composite endpoints and their individual components, were analyzed in a similar manner as the primary endpoint using a Cox proportional hazard model, with the meta-analysis treatment group as the independent variable, stratified by meta-analysis study group. The estimated HR and its associated 95% CI were to be reported for these outcomes. The upper bound of the 95% CI for the hazard ratio was to be compared with 1.3. If the null hypothesis was rejected for both the primary and first key secondary endpoints, the upper bound of the 95% CI for the hazard ratio was to be compared with 1.0 to conclude whether exposure to bexagliflozin resulted in a reduced risk of CV death or hospitalization for heart failure in T2DM subjects.
L2788: Time-to-event analysis was conducted for Trial C-476 and for the combined phase 2/3 studies excluding Trial C-476, separately for the secondary CV endpoints.
L2789: ## 17.1.5. Subject Disposition, Demographics and Baseline Characteristics
L2790: ## 17.1.5.1. Subject Disposition
L2791: The FAS consisted of 4090 T2DM subjects, with 2437 (59.6%) randomized to receive bexagliflozin and 1653 (40.4%) randomized to receive active comparator drugs or placebo. An aggregate summary of the disposition including reasons for study dropout and premature discontinuation of study drug is provided in Table 194.
L2792: The disposition of subjects in the combined bexagliflozin group was similar to that of the combined comparator group. Among the 4090 FAS subjects, 2148 (88.1%) in the combined bexagliflozin arm and 1442 (87.2%) in the comparators arm were followed until the completion of the studies, regardless of their adherence to randomized treatment. Across both arms, 500 subjects (12.2%) discontinued study participation prior to the end of the studies; premature study dropout was similar in both arms in terms of percentages (11.9% in bexagliflozin versus 12.8%
L2793: in control), as well as reasons for study dropout. The most common reason given for study discontinuation was withdrawal of consent which occurred in 122 subjects (5%) in bexagliflozin group and 91 subjects (5.5%) in control group, followed by lost to follow-up for 59 subjects (2.4%) in the bexagliflozin group and 48 subjects (2.9%) in the comparators group. The percentages of early study withdrawal due to adverse events are comparable between the two arms (bexagliflozin: 1.5%; control: 1.4%).
L2794: Reasons for treatment discontinuation were also provided in Table 194. Fractions of premature treatment discontinuations were generally similar across the two comparison arms; a slightly larger fraction (108; 4.4%) of subjects on the bexagliflozin arm ceased doses due to adverse events compared to that in the control arm (59; 3.6%).

L2804: The aggregate summary of study follow-up in the FAS is depicted in Table 196. In the pool of all studies, subjects in the bexagliflozin arm were followed for an average of 2 months longer than subjects in the comparator arm. The reason for this apparent imbalance is that subjects in Trial C-476 had longer mean follow-up time (approximately 900 days) than any of the other trials and Trial C-476 contributed twice as many subjects to the bexagliflozin arm than to the comparator arm in the pool of all studies due to its 2:1 randomization ratio. The mean and median follow-up duration was comparable between bexagliflozin and placebo in Trial C-476 as shown in the lower panel of Table 196.
L2805: Approximately 54% of subjects had at least 48 weeks of study follow-up, 48% had 96 weeks or longer of follow-up, and around 16% had a follow-up duration longer than 144 weeks. The CVOT Trial C-476 contributed about 69% of the total subject-years of follow-up in the meta-analysis.

L2815: ## 17.1.5.2. Demographics and Baseline Characteristics
L2816: Table 198 summarizes the demographics and baseline characteristics of the FAS subjects pooled across all studies included in the CV meta-analysis and in Trial C-476 alone. The demographics for the 4090 subjects in the FAS were generally well-balanced between the comparison groups in all studies combined and in the standalone Trial C-476.
L2817: For all studies combined, imbalances between comparison arms were observed for baseline cardiovascular history and history of insulin prescription, due to the 2:1 randomization ratio in Trial C-476 which enrolled an enriched population with elevated CV risk or insulin use. Besides higher proportions of prior CV disease, subjects in C-476 had a longer history of T2DM diagnosis, older age, and a greater proportion of insulin use at baseline, compared to subjects from other studies included in the meta-analysis.
L2818: In the FAS, there were more male subjects than female subjects (63% versus 37%). Approximately 70% of subjects were white and about 7% were black, while 17% were Asian and 6% of subjects belong to other races. About 41% of subjects were at least 65 years of age, while the mean age was about 61.7 years. About 40% of subjects were from the United States. The mean BMI was 31.6 kg/m2. The mean HbA1c at baseline was 8.1%. The mean duration of T2DM was 11.6 years with baseline insulin usage in 26% of the FAS subjects.

L2903: ## 17.1.7. Findings in Subgroup Populations
L2904: In this section, analysis results for the primary CV endpoint MACE+ are presented for specific subgroups in the FAS based on the on-study censoring scheme. Subgroups presented in this section are defined by baseline demographic factors and clinical factors including age, gender, race, region, baseline eGFR, baseline BMI, history of CV disease, duration of T2DM diagnosis, and insulin use at baseline. Analyses of subgroups were based upon a Cox proportional hazards model stratified by meta-analysis study group (C-476 or not) with a fixed effect for treatment group to estimate the hazard ratio and its corresponding 95% confidence interval. There were no protocol-defined multiplicity corrections for these exploratory analyses and as such results are presented using unadjusted 95% confidence intervals for each of the subgroups.

All hazard ratio estimates were below 1 except for the estimate of the race category “Asian” (1.21); however, the number of events is relatively low and the confidence interval was wide for this subgroup.
